Crews of motorized bike-riding thieves — some of them illegal migrant gang-bangers — are terrorizing New York City, viciously snatching thousands of dollars in jewelry from the necks of unsuspecting cops and civilians alike, The Post has learned.

There have been more than 20 motorized bike chain-snatchings since September, with at least 10 of them turning violent, according to the NYPD — and police sources say that’s just a drop in the bucket.

“There are hundreds of chain snatchings around the city,” said a law enforcement officer, who asked to remain anonymous because he’s not cleared to talk to the news media.

“A lot of it has to do with the Trinitarios,” said the officer, referring to the violent street gang founded by Dominican inmates at Rikers Island in the early 1990s that has since grown into a crime empire plaguing the Bronx and upper Manhattan for decades.

“That’s one of their big things, chain snatchings, and two people on a bike doing robberies.”

The most notable mobile mugging happened when an NYPD detective was stabbed 10 times after he tried to fight back against two illegal migrants earlier this month.

Nine other chain-snatching victims reported being punched, knifed or thrown to the ground during the terrifying, lightning-fast robberies.

Two reputed Trinitario gang members on scooters were also responsible for shooting an off-duty federal border patrol agent at a Manhattan park on July 9, 2025, sparking a massive roundup of Big Apple gangbangers in January, federal officials said.

“Operation Salvo” took 54 members of the crew off the streets after the 42-year-old law enforcement officer was shot and wounded at Fort Washington Park in Washington Heights at West 155th Street, the officials said.

In Gotham, the thieves often have the advantage.

If they are caught, lefty judges often spring the crooks just as fast.

And they are never handed over to ICE if their immigration status is in question because NYC is a sanctuary city, an NYPD officer said.

“We’re not allowed to confer with ICE so we just arrest them,” said the cop, who also asked to remain anonymous so he wouldn’t get in trouble. “They get released on their own recognizance [by a judge] and they go back and do it again.”

The revolving-door system was spinning in the case of Jorge Beltre, a Bronx bodega worker and Uber driver who was attacked by two scooter-riding bandits as he walked his 5-year-old son home from school near Mount Eden Parkway and Sheridan Avenue in Claremont on Oct. 8.

Beltre, 30, fought back to save his 14-karat gold Cuban-link chain when one of the attackers pulled a knife and stabbed him in the leg, according to police.

Despite his wound, the Domincan Republic native was able to hold the 17-year-old thief — with the help of eight onlookers — until cops arrived, he said. Beltre’s son was unharmed.

The teenager was charged with robbery and weapon possession, according to police. He was released on $900 bail, Beltre said the Bronx District Attorneys Office told him.

“The community and I caught one,” he told The Post in Spanish. “Why did they let him go? He didn’t say where the other guy is. He didn’t say who the other guy was. I feel outraged. Why do they grant him release?

“It fills me with outrage because I felt my life was in danger,” Beltre continued. “We are living through a scourge. The Bronx is practically being ravaged by these criminals. People are getting their chains snatched — two or three incidents a day. The community is fed up.”

The experience has been “unsettling” for his son, who asked his mom to send him back to school with a baseball bat “so he could hit the criminals if he saw them,” Beltre said. He said his muggers were also from the Domican Republic.

Beltre needed five stitches to close his wound.

The Bronx District Attorneys Office didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.

In another incident on Sept. 13, a 54-year-old victim told cops he tried to hold onto the motorbike-riding thief who ripped a chain off his neck on Grand Avenue near West 180th Street in the West Bronx.

But the thief accelerated, dragging the victim, who suffered minor injuries and lost his $2,700 chain, cops said.

Two robbers on e-bikes approached a 60-year-old man near Duncan Street and Laconia Avenue in the East Bronx on Sept. 28, displayed a firearm and punched him in the face before snatching $8,000 of jewelry from his neck. He suffered minor injuries.

The motorized muggers are brazen enough to target cops.

An off-duty female office, had her chain snatched at the corner of Arlington and Barbey streets in Brownsville, Brooklyn, on Oct. 10, police sources said.

The crook grabbed a gold necklace that read “Angie” from the 25-year-old’s neck before riding off on a scooter, the sources said. The necklace was worth about $800, the cop reported.

The female officer’s attack came eight days after two criminals stabbed Detective Jose Mercedes, 33, near East 206th Street and Rochambeau Avenue in Norwood in the Bronx as they tried to rip the necklace given to him by his mom off his neck, he told reporters this week.

Mercedes told the crooks several times in both English and Spanish that he was a detective — but “they didn’t care,” he said.

The accused robbers, whom police identified as D’Angelo Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia, 24, fled the scene on an e-bike. Mercedes chased them but collapsed because he was losing so much blood, he said.

Police hunted the duo down outside of Boston and brought them back to New York to face attempted murder charges.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE said both men have prior criminal records, and are Dominican Republic natives living in the US illegally.

An NYPD spokesperson said the chain-snatchings had been decreasing in the Bronx recently.

“Since the attempted murder of Detective Mercedes, there has been a significant decrease in chain snatches within the confines of Patrol Borough Bronx North,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that major crime declined 7% in all five boroughs of the city so far this year, with the Bronx continuing to lead the city with a 12% reduction — to 20,751 so far this year, versus 23,545 in the same period last year.

Surveillance photos released by the NYPD show the robbers often have their faces completely covered and are difficult to identify, police sources said.

Critics lay some of the blame for the troubling trend at the feet of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has called for less enforcement of e-bikers — in purported support the multi-million food app industry. Their lawlessness has surged as cops write fewer tickets.

“Mamdani doesn’t want to enforce summonses against these moped guys because they’re working, but then everyone’s taking advantage of it,” said Michael Alcazar, a former NYPD detective and an adjunct professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice.

“This is what they do in Third World countries,” he added.

Alcazar thinks the NYPD needs to use the broken-window theory of policing to staunch the epidemic.

“Bad guys have to know we’re enforcing these things,” he said of the tactic in which cops write summonses for small infractions to prevent larger crimes. “That will nip this in the bud.”

A return to the NYPD’s plainclothes anti-crime units, which were disbanded in 2020 under self-described Marxist Mayor Bill de Blasio following protests over George Floyd’s death in Minneapolis, would also help, he said.

“Nobody wants to talk about bringing back anti-crime but it’s an effective tool,” Alcazar said of the plainclothes cops. “This is what we did when crime was spiking.”

On Friday’s broadcast of MS NOW’s “The Moment,” guest host Eugene Daniels stated that Oregon already has “some of the strictest gun laws in the country.”

While speaking with Deschutes County Commissioner Phil Chang, Daniels asked, “What needs to change in this country, in your view? Because, even in Oregon, you guys have some of the strictest gun laws in the country. And yet, we see what happened yesterday, still.”

Chang answered, “The county has developed a healthy schools partnership with the Bend-La Pine School District that tries to make sure that our schools are supportive and welcoming places, where kids feel like they belong. We offer school-based health centers with behavioral health clinicians at our schools, throughout the Bend-La Pine School District, throughout Deschutes County. Our community makes some of the most active use of extreme risk protection orders under Oregon’s red flag law in the state of Oregon. So, we have some of the highest numbers per capita of people of use of ERPOs, extreme risk protection orders, to remove guns from people who are going to harm themselves or others. We have very active programs to support our community in safely storing their guns, getting access to gun locks. And so, we have done all of these things, which maybe helped prevent something like this from happening in our community sooner, but they were not enough to prevent something like this from happening to our community yesterday.”

village-installs-knitted-traffic-cops:
Villagers have knitted speed cameras and life-sized traffic cops to fake-out reckless motorists, in a bid to slow down drivers.

The locals in Fillongley, Warwickshire, dressed the mannequins in high-visibility vests to look like traffic cops in a crafty bid to cut down on accidents.

Members of the town’s Knit and Natter group created the realistic cameras and mannequins after a spate of crashes along the villages main street.

The group’s latest recruit is a knitted officer stationed beneath a 30mph sign, complete with a mock speed gun aimed at oncoming traffic.

And locals believe the effort is working with many drivers falling for the mock speed cameras.

Heather Badham, the town’s councillor/mayor, said their realistic creations have been faking out drivers all week since they were installed on October 13 following four months of preparation.

“It has had a massive impact,” said the 58-year-old.

“90% of the accidents are caused by people coming down the Nuneaton road, not seeing the signs and then hitting someone.

“Since putting these up, we’ve been chuckling as people saw the man and thought he was real. You could see the brake lights coming on.

“They don’t take notice of the flashing 30 sign and go too fast—but they see the cameras and slow down.

“It probably did surprise a lot of people.”

Topic:Cricket

Matt Renshaw's shot selection and dominant batting in Durban helped win the Test and lock in his spot in the order.

  (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

Australian Test captain Pat Cummins expects Matt Renshaw to stay in the middle order for the second Test against South Africa.

Renshaw's 272-run total in the first Test means the batting line-up is set to remain, but the bowling attack may depend on how much rain is likely on the first two days.

ABC Sport will live blog the second Test in Gqeberha, starting on Sunday evening, with the first ball at 7pm AEDT.

Matt Renshaw is set to remain at number five for the second Test against South Africa, as Australia waits on the opening day's weather to name the team.

Captain Pat Cummins confirmed on Saturday he expected Renshaw to again bat in the middle order after his match-winning heroics in Durban.

That all but ensures Nic Maddinson will stay in the side and open with Travis Head, after scores of 0 and 48 on his shock Test recall last week.

Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 came after he'd originally been recalled as an opener in Australia's previous Test against Bangladesh, the position where he has batted for most his career.

Australia started the first Test against South Africa on the back foot, but its 214-run victory has silenced any critics of the selection strategy.

"After what Renners did last week, I presume he'll stay at number five," Cummins said on the eve of the Gqeberha Test.

"What he deserved even more credit for is that we'd asked him to do a different role, and he just said straight away, 'Yep, no worries, whatever the team needs.'

"So many positives in addition to the runs he scored last week. He was a delight, and really helped me and [Nathan] Lyon get through those partnerships."

Cummins also confirmed Cameron Green remained sidelined with an abdominal strain, while Josh Inglis was close to being declared fit.

Josh Inglis is unlikely to return despite recovering from a fractured finger.

Even if Inglis is cleared to play following his fractured finger, it is unlikely he will be able to force his way into Australia's side.

Rain is expected across the opening two days in Gqeberha, with the prospect that both sides will be able to factor that into their XIs should the toss be delayed.

That could potentially reduce the need for spin and provide the option of a fourth quick in Scott Boland, with extra grass also left on the St George's Park wicket.

Depending on the weather in Gqeberha, Scott Boland could get one of his rare chances to break into the Australian side.

  (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor, file photo)

But Cummins gave every indication that Lyon would remain as a key part of the attack.

"We always look at all options," Cummins said when asked if it was conceivable that they could go in without a specialist spinner.

"We love playing with Nath. We saw last week, a couple of key wickets in the first innings.

"And even the control he gives. It makes the rest of us fast bowlers be able to function around him."

Winston Lee, one of the seven fraternity brothers at Cornell University accused by a fellow student of gang rape, is the grandson of a former South Korean prime minister and ambassador to the U.S.

The ex-Chi Phi fraternity bro was accused by Cornell student known only as “Jane Doe” of snorting ketamine off her and forcing oral sex on her during the alleged gang rape.

Cornell suspended him for two years.

Winston’s grandfather is Lee Hong-koo, who served as South Korea’s leader between 1994 and 1995, and the country’s ambassador to the US from 1998 to 2000, during Bill Clinton’s presidency.

The two statesmen and power players often crossed paths, including at a 2000 commemorative ceremony at the Korean War Memorial in Washington, marking the 50th anniversary of the Korean War, where they posed for photos alongside each other.

Even after Clinton left the presidency, they appeared to remain close — like when Lee invited Clinton for bibimbap, a dish Bubba was a “huge fan” of, at a Seoul hotel in 2005 when the former president was in town to promote his autobiography.

Lee died in May, and Winston served as the chief mourner at the high-profile Seoul funeral — overseeing key rites, greeting guests and receiving condolences on behalf of the family, who are descendants of Korea’s former royal family.

Winston is seen prominently in photos wearing white gloves as he holds up his grandfather’s portrait.

The former prime minister’s only son is Winston’s father, Barton Lee, a Yale University-educated investment banker who is the managing director and head of Asia at EIG in Hong Kong.

The family is among the most prominent in the South Korean expat community in Hong Kong and have been consumed with shame since an unnamed student at Cornell known only as “Jane Doe” filed a lawsuit alleging she was gang raped by a group of seven, including Winston, sources have said.

Winston’s mother, Ji Young Hwang, is president of the Korean Women’s Association of Hong Kong, a nonprofit officially recognized by the South Korean government whose mission includes “supporting women’s integration and personal growth.”

The women’s association deleted its Instagram page in the wake of the scandal, prompting even more backlash.

“Shutting down their Instagram account feels like a move to protect one of their own rather than stand by their mission,” wrote popular Hong Kong Instagram account Cantonese Lesson Daily.

“It is especially troubling given that the person involved is the president of the organization. The behavior her son is accused of is fundamentally antithetical to the core principles of any group dedicated to supporting, protecting, and empowering women.”

This article was produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network in partnership with The Philadelphia Inquirer. Sign up for Dispatches to get our stories in your inbox every week.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In 2020, seven years after he was appointed to represent a client who claimed he was wrongly convicted, attorney Scott Galloway told the judge that he was still looking into the case and needed more time.

“I am still in the process of interviewing individuals,” the lawyer wrote to the judge in Delaware County, outside Philadelphia, who had already granted him 32 extensions.

His client, Nolan O’Neal, had been a 20-year-old high school student when he was arrested for murder by Chester police, who had four eyewitnesses identifying him. At his 2005 trial, those witnesses all recanted, saying police had pressured them to accuse O’Neal.

By the time Galloway joined the case, in 2013, O’Neal had already spent eight years in prison insisting he was innocent. The lawyer’s job was to help him file a petition under Pennsylvania’s Post Conviction Relief Act. That law provided a narrow path to freedom if Galloway could find crucial new evidence or prove that previous lawyers had mishandled the case.

But court records do not show that the attorney did much other than ask for more time.

In 2022, after nine years, one unsuccessful request to access evidence and 41 extensions, Galloway filed a two-page petition addressing just one of the many issues O’Neal had wanted him to raise. It would not be enough to get O’Neal his day in court.

For more than half a century, Pennsylvania has promised people who claim they didn’t get a fair trial the right to “effective” post-conviction legal representation, regardless of their ability to pay. That’s more than most states promise people after they have been convicted and lost their appeals.

Yet Pennsylvania has done little to fulfill that promise. The Philadelphia Inquirer and ProPublica previously reported that Pennsylvania lets lawyers resolve cases quickly using a practice that is discouraged in several states: filing “no-merit” letters, also known as Finley letters, urging judges to reject their clients’ handwritten or typed claims. In Philadelphia, dozens who had received such letters later had their convictions or sentences overturned based on issues their lawyers had rejected or overlooked.

But the problems go deeper than that: The state’s loose rules and its failure to fund post-conviction work have made the type of breakdown O’Neal encountered a recurring feature of this system.

By filing public records requests with courts serving all 67 Pennsylvania counties and analyzing a decade of court dockets, an Inquirer and ProPublica investigation found that the system Pennsylvania set up to protect the right to counsel instead allows, or even encourages, shoddy representation.

The news organizations found that:

While almost every county in the state has a public defender office, most post-conviction cases are handled by private lawyers who are paid hourly, by the case or by the year and work with little to no supervision. Our review of court records found pay as low as $500 per case and delays as long as 19 years without a single court filing.

In some counties, contracted lawyers’ backlogs spanned dozens of cases. In Chester County, an affluent region west of Philadelphia, a lawyer left cases untouched for as long as two years before the county ended his contract last fall.

Delaware County, where O’Neal was convicted, relies on a group of part-time lawyers to handle most of its post-trial matters. One is Galloway, who has handled 20 or 30 post-trial cases per year for the county in addition to running his own law practice and, for a time, holding local elected office. Galloway said that his ethical obligation to confidentiality prevented him from commenting on O’Neal’s case. Judge George A. Pagano, who granted him 41 extensions on O’Neal’s case, declined to comment.

In the years Galloway was on the case, O’Neal wrote him dozens of letters from state prison, proposing legal arguments and sending leads to investigate.

“It is a daunting and exhausting task to navigate this legal process and be heard,” O’Neal said in an interview. “We at times even have to fight the attorneys who are supposed to represent us.”

In 2020, he received a letter from the brother of the murder victim, admitting that his testimony against O’Neal was a lie. “I want to fix it. I know my brother would want me to. It’s been long enough,” he wrote. O’Neal said he pleaded with Galloway to track down the man.

In 2022, Galloway attached the brother’s signed statement to a sparse two-page brief, which mentioned none of the other issues O’Neal had raised nine years earlier or the other witnesses who’d come forward over the years. The judge started the process of dismissing the claim. One reason: The filing had been made too late. O’Neal is still fighting his case, now with a new court-appointed lawyer.

Dear Judge Pagano: I am writing to your attention as I have grave and urgent concerns about my current appointed attorney Scott D. Galloway, who you have appointed to represent me on my PCRA petition pending in your court. This is the best I can do to bring matters to your attention as my filings are going unanswered.

Before they are assigned a lawyer, Pennsylvania prisoners must write the first draft of their post-conviction filing on their own within a strict one-year deadline. The lawyers appointed to revise their petitions, on the other hand, are not generally held to any timeline. The state courts say lawyers should act “expeditiously so as to reduce unnecessary delays.” Yet judges have granted extensions liberally, court dockets show, and in many cases failed to impose any deadlines at all.

An Inquirer and ProPublica review of court dockets found that hundreds of people have waited two years or longer, only to receive no-merit letters. That analysis is an undercount, since many court clerks don’t clearly label attorney filings on their dockets. In Philadelphia alone, some 65 people have waited three to eight years for lawyers to take action before reaching that same outcome. Similarly, across the state, dockets show that lawyers received seven or more extensions in dozens of cases before filing Finley letters or nothing at all.

In 2017, Lee Mandell, who has been practicing law in Philadelphia for more than 50 years, sent a Finley letter saying that he’d written to but never spoken with his client of four years and did not understand his claims.

“It is entirely unclear as to what the defendant really means,” wrote Mandell. In his own review of the case, Mandell failed to flag an erroneous jury instruction that four years later would lead to the conviction being overturned. Mandell was later formally reprimanded for allowing another client’s hearing to be delayed by six years, during which time two witnesses died. He did not return calls seeking comment.

Judges’ inaction added to lawyers’ delays, leaving matters to stagnate for years on end. In 2023, the state’s Superior Court registered such concerns about a case from Wayne County, where a lawyer filed a “two-page, deficient motion to withdraw, and the PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.”

To be sure, there can be good reasons for delays, since investigations can be complex. Lawyers have spent years chasing down missing witnesses, litigating requests for DNA testing or combing through police files.

But in almost 200 post-conviction cases across Pennsylvania in the last 15 years, lawyers were appointed, then filed nothing at all over the span of a year or longer before being replaced with a new appointed lawyer. One of the cases stagnated for almost seven years, only for a new attorney to pick up the file. Another man was appointed five lawyers over eight years, dockets show, none of whom filed anything on his behalf.

Court officials have long been aware of the backlogs wracking this system, even publishing a law review article about it in 2003. The study outlined needed reforms but acknowledged the lack of political will, saying the “low status” of these cases stems from a bias among judges and lawyers who believe “that most post conviction claims are frivolous.”

The loose timeline is just one dimension of a system with few standards. The state has published no best practices for indigent defense or guidelines on how many cases a lawyer can take; it has provided no training and instituted virtually no guidelines to ensure that court-appointed lawyers are qualified. As a result, lawyers hold widely diverging views on just what obligations they have to their clients.

The Inquirer and ProPublica previously found that about three-quarters of the time, Philadelphia lawyers who ended up filing Finley letters did not take basic steps such as meeting with their client, tracking down the trial lawyer’s file and obtaining all available discovery.

“I do not know how you can evaluate trial counsel’s performance, which is the main role of post-conviction counsel, without talking to your client and reading trial counsel’s file,” said Jennifer Merrigan, a co-founder of Phillips Black, a nonprofit law firm. That file would reveal whether the lawyer consulted with experts, received all relevant evidence from the prosecutor and investigated potential witnesses.

The state’s lack of vetting and training stands in contrast with national norms. A majority of other states have centralized defender services or support offices that provide resources, education and oversight. For instance, in North Carolina, appeals lawyers seeking court appointments must apply with the state appellate defender and submit references, work history showing the lawyer is qualified to litigate appeals and legal writing samples. They’re also required to take a training course covering strategy and best practices.

Even without a statewide office, Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court could establish minimum qualifications for lawyers handling indigent defense. In August, a state court committee published such a proposal, but it recommends only that lawyers have relevant work experience “to the extent practicable.” Work experience requirements have been enforced in some other states, such as Ohio, for years. But the committee’s proposal argued that work experience is not “possible to quantify” and that “less-than-experienced representation is better than no representation.”

Ted Skaarup, a public defender who has advocated for training and qualification requirements, said inexperienced and untrained lawyers are more likely to default to writing Finley letters. New lawyers, he said, are left to consult with older attorneys who may pass on bad practices. “You go to them for advice and they say, ‘I’ll send you a copy of my [no-merit] letter.’”

Only one of the state’s 67 counties provided written criteria requiring specific work experience for lawyers to be appointed to post-conviction cases in response to records requests. Philadelphia court leadership says that lawyers must complete a training session and show they’ve recently handled three hearings involving disputed evidence. A volunteer panel tasked with approving prospective lawyers there rarely meets and is not empowered to approve or reject candidates based on writing samples, a core part of screening appeals lawyers in some other places.

In Pittsburgh, the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice has urged local court officials to set up a system to screen and supervise appointed lawyers. For now, the organization is running its own voluntary trainings, as well as a resource center with office hours, a library of sample motions and help with social service referrals.

Without such systems, the organization’s executive director, Rob Perkins, said, “There’s no quality control.” Lawyers can get away with “doing a poor job in these cases for years without anyone really paying attention.”

When attorney Corrie Woods took over Washington County’s post-conviction caseload in 2020, he was startled to discover about a dozen files that had been untouched since being assigned to the previous lawyer in 2019 or earlier. In some, the lawyer’s inaction had caused the clients to lose their appeal rights.

Looking back, Woods said, it’s not surprising, given that the western Pennsylvania county was paying him $25,000 a year as a part-timer for up to 24 cases. “These cases are not going to take priority in most law offices,” said Woods, who now handles mostly personal injury cases.

Under such a contract, he said, “Your incentive is to do the least work. You’re not getting more for doing more.”

The American Bar Association has long opposed such flat-fee pay structures for that reason. States including Colorado, Idaho and Nevada have banned them.

Not Pennsylvania. The state began contributing any money to indigent defense only in 2023. Today it kicks in just 57 cents per capita; neighboring states, on average, pay $26 per resident. Counties provide the rest as they see fit. A pending American Civil Liberties Union lawsuit claims that has resulted in widespread violations of the right to counsel.

At 57 cents per resident, Pennsylvania’s state-level contribution toward funding legal defense for poor people is a fraction of what neighboring states pay.

About three-quarters of Pennsylvanians live in counties that use flat-fee arrangements or cap the amount a lawyer can bill for a case. Daniel Buzard, the court administrator in the county where Woods held the contract several years ago, said in an email, “This provides financial stability for both parties.”

Some counties pay as little as $500 per case. Based on time estimates from Maine, one of the only states to publish post-conviction workload standards, that would come out to $11 per hour.

Twenty-one Pennsylvania counties offer flat annual pay for part-time lawyers — sometimes then assigning them caseloads that exceed Maine’s standard for full-time work.

“We at times even have to fight the attorneys who are supposed to represent us.”

Only five of the 18 contracts obtained in response to public records requests included a limit on the number of cases the court could heap onto a lawyer. None of the contracts set deadlines, specified a time commitment or described any oversight mechanism.

Stuart Wilder said his contract to handle post-conviction cases in Bucks County, outside Philadelphia, kept the lights on in his office for years. He worked hard for clients, he said, and won several challenging cases. But he said the flat-fee structure did require him to deprioritize cases where he didn’t see merit.

“Being able to file Finley letters gave me the time to work on cases I could fix,” said Wilder, who recently retired.

But in at least three counties, contract lawyers left multiple clients stranded for a year or longer with no progress on their cases, dockets show.

In 2021, the court in Erie County yanked 50 cases from attorney James P. Miller and eventually reported him for discipline, citing extreme delays that cost some clients their appeal rights. Miller, whose law license was suspended as a result, declined to comment. But Erie court administrator Robert Catalde said the debacle spurred the county to double lawyers’ pay to $46,800 and provide benefits.

A similar situation played out last year in Chester County, which abruptly ended its contract with the lawyer handling all its post-conviction cases, Charles Thomas Jr., after discovering that he had been putting in an average of just five hours a week across his roughly 25 cases.

One client, Patrick Hickson, said he spent two years trying to get Thomas to track down evidence that could clear him of a 2018 shooting or at least prove he didn’t get a fair trial. His defense lawyer had failed to call a single witness — admitting to the judge, mid-trial, that he’d wrongly assumed the prosecutor would send a summons to an eyewitness who had told police Hickson wasn’t the shooter.

To raise the issue, Hickson needed Thomas to track down the missing witness. But when he reached Thomas by phone in August 2025, for the first time in months, the lawyer told him he was off the case. “He said the courts told him he was taking too long,” Hickson said. Thomas declined to comment.

Chester County criminal court administrator Jordan Ludwick acknowledged concerns about the delays but said he resolved the problem by finding a qualified lawyer to take over the contract.

That attorney, Shannon McDonald, said it was “not an easy transition.”

“There were many cases that had not been touched at all,” she said.

She cut through the backlog by filing 17 briefs in just over three months. All but three were Finley letters.

“The case has to survive on the merits,” she said, “and, frankly, the deck is stacked against overturning a case.”

This March, she also sent Hickson a Finley letter. McDonald said ethics rules prevented her from discussing Hickson’s case, but in the letter she blamed Hickson for failing to track down the would-be witness and said his trial lawyer had a strategic reason for not sending the subpoena.

Reading the letter, Hickson said, “I felt defeated.”

Since McDonald asked to drop the case, he is pursuing exoneration alone.

He worked hard for clients, he said, and won several challenging cases. But he said the flat-fee structure did require him to deprioritize cases where he didn’t see merit.

“Being able to file Finley letters gave me the time to work on cases I could fix,” said Wilder, who recently retired.

But in at least three counties, contract lawyers left multiple clients stranded for a year or longer with no progress on their cases, dockets show.

In 2021, the court in Erie County yanked 50 cases from attorney James P. Miller and eventually reported him for discipline, citing extreme delays that cost some clients their appeal rights. Miller, whose law license was suspended as a result, declined to comment. But Erie court administrator Robert Catalde said the debacle spurred the county to double lawyers’ pay to $46,800 and provide benefits.

A similar situation played out last year in Chester County, which abruptly ended its contract with the lawyer handling all its post-conviction cases, Charles Thomas Jr., after discovering that he had been putting in an average of just five hours a week across his roughly 25 cases.

One client, Patrick Hickson, said he spent two years trying to get Thomas to track down evidence that could clear him of a 2018 shooting or at least prove he didn’t get a fair trial. His defense lawyer had failed to call a single witness — admitting to the judge, mid-trial, that he’d wrongly assumed the prosecutor would send a summons to an eyewitness who had told police Hickson wasn’t the shooter.

To raise the issue, Hickson needed Thomas to track down the missing witness. But when he reached Thomas by phone in August 2025, for the first time in months, the lawyer told him he was off the case. “He said the courts told him he was taking too long,” Hickson said. Thomas declined to comment.

Chester County criminal court administrator Jordan Ludwick acknowledged concerns about the delays but said he resolved the problem by finding a qualified lawyer to take over the contract.

That attorney, Shannon McDonald, said it was “not an easy transition.”

“There were many cases that had not been touched at all,” she said.

She cut through the backlog by filing 17 briefs in just over three months. All but three were Finley letters.

“The case has to survive on the merits,” she said, “and, frankly, the deck is stacked against overturning a case.”

This March, she also sent Hickson a Finley letter. McDonald said ethics rules prevented her from discussing Hickson’s case, but in the letter she blamed Hickson for failing to track down the would-be witness and said his trial lawyer had a strategic reason for not sending the subpoena.

Reading the letter, Hickson said, “I felt defeated.”

Since McDonald asked to drop the case, he is pursuing exoneration alone.

Dr. Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, reacts to the Pope's diagnosis and how lung cancer can occur in never-smokers.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after a scheduled surgery, the Vatican announced Tuesday.

After undergoing thoracic surgery, where surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.

The diagnosis had been suspected based on testing conducted before the procedure, according to the Holy See Press Office.

POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS

The Pope reportedly does not smoke and does not have a known history of smoking. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicates that most lung cancer deaths (80%) are caused by smoking.

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, representing about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. It is also the most common type among non-smokers.

NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Lary Robinson, M.D., an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the Pope’s health status, as the lung nodule was "felt to be malignant."

About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the Pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers — including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients.

Newly elected Pope Leo XIV, Cardinal Robert F. Prevost of the U.S., appears on the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica at the Vatican, on May 8, 2025. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

"But [the Pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a stage 1 cancer," the doctor added.

If the Pope’s cancer is stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90%, depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread.

HEALTHY DIETS SPARK LUNG CANCER RISK IN NON-SMOKERS AS PESTICIDES LOOM

"We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he had a stage 1 cancer and whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said.

"Size matters in lung nodules and lung cancer – the larger the cancer, the worse outlook it is, because it's more likely to be advanced and have spread."

Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking, according to experts. (iStock)

Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking. Other factors like family history and genetic predisposition can play a role, experts say.

Recent research discovered that a rare genetic mutation in the gene EGFR T790M increased lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to findings published in the journal Science.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who were not carriers.

Family history and environmental exposures can increase lung cancer risk. (iStock)

Robinson added that other types of smoking, like pipes and cigars, can increase the risk of lung cancer, as well as heavy use of marijuana.

Another risk factor is exposure to environmental toxins, such as diesel exhaust and radon, according to the oncologist.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Unfortunately, probably over half of the people who are never-smokers with lung cancer come into stage 4 disease," Robinson said. "And that's higher than people who are smokers or former smokers, so they start out at a worse stage in general."

In most cases, early-stage lung cancer will not come with any symptoms, according to Robinson. In those who do have symptoms, however, the most common are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Unexplained weight loss can result from any form of cancer, the oncologist noted. Neurological symptoms, like persistent headaches, may also warrant seeing a doctor.

The most common symptoms are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood. (iStock)

Lung cancer is rare in younger adults, which is why annual CT screening is generally recommended starting at age 50 for those at high risk, the doctor said.

People considered at high risk include current smokers with at least a 20 pack-year history, as well as former smokers who quit within the past 15 years.

"Only about 15% of the people who are eligible get screened, unfortunately," Robinson said.

"I'm hoping that within four or five years, a screening CT scan will only be confirmatory after they have a positive blood test done at your doctor's office." That approach could make screening easier and potentially help detect more lung cancers, according to the doctor.

The details are harrowing: An 11-year-old boy, wrists and ankles bound tightly with zip ties, is picked up and then slammed into the hard concrete floor of an unfinished basement.

He can feel the circulation cutting off in his arms and legs, a dull burning at his wrists and ankles from where the sharp plastic of the too-taut zip ties is digging into his skin. His tailbone is bruised and sore from breaking his fall onto the floor.

'You're a burden, Collin! You're a burden to this whole family.'

It's a recollection that feels like a horror story, but according to Collin Gosselin, it was just another day in his childhood as a reality TV star once the cameras were no longer rolling.

This shocking story is just one of many chilling allegations that Collin, 22, makes about his upbringing with his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, 51, in his new memoir called In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood. The book recounts his time on the TLC reality show, Jon & Kate Plus 8, which catapulted Collin, his seven siblings – fellow sextuplets Aaden, Alexis, Hannah, Joel and Leah, and twin sisters, Mady and Cara – and their parents, Jon and Kate, to fame.

Filled with horrific allegations of physical, verbal and emotional child abuse, the narrative he presents is a far cry from the sometimes chaotic but always cheery family life in suburban Pennsylvania that was sold to millions of viewers each week.

Indeed, the picture he paints is of a childhood rife with alleged violence and casual cruelty – treatment for which, Collin claimed, he was singled out as retaliation for his reticence to being filmed for the show.

Collin first appeared on-screen at 15 months old, in a Discovery Health one-hour special called Surviving Sextuplets and Twins in 2006. The couple turned to fertility treatments, specifically Intrauterine Insemination (IUI), and twins Mady and Cara were born in 2000.

Speaking in 2009, Kate recalled in an interview: 'I had everything I had ever hoped and prayed for: a loving and devoted husband, two chubby-cheeked, silky-haired, pint-sized daughters, a cozy home and a rewarding career as a neo-natal nurse. Two men allegedly arrived at a Sydney car park to collect what they believed was a $17 million shipment of cocaine, only to discover the drugs had already been seized in Chile and replaced with a fake substance by police.

The delivery was part of an AFP sting operation, with investigators swapping the 23kg haul for an inert substance before transporting the replica packages to a Port Botany car park on Tuesday.

Police allege the two men, both 33, attempted to take possession of the packages before they were arrested.

The operation followed a tip-off from Chilean investigators, who allegedly uncovered an organised crime network planning to send cocaine to Australia aboard a commercial aircraft.

Officers seized the shipment before it reached Australia and shared intelligence with the AFP, setting the sting in motion.

Both men were charged with attempting to possess a commercial quantity of a border controlled drug - an offence which carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

The men faced Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday and were both refused bail.

They are set to appear before Downing Centre Local Court on December 9.

Two other people, including a Bolivian national and an Argentinian national, were also arrested for their alleged involvement in the attempted cocaine importation plot.

The individuals have each been charged with drug trafficking and criminal association offences.

Employers who try to extend the visas of their temporary foreign workers must file new justifications for not hiring skilled Americans, say new regulations from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The rule change ended the prior deference rules, which say agency examiners must defer to years-old corporate justifications for foreign workers. The likely result will be many more denials of requests for visa workers, such as the H-1B and J-1 workers being targeted by Vice-President JD Vance’s anti-fraud campaign.

“DHS believes that removing deference [to prior justifications] would enhance program integrity and thereby better protect the interests of U.S. workers, consistent with this Administration’s priorities,” said the DHS statement.

The priorities were sketched on October 8 by Vance:

I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played: You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers, and if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with. This is a terribly pernicious system. It’s gone on for too long.

Vance’s growing criticism of the visa programs is spurring more public opposition, despite a near-blackout by the establishment media.

In 2024, the DHS received almost 600,000 new and renewal applications for foreign workers, titled “Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker.”

The 38-page application does not ask for evidence that employers tried to hire Americans before asking for the foreign worker.  “There isn’t anything like that,” said John Miano, an immigration lawyer who defends Americans.

The key factor is enforcement, Miano told Breitbart News: “They’ve got to actually check … [and] the cynic in me says they are announcing stuff that won’t have any effect on the companies.”

RELATED: Inspector General: Many Recipients of H-1B Are Pawns in Chess Game Run by Corps. Seeking Cheap Labor

Currently, “they’re not even checking if the [workers’ claimed] worksite is valid,” he added.

The visa numbers are high because the many visa programs are huge and strongly supported by many executives. For example, the government allows U.S. employers to keep a workforce of roughly 2.5 million foreign graduates, including almost 1 million H-1B workers and spouses.

Those white collar migrants get good jobs — partly via Indian favoritism, fraud, and hidden kickbacks — that would otherwise go to American graduates.

The deference rules were established in 2004 by President George Bush, ended by President Donald Trump in 2017, and restarted by President Joe Biden in 2021.

The end of deference is likely to expose fraud, Trump’s deputies noted:

Specifically, for H-1B extension cases from FY 2022 through FY 2025, the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among H-1B sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits was 22.39 percent. In comparison, when USCIS had a policy of no deference, the overall combined percentage of H-1B non-compliance and/or fraud among H-1B sites visited during FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 16.77 percent.

For L-1A extension cases,  the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits from FY 2022 through FY 2025 was 24.46 percent. In comparison, the overall combined percentage of L-1A noncompliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited from FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 18.37 percent.

The visa programs are set in law, and are strongly backed by business groups. But Trump’s deputies are setting many partial curbs on many visa programs. For example, they are curbing the ability of foreign students to stay in the United States and setting large fees on universities that get work permits for foreign students.

Officials are also setting large fees on H-1B work permits, and forcing migrants to submit justification if they want to extend work permits.

So far, corporate lawyers have persuaded friendly, lower-court judges to block nearly all of Trump’s reforms.

Lobbies for more business migration lamented the Trump reforms. For example, the leading migration firm, Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy, complained:

If the regulation is implemented, employers are likely to see a marked increase in Form I-129 requests for evidence (RFEs) and an increased risk of denials, with a particular impact on extension of status petitions; this in turn could disrupt the ability of employers to retain sponsored foreign talent and impede projects and workforce planning.

“The administration wants to discourage immigration,” immigration lawyer Jonathan Grode of Green & Spiegel told Forbes.com.

The Times of India worried the reform could constrict India’s economic strategy of sending Indian migrants into foreign jobs:

This means there will be more denials, more documentation, more RFEs. USCIS could reexamine whether the employee qualifies for the position and whether the job meets H-1B requirements. Employers and employees may face additional requests for evidence and documentation.

A growing number of investors and CEOs admit the deep fraud within the visa programs.

India’s tech economy has grown because “a big part of the business was gaming the US visa system to cheaply onshore Indian IT workers into American companies,” Umar Saif, the CEO of a Pakistani tech firm, said on X. He added:

Basically, staffing firms masquerading as IT companies. Washington has finally caught up with this back door. First came the $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B applications. Now, major IT outsourcing firms, Microsoft and Adobe have been suspended from the PERM green-card process over alleged abuse. A visa programme meant to attract skilled talent should never become a back door for cheap staffing.

Few Pakistanis are hired via the Indian-dominated H-1B program.

If you’re a watch enthusiast, you probably don’t want to exchange your prized timepiece for a bulky fitness tracker. But Hiyd founder Salah Batroukh doesn’t think people should have to sacrifice fashion for function.

“We don’t think that health tracking needs to be this overly conscious decision where you have to change something about the way you look,” Batroukh told TechCrunch. “That’s the ethos of the entire company. Our plan is to build out this product ecosystem of invisible health tracking.”

Hiyd’s first device to make health tracking look cooler is a small, slim disc that attaches to the back of your watch via microsuction, a material technology that allows the sensor to sit flush under your watch without magnets or adhesive. That way, it won’t leave any residue or mess with the mechanics of watches that keep time using magnets.

“Microsuction is essentially a textured silicone, with hundreds of tiny pockets per square inch molded into a pliable sheet. So when you press on it, it pushes air out of all those pockets, and you end up with a vacuum — just like traditional suction cups but scaled down incredibly,” Batroukh explained. “It works incredibly at stopping shear forces, but a little bit of prying allows it to pop right off, which is ideal for us. It’s also incredibly thin at just 0.3 mm with our manufacturing processes.”

According to Batroukh, the sensor, which measures 2.7 mm thick and weighs 7 grams, collects biometrics similar to those of leading wearables, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep staging, movement, calories burned, and VO2 max estimations, then syncs to an iOS or Android app. In order to fine-tune the sensor, Hiyd’s team is filming themselves doing various activities, then labeling those datasets to train its AI.

“We go for a walk and say, ‘This is somebody walking, this is somebody jogging, this is somebody running,’” he said. “The one thing that AI is really good at is data analysis, so we can basically fit a lot of heuristic analysis into our sets really quickly.”

On its app, Hiyd is also working to incorporate nutrition tracking. The goal isn’t to count calories, but rather to help users glean insights about how their eating habits impact their sleep quality or workout performance.

“What we will do is say like, ‘Hey, on days where you work out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m., your sleep quality is actually worse,’ and that’ll be specific to you,” he said. “Or it’ll say, ‘Hey, we think you had a less deep sleep last night because you had a slice of cake before you went to bed, and the sugar affected it.’”

Batroukh spent about seven years as a manufacturing design engineer at Apple, a company synonymous with iconic hardware. But he wanted to know if he could design something great without the support of a global brand and a multitrillion-dollar market cap.

“One of the reasons I left Apple was a lot of the products became a little bit more about being an Apple product, rather than being something for the customer,” he said. “[Hiyd] gives me the opportunity to do the exact opposite.”

Batroukh is joined by fellow founders Omar Shakir, an experienced mechanical engineer who is the startup’s CTO, and Mahamad Charawi, who is its head of software. (Charawi previously co-led the Y Combinator-backed startup Laudspeaker through its sale.)

Hiyd is bringing its tiny sensor to the big stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where the company is competing as one of the top 20 companies at Startup Battlefield on Wednesday. (Don’t miss out on the action.) In November, the company plans to launch a Kickstarter. So far, over 16,000 people have made deposits to secure Hiyd’s first units.

nyt-op-ed-democrats-affordability:
The affordability shtick is nothing more than a campaign myth.

For Americans considering voting Democrat because they want cheaper groceries and lower gas prices, a New York Times op-ed offers a warning about what a Democrat victory would actually deliver: another round of get-conservatives lawfare, resource-squandering impeachment witch hunts, and performative stonewalling of Trump’s judicial nominees.

Democrats have spent months positioning themselves as the answer to Americans’ affordability concerns. But voters — particularly independents, moderates, and frustrated Republicans — should pay attention to what Democrats say they would actually do with control of Congress.

Writing for the Times, Jamelle Bouie says if Democrats win back the House and Senate, they “would have an opportunity not just to check the Trump administration but to neuter it: to halt the confirmation of new judges, to block the president’s attempts to appoint more unqualified toadies to key offices and to focus the investigative fire of both chambers on every aspect of this White House.”

Bouie all but salivates at the prospect of lawfare, writing, “Should Democrats find the will to do so, they could launch the kind of full-court press that no president has faced from the opposition since Barack Obama had to contend with a Republican Congress in the last two years of his administration. The difference is that Democrats will have real corruption and malfeasance to work with.”

Bouie also warns Democrats against imagining they can have a “constructive relationship … with either Trump or the Republican Party over the next two years.” Instead, Bouie suggests Democrats wield “the full suite of Congress’s powers to constrain the president and restore constitutional government.”

In a lot more words than needed, Bouie is arguing for a two-year-long lawfare campaign against the president and his agenda. Elect Democrats, and you’ll get political lawfare, Bouie hopes. Voters anticipating a Democrat Congress would focus on affordability — which certainly would include working with Republicans and the president despite Bouie’s desire for no bipartisan work — should be wary.

And while Bouie is an opinion columnist, some of the very Democrats who campaign on affordability are also promising the same obstruction and lawfare that Bouie stumps for.

Ohio Democrat Senate candidate Sherrod Brown recently told voters: “I’m in this fight to make life more affordable. Ohioans are working harder than ever and they deserve to get ahead.” But appearing on MSNow, Brown also promised that no matter the qualifications of a candidate, a Democrat-controlled Senate will not confirm any Trump judges.

“We’re not, obviously, confirming judges that are Trump judges,” Brown said. How refusing to confirm a judge because Trump nominated him makes life more affordable for Ohioans is not clear, but what is clear is that Brown’s focus isn’t exactly on affordability.

Rep. Ro Khanna has similarly framed this upcoming election as a referendum on affordability, saying in a post in July: “American families are paying $3500 more a year because of Trump’s war in Iran, his blanket tariffs, and his tax breaks for the wealthy. We need Democrats back in power.”

Yet when asked in a Sept. 27 interview on Meet the Press if impeaching Trump for a third time would be “a mistake,” Khanna said, “No, it’s not,” and said impeachment would set a “standard.” Khanna claimed Democrats could pursue impeachment and also focus on the cost of living.

Democrats keep offering promises of political lawfare to stop Trump with vague assurances that they will make life more affordable. Voters can be frustrated with prices, disappointed in Republicans (for not doing enough), or unhappy with Trump without wanting to give Democrats two years to pursue lawfare. Democrats’ affordability pitch is merely a mask for their real goals: obsessively obstructing Trump and ushering in their radical socialist plans, including free health care for illegal aliens, wide-open borders, and get-the-“rich” schemes that will harm everyday Americans.

Virginia offers a warning about accepting the affordability pitch at face value. Last fall Abigail Spanberger turned the Virginia gubernatorial race into a referendum on affordability.

“Affordability takes center stage in New Jersey, Virginia governor races,” ABC News’ Benjamin Siegel wrote on Nov. 2, 2025. Politico’s Erin Doherty and Brakkton Booker wrote on Oct. 29, 2025, that “Spangberger has stuck to a message on the economy, specifically the cost of life for Virginians.”

Spanberger ultimatey won the race, and yet life has not gotten any more affordable in the commonwealth. July polling found that 47 percent of Virginians disapprove of Spanberger (compared to 42 percent who approve), and affordability issues are still the leading concerns. The Democrat-led state government has put forward proposal after proposal that would raise taxes on everyday services like gym classes, dry cleaning, home repairs, delivery and shipping services, and other items. Spanberger also announced plans to return Virginia to the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative from which Republican Gov. Glenn Youngkin withdrew the state during his tenure. The Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative raises Virginians’ electricity costs, as admitted by the Virginia Energy Efficiency Council.

The affordability shtick was nothing more than a campaign myth meant to deceive voters into voting for Spanberger. It’s the same playbook Democrats are running now. Impeaching Trump, blocking judicial nominees, and performatively opposing Trump regardless of the policy are all the real goals of Democrats, as made clear by Democrats themselves as well as Bouie.

It’s no surprise that Americans are frustrated with high gas prices. But electing Democrats — whether because they promise to make life affordable or to punish Republicans for inaction on other fronts — will not result in lower gas prices. It will, however, bring an end to deportations, an end to secure borders, an end to shrinking government, and an end to any other campaign promise the president is working on now.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.

Nobody needs to follow you to know where you went this week. The phone in your pocket can already keep a record of your movements. And parts of that information can end up in the hands of other companies.

Your pharmacy. Your cardiologist. The church you attend on Sunday morning. The support group you'd rather nobody knew about. None of it necessarily comes from hacking. It can come from ordinary apps you installed yourself and the permissions you gave them. Here's how your movements can get out, who buys location data and the settings that can limit how much gets shared.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

A smartphone can share location and other device data that may reveal sensitive details about where you go. (Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images)

Smartphones can use advertising identifiers that help advertisers and developers measure ads and activity. On Apple devices, the system advertising identifier is known as the IDFA. Android devices can use Google's advertising ID.

Advertising identifiers can help connect activity across apps when apps and advertising systems are permitted to use them. Combined with location data and other signals, those identifiers can help companies build a much more detailed trail of where a device has been.

And a trail stops being anonymous fast. A device that sleeps at your address every night and turns up at a dialysis center every Tuesday and Thursday isn't much of a mystery to anyone who can connect those locations with other identifying information.

An app asks for your location. Often for a fair reason, like providing a local forecast or showing the nearest pharmacy. What many people don't realize is that apps can include advertising and analytics software from outside companies. Depending on the app, its permissions and its privacy practices, that technology may collect or receive information about your device and location. Location information can also become part of the digital advertising ecosystem, where information about a device can pass among multiple companies. Once location data leaves your phone, controlling where it goes next becomes much harder.

This isn't a theory about what could happen. The government spent years fighting one such case in court. On May 4, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement that bars the data broker Kochava and its subsidiary, Collective Data Solutions, from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without people's affirmative express consent, subject to the terms of the order. The FTC alleged Kochava sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track people to health facilities, places of worship and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not admit wrongdoing. Kochava wasn't alone. In December 2024, the FTC took action against two more location data companies, Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla, over allegations involving the sale of sensitive location data.

In January 2025, Gravy Analytics was breached. A hacker posted what they claimed was 17 terabytes of stolen data on a Russian cybercrime forum. Security researchers examining a sample found more than 30 million location points, including phones at the White House, the Kremlin and military bases around the world. The data reportedly came from everyday apps, including games and dating apps. Think about what that means. A company collects movements. Regulators take action over how sensitive location data gets handled. Then criminals allegedly obtain a massive collection of data anyway.

Strip out the technical language. A few weeks of location data can potentially reveal:

Those last few can turn a privacy problem into a safety concern. A device that regularly leaves a home at the same time and returns two hours later can reveal patterns about when someone may be away. Location information can also make a scam call more convincing. "I'm calling from the billing office at the clinic on Oak Street about your visit last week" is much harder to dismiss when the clinic and timing happen to be correct. And with Medicare Open Enrollment beginning October 15, a caller who seems to know your doctor or pharmacy may sound more convincing than a random scammer.

If you've ever tapped "Allow" on a weather app, a store app or a game, you may have shared it. You might have granted that permission years ago and forgotten about it. Even apps without precise location permission may be able to estimate your general area through information such as your internet connection. You can't make yourself invisible, but you can make your movements harder to track.

You can't stop your phone from knowing where you are and still use every location-based feature. But you can limit which apps get that information and reduce some of the identifiers used for advertising and tracking. None of this takes technical skill, and you can tackle one part at a time.

Advertising identifiers aren't the only way companies can recognize a device, but limiting them can remove one tool used to connect activity for advertising purposes.

First, control whether apps can request permission to track you across other companies' apps and websites:

When this setting is off, apps that request permission to track are treated as though you selected Ask App Not to Track. They cannot access Apple's system advertising identifier, known as the IDFA.

Apple also has a separate setting for ads that Apple itself delivers:

This second setting limits how Apple personalizes the ads it delivers in services such as the App Store, Apple News and Stocks. It is separate from the app-tracking control above.

THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE

Social media apps collect more data than many users realize, from clicks and contacts to location history. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)

To check your advertising ID controls:

Depending on your Galaxy model and software configuration, you may also find Google's advertising controls through Settings > Google > All services > Ads.

Deleting the advertising ID prevents apps from accessing that particular Google advertising identifier. It does not prevent every form of advertising, analytics or device identification.

Google says deleting the advertising ID removes that identifier. Apps that try to access it receive a string of zeros instead. Apps can still have their own privacy and advertising settings, so this does not eliminate every form of tracking.

Now look at which apps can see where you are and whether they really need that access.

You don't have to turn Location Services off completely. Doing so can interfere with useful features. Instead, focus on apps that have more access than they need.

That’s an explosive find.

A Texas man found live World War II-era grenades inside a box he bought at an estate sale, prompting police to send in the bomb squad.

The Austin Police Department said it got the “unusual call” Monday after the man was rummaging through boxes he had bought and noticed one contained the handheld explosives.

“Our patrol officers, who quickly secured the scene, set up a perimeter, and kept neighbors safe while they waited for EOD [Explosive Ordnance Disposal],” the department wrote on Instagram.

The bomb squad confirmed the grenades were “live and active.”

A photo shared by police shows at least three loose US Mk 2 fragmentation grenades in the box, known as “pineapples” because of their shape and grooved cast-iron bodies.

The Mk 2 was the US military’s standard-issue fragmentation grenade from World War II through the Korean War and into the Vietnam War.

The box also appeared to hold shipping tubes and containers, including one marked for an M21 practice grenade.

The bomb squad safely removed the devices, police said.

An Austin Police Department spokesperson told Chron that six grenades were recovered in all, each appearing to date to World War II and in good condition for its age.

“Bomb Squad personnel assessed the devices, including X-ray examination. Based on their interpretation of the X-ray images, the grenades appeared to be live and were treated accordingly,” the spokesperson told the outlet.

The department said the bomb squad “subsequently conducted render-safe procedures to eliminate any potential hazards,” and that there is no ongoing investigation.

“A big shoutout to our APD Bomb Squad. These officers bring a level of training, expertise, and steady nerves that most people never see,” the department wrote on Instagram.

“Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on.”

Police noted that “no crime” was committed but urged the public to call them if they ever find themselves in a similar situation.

“If you ever come across old military ordnance (grenades, shells, mortar rounds, etc.), even if you think it’s inert, don’t touch it, don’t move it, and call 911. Let the experts handle it,” the department said.

While the man who bought the box was not charged with any crime, it’s still illegal to own hand grenades and other explosive devices classified as prohibited weapons in Texas.

Unlawfully possessing an explosive weapon such as a grenade is a third-degree felony that carries 2 to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000, under Texas Penal Code Section 46.05.

This isn’t the first time an unlucky buyer has stumbled upon live grenades while secondhand shopping.

In 2025, employees at a Maine Goodwill store discovered military-grade grenades and mortars hidden in a donation box.

The store was evacuated while the Maine State Police Bomb Squad assessed the devices, which were found to be inactive.

VATICAN CITY— Question: Who runs the Catholic Church when the pope is unconscious, incapacitated or otherwise unable to govern?

Answer: The pope.

Pope Leo XIV arrives at hospital ahead of surgery to remove lung nodule

The Vatican has detailed laws, rituals and norms to transfer papal power if a pope dies or resigns. But none of them apply when he is sick or even unconscious, as Pope Leo XIV will be when he undergoes surgery Tuesday to remove a nodule on his lung.

As a result, Leo remains pope and very much in charge even when he goes under general anesthesia at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he arrived Tuesday afternoon for what is expected to be a weeklong stay.

The pope is the successor of the Apostle Peter, the head of the college of bishops, the Vicar of Christ and the pastor of the universal Catholic Church on Earth, according to the church’s in-house canon law.

Nothing changes in his status, role or power since Leo was elected the 267th pope on May 8, 2025.

Leo may be in charge, but he already delegates the day-to-day running of the Vatican and church to a team of officials who operate whether he is in the Apostolic Palace or not, and whether he is conscious or not.

Chief among them is the Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin. In a sign that Leo’s hospitalization foresaw no change to the governance of the church, Parolin wasn’t even in the Vatican on Tuesday. He was speaking at a conference nearby.

“We were all struck by the serenity with which the pope announced this procedure,” Parolin told reporters as he arrived for the conference. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.”

But Parolin said he had spoken with the pope Monday night and was reassured.

“It’s something that, thank God, we noticed right away. And normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved,” he said. “But these are, as the pope said, God’s surprises.”

Other Vatican functions are proceeding normally, including the announced appointments of two new bishops on Tuesday, albeit with some modifications for events where the pope had been expected to attend.

Canon law has provisions for when a diocesan bishop gets sick and can’t run his diocese, but none for a pope. Canon 412 says a diocese can be declared “impeded” if its bishop — due to “captivity, banishment, exile, or incapacity” — cannot fulfill his pastoral functions. In such cases, the day-to-day running of the diocese shifts to an auxiliary bishop, a vicar general or someone else.

Even though Leo is bishop of Rome, no explicit provision exists for the pope if he similarly becomes “impeded.” Canon 335 declares simply that when the Holy See is “vacant or entirely impeded,” nothing can be altered in the governance of the church. But it doesn’t say what it means for the Holy See to be “entirely impeded” or what provisions might come into play if it ever were.

In 1965, Pope Paul VI wrote letters to the dean of the College of Cardinals hypothesizing that if he were to become seriously ill, the dean and other cardinals should accept his resignation.

Paul foresaw the possibility that as popes continued to live longer, they could become incapacitated by stroke, dementia or another long-term, progressive ailment that would make it impossible for them to do their job and unable to freely resign. The letter was never invoked, since Paul lived another 13 years and died on the job.

Pope Francis confirmed in 2022 that shortly after he was elected pope he wrote a letter of resignation, to be invoked if he became medically incapacitated. Francis said he gave it to the then-secretary of state, Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, and assumed Bertone had delivered it to Parolin’s office when he retired.

The text was never made public and the conditions Francis contemplated for a resignation were unknown. It also is not known if such a letter would be canonically valid. Canon law requires a papal resignation to be “freely and properly manifested,” as was the case when Pope Benedict XVI announced his resignation in 2013.

The only time papal power changes hands is when a pope dies or resigns. At that time a whole series of rites and rituals comes into play governing the “interregnum,” the period between the end of one pontificate and the election of a new pope.

During that period, known as the “sede vacante,” or “empty See,” the camerlengo, or chamberlain, runs the administration and finances of the Holy See. He certifies the pope’s death, seals the papal apartments and prepares for the pope’s burial before a conclave to elect a new pope.

The position is currently held by Cardinal Kevin Farrell, the head of the Vatican’s laity office.

The camerlengo has no role or duties if the pope is merely sick or otherwise incapacitated.

In fact, in these days Farrell is presiding over a Vatican conference on family ministry that Leo had been attending up until his surprise hospitalization.

By 2050 an estimated 24.7 million people will be diagnosed with dementia each year and women will be disproportionately affected, according to a landmark new study.

The research found approximately 11.4 million people developed dementia globally in 2023 and that by 2050 that figure will double and demand for care will explode.

The study's authors said women's brain health needed to be prioritised and risk factors like hormonal changes and unequal education or job opportunities needed investigating.

"Understanding these differences is critical if we are to develop dementia prevention, diagnosis and care strategies that respond to the populations facing the greatest future risk," lead author Dr Ashleigh Vella said.

The research from the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at the University of NSW analysed 38,418 people through population-based studies from 18 countries and territories.

It is one of the most comprehensive studies looking at the incidence rate of dementia. The study found cases were highest among women and people living in low income and middle income countries.

Higher rates of depression, anxiety and obesity among women could also be contributing factors. (Unsplash: rawpixel)

Nearly two thirds of current dementia diagnoses in Australia are women and this has long been considered a symptom of their longer life expectancy but researchers said there may be more at play.

Co-director of the CHeBA and Senior Australia of the Year Professor, Henry Brodaty, said historically women had less access to education and fewer career opportunities which could lead to poorer cognitive resilience.

"[Studies have shown] people who are in more complex occupations, particularly where they have complexity in managing people, they have a lower rate of cognitive decline and dementia," he said.

Professor Brodaty, whose father passed away with Alzheimer's at just 52, said having a clear idea of what was coming meant there must be more investment in diagnosis, care and prevention.
