Hey everyone,

Welcome to State of the Day,

As Election Day inches closer, the Republican Party’s post-midterm future is coming into focus.

Republicans Have A Trump Dilemma. What Comes Next Is Harder

Say you’re running as a Republican in 2026. Do you align yourself with the president in hopes of earning support from the base that helped him win the White House last time around, or do you distance yourself from the administration, hoping to appeal to independents and disaffected Republicans?

Well, there’s no perfect answer. In fact, from a purely electoral perspective, it’s probably best to do a bit of both — walk the line, if you will.

A Friday Politico poll found that a quarter of Trump voters want Republicans to break with President Donald Trump to win. Half want candidates to remain close to the commander-in-chief. And the last quarter can’t make up their minds.

Quite the Trumpian pickle.

The trouble is that this isn’t just a question of how much Trump a candidate can afford to embrace this cycle. It’s a question of what comes after Trump, and what American conservatism will look like when the president is no longer the standalone, defining figure on the right.

For nearly a decade, Republicans have been able to define themselves largely by their relationship with Trump. But loyalty to one man is not a governing philosophy, and sooner or later, the party will have to reckon with that distinction.

Nov. 3 is barreling toward us, and candidates can only spend so much time calculating their proximity to the president.

Eventually, they’ll have to decide what they stand for and what the future of their party will look like.

Will the next generation of elected conservatives support or oppose sprawling data centers?

Will they back federal AI regulations or leave the industry to regulate itself?

Where will they draw the line between mass surveillance and individual liberties?

Will they favor an interventionist or isolationist approach to foreign policy?

When the interests of corporations clash with the interests of the average American, whose side will they take?

These aren’t exactly small questions, and their answers will shape the future of American conservatism, determining not just what the Republican Party campaigns on, but what it actually accomplishes.

Trump has taken positions on some of these issues. Others remain unsettled. His eventual departure from the political stage won’t resolve these debates. If anything, it’ll bring them into sharper focus.

Of course, getting there means navigating the present political environment where Trump still makes politicians and breaks them.

And none of these questions about the party’s future will matter much to candidates if they can’t win their elections anyway.

That means maintaining a careful balance between a president who commands fierce loyalty among a vital part of the GOP base and disaffected voters signaling they are ready for something different.

Breaking with Trump could alienate the one group; sticking too close to him could scorn the rest.

So the question facing Republicans is twofold: How much distance can they afford to put between themselves and Trump today, and what kind of party do they want to build for tomorrow?

The next generation of Republican politics is already taking shape.

Whether candidates recognize that — or are too busy figuring out how to survive the Trump era to think about what comes next — is another question entirely.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson spoke with Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, about how attitudes toward autonomous trucks have shifted over time.

You could soon be driving down a Texas highway, look over at a massive delivery truck and realize the driver's seat is completely empty. Kodiak AI plans to start hauling IKEA products between the Dallas and Houston areas later this year with nobody in the cab. The company has spent years preparing for this step, but removing the safety observer changes the equation.

What happens if something breaks while the truck is moving at highway speed? Is someone secretly driving it from a control room? How does it react to a police car or ambulance? And, yes, I wanted to know what keeps a hacker from getting anywhere near something as important as the steering or brakes. So, I took those questions directly to Kodiak founder and CEO Don Burnette to find out how the company says these driverless trucks will handle them.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

Kodiak’s self-driving semi sits outside an IKEA store as the company prepares to haul freight with nobody in the cab. (Kodiak AI)

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com

"The decision to remove the driver isn't based on any single test or milestone," Burnette told CyberGuy. "It's the result of years of operating experience, rigorous validation and a clear safety case that gives us a clear, evidence-based framework for determining when the Kodiak Driver is ready to operate safely without anyone in the cab."

Kodiak calls its autonomous driving system the Kodiak Driver. The company also uses something called an Autonomy Readiness Measure, or ARM, to track its progress toward running long-haul trucks without anyone aboard.

As of the end of September, Kodiak said 96% of the claims and evidence required for its long-haul safety case were materially complete, up from 93% at the end of August. The remaining work includes engineering verification, validation and final safety assessments. Kodiak expects to complete that work before launching driverless long-haul service by the end of 2026. The company also has experience running trucks commercially with empty cabs.

Kodiak-powered trucks have been operating for Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin without anyone aboard since December 2024. Burnette says that by the end of the second quarter, 35 driverless trucks were operating there commercially and had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations. To put things in perspective, that is the equivalent of more than 4 ½ years of nonstop driving. So, the IKEA route will take Kodiak into a different setting, but removing the driver itself will not be new territory for the company.

I asked Burnette what drivers on I-45 will actually notice once the new service starts. His answer was pretty straightforward. "The biggest difference is that there won't be anyone in the cab," he said.

The driverless section will cover 219 miles, primarily along Interstate 45 between Kodiak facilities in the Dallas and Houston areas. That stretch is part of a longer 292-mile delivery route connecting IKEA's distribution center in Baytown with its store in Frisco.

Kodiak has been carrying IKEA products along the route for four years with a safety observer aboard. During that time, the companies have also been figuring out the less obvious parts of running autonomous freight, such as when trucks should leave, when they will reach the destination and how maintenance should be scheduled.

The trucks themselves have redundancy systems built into safety-critical components including braking, steering, power and computing. "From the outside, the drive itself should look pretty boring, and that's exactly what we want," Burnette said. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to be predictable, courteous, conservative and defensive." Frankly, boring is exactly what I think we all want from a giant truck with nobody sitting behind the wheel.

This was high on my list of questions. "We've designed the Kodiak Driver around the idea that something will eventually go wrong, whether that's a mechanical issue, a damaged sensor or an unexpected situation on the road," Burnette said. "The important thing is that the truck already knows what to do when that happens."

Burnette says the Kodiak Driver continuously monitors more than 1,000 safety-critical components across the truck, its sensors, hardware and autonomy software. If the system detects a serious issue, it can switch from normal driving into what Kodiak calls a fallback maneuver. That process is designed to bring the truck to a controlled stop in a safe location.

Kodiak also puts limits around where and under what conditions the truck can operate. In the autonomous vehicle world, that is called an Operational Design Domain, or ODD. You can think of the ODD as the truck's approved operating boundaries. If the situation falls outside what the system has been designed and tested to handle, Burnette says the truck can fall back rather than continuing as though nothing has changed.

DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES

Kodiak plans to run driverless IKEA deliveries along a 219-mile stretch of I-45 between the Dallas and Houston areas. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

No one will be in the cab, but people will still be watching what is happening. Kodiak has a command center just south of Dallas. However, Burnette does not describe those workers as remote drivers waiting to take control. If the Kodiak Driver runs into a situation it cannot safely resolve, it can activate its fallback system and then, as Burnette puts it, "call home for help." The command center can provide guidance about what the truck should do next.

That is different from a person taking over the steering wheel from miles away. "We use redundant communications channels to ensure we remain in contact with the truck, but if connectivity is lost, the Kodiak Driver still has to be able to respond safely on its own," Burnette said.

That last part is especially important. If the cellular or communications connection goes down, the truck cannot simply sit there waiting for someone at the command center to tell it what to do. Kodiak says the vehicle still has to get itself into a safe state.

Highway driving involves situations that go well beyond staying between the lane lines. Police pull vehicles over. Ambulances approach from behind. Accident scenes can suddenly change the flow of traffic. A truck with nobody in the cab still has to recognize what is happening around it and respond.

Kodiak says its autonomous system is designed to identify emergency vehicles, stopped vehicles, lane closures and accident scenes. The system can slow down or move over when appropriate. The company has also spent time working directly with first responders.

Kodiak employs a retired California Highway Patrol officer who works with law enforcement on how to interact with driverless trucks. The company also has a written First Responder Interaction Plan that explains what responders should do if they encounter one of its vehicles.

Another piece of technology comes into play if a Kodiak truck stops along the road. Kodiak has integrated HAAS Alert's Safety Cloud. That system can send digital warnings about a stopped truck to nearby motorists through compatible navigation apps and vehicle systems.

You knew I was going to ask this one. Once software has control of an 18-wheeler, cybersecurity becomes a major part of the conversation. I asked Burnette what keeps someone from hacking into a truck and interfering with systems like the steering or brakes. "Cybersecurity is something we take very seriously," he said.

Burnette says cybersecurity is one of six pillars in Kodiak's safety case. The company says its approach follows guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology and vehicle cybersecurity best practices from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. But the part that really stood out to me was how Burnette described limiting access to the truck. "First, we've minimized the number of ways into the truck," he said. "We limit data entry points to only what's necessary, and we isolate safety-critical functions like steering and braking from external communications."

That isolation is important because communication with the outside world should not provide a direct doorway into critical driving systems. Burnette says Kodiak also monitors for threats and maintains an incident response process. Burnette also addressed what happens if the truck loses connectivity. "The truck's safety doesn't depend on connectivity, and it's designed to bring itself to a safe stop if something isn't right," Burnette said. No connected vehicle comes with a promise that hackers will never target it. That is why I will be watching how these protections hold up as more driverless trucks begin traveling public highways.

AUTONOMOUS EXCAVATORS ARE DIGGING WITH EMPTY CABS

The Kodiak truck uses autonomous driving technology with backup systems for critical functions including steering and braking. (Kodiak AI)

With a traditional truck, investigators can look at what the person behind the wheel did before a crash. But what happens when nobody was behind the wheel? I asked Burnette who would ultimately be responsible if a driverless Kodiak truck were involved in an accident. "Responsibility for a driverless vehicle works similarly to responsibility for any vehicle: it depends on the circumstances surrounding the crash," he said.

Burnette says Kodiak trucks have more than a dozen sensors aboard. Those sensors can give the company a detailed record of what happened around the vehicle. That information could be especially useful when investigators need to reconstruct the moments leading up to a crash.

I wanted to push on the limits too. Autonomous driving companies spend plenty of time telling us what their technology can do. I think it is just as useful to ask what it cannot do.

Burnette pointed back to the Operational Design Domain. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to operate under specific conditions," he said. "If the truck leaves its ODD, it will simply achieve a fallback. That's intentional." At launch, Burnette says the ODD will cover the Dallas-Houston corridor. Kodiak plans to expand the operating area during 2027 and beyond.

This may be the biggest question of all for someone who makes a living driving a truck. If a semi can travel hundreds of highway miles without a person in the cab, what happens to the person who used to sit there? "We see autonomous trucks supplementing the workload rather than eliminating the need for them," Burnette said.

Burnette also explained why Kodiak is targeting this type of work. "Our focus is on the long, repetitive highway miles that can keep drivers away from home for days or weeks at a time," Burnette told CyberGuy.

There is still a much larger question about what happens if driverless freight eventually spreads across the country. Companies could change the way they divide routes and use drivers. Some jobs could change with them. We will know much more once autonomous trucking gets beyond a limited number of routes and starts becoming part of larger freight networks.

The part I keep coming back to is that there will actually be nobody in the cab. Kodiak has spent four years hauling IKEA freight on this route with a safety observer aboard. Taking that person out changes the stakes, especially when you are talking about an 18-wheeler traveling alongside the rest of us on a busy interstate. I also give Burnette credit for answering our tougher questions. What happens when something breaks? Can somebody remotely drive it? How are the steering and brakes protected from hackers? Kodiak has built systems around each of those concerns, but now comes the test that counts. Once these trucks start piling up driverless highway miles with nobody there to step in, we will get a much clearer idea of how ready this technology really is.

Would you feel comfortable driving next to an 18-wheeler with nobody behind the wheel, or would you keep your distance until driverless trucks have a much longer safety record? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

good-news-in-history-october-12:
81 years ago today, Desmond Doss became the only conscientious objector to win the Medal of Honor after saving an estimated 75 men during the Battle of Hacksaw Ridge in the invasion of Okinawa. Doss refused to carry a weapon into combat because of his personal beliefs as a Seventh-day Adventist against killing. He consequently became a medic assigned to the 307th infantry in the 77th infantry division. READ about his heroism… (1945)

Raised as a Sabbath-keeping non-violent vegetarian, Doss joined the army as a medic and never carried a weapon. In Guam and the Philippines, he was awarded two bronze stars with a V on them for valorous deeds rather than meritorious achievement.

During the Battle of Okinawa, he saved dozens of wounded soldiers atop an area known as the Medea Escarpment, or Hacksaw Ridge, inspiring a film of the same name in 2016.

The citation for his award opened thusly.

As our troops gained the summit, a heavy concentration of artillery, mortar, and machinegun fire crashed into them, inflicting approximately 75 casualties and driving the others back. Private First Class Doss refused to seek cover and remained in the fire-swept area with the many stricken, carrying them one by one to the edge of the escarpment and there lowering them on a rope-supported litter down the face of a cliff to friendly hands.

More Good News on this Day:

And, on this day in 1868, the German engineer and auto pioneer August Horch was born. After working for Karl Benz, he founded the manufacturing giant that would become Audi—and his cars were winning races in Europe before there even was a Model T. His autobiography, published in 1937 was titled, I Built Cars (Ich Baute Autos).

46 years ago today, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, a humorous science fiction book by Douglas Adams, was published. It became an international multi-media phenomenon after the novels were widely distributed and translated into more than 30 languages. The story follows the misadventures of the last surviving man, Arthur Dent, following the demolition of planet Earth who is is rescued via spacecraft by Ford Prefect—a human-like alien writer for the eccentric, electronic travel guide The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. (1979)

215 years ago today, the first Oktoberfest was held when Bavarian royalty invited the citizens of Munich to join together in celebration of the marriage of the Crown Prince.

The outcome was so successful, they decided to celebrate every year—though there have been cancellations due to war, and in 2020 because of the coronavirus pandemic.

The German folk festival runs in early October for 16-18 days, with more than six million people from around the world attending the event, drinking more than 60,000 barrels of Oktoberfest beer. (1810)

55 years ago today, Jesus Christ Superstar, the rock opera by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice, opened on Broadway—a musical story told entirely through song, with no spoken dialogue.

Loosely based on the biblical account of the last week of Jesus’s life—but with psychological and social commentary—the play was nominated for five Tony Awards, and starred Jeff Fenholt as Jesus, and Ben Vereen as Judas.

Initially unable to get funding for a stage production, the composers released it as a rock opera concept album musical. The success of the LP proved its viability and led to its Broadway debut. By 1980, the concert-like play had grossed more than $237 million worldwide. Running for over eight years in London between 1972 and 1980 it held the record for longest-running West End musical until it was overtaken by Cats. (1971)

7 years ago, Eliud Kipchoge completed the first ever sub-2-hour marathon in history when he crossed the finish line in Vienna. Long considered a possible yet near-mythical feat of athletics, Eliud dedicated his effort, which came in at 1 hour 59 minutes 40 seconds, to an attempt to ensure no human being ever feels limited. He described it as like the first man on the moon, both in scale of achievement, and in scale of hope for future generations.

In 2018 Eliud had tried to break the record in Monza, Italy, as part of a special race designed to see if someone could log a sub-2-hour marathon. However, it was partially-assisted, and wasn’t overseen by World Athletics.

In 2019, Eliud completed an incredible 21 kilometers in just 59 minutes. The President of Kenya, Uhuru Kenyatta tweeted out “Hearty congratulations @EliudKipchoge. You’ve done it, you’ve made history and made Kenya proud while at it. Your win today, will inspire tens of future generations to dream big and to aspire for greatness. We celebrate you and wish you God’s blessings.” – President Kenyatta.

Nithya Raman has issued a word-salad denial on whether she will make controversial former District Attorney George Gascón head of the LAPD if she becomes mayor of Los Angeles.

The DSA-backed candidate appeared to panic during a TV appearance and said “I don’t know him personally” when grilled over bringing back the ultra-liberal former cop.

It comes just a day after she issued an outright denial to the California Post on appointing him, further muddying the water on what she plans if she gains office.

Raman sparked fury last week when The Post unearthed a since deleted “fascist liars” video featuring LAPD chief Jim McDonnell with a giant red X across his face.

During her NBC appearance Sunday, Raman was quizzed on the rumors she wants to bring back Gascón, who was dumped as LA County DA in 2024.

Raman said: “No, no. I don’t know where the rumors are coming from. I don’t know him personally.”

The rumors are the latest headache for Raman, who spent much of the past week explaining a since-deleted social media video featuring McDonnell’s face crossed out with a giant red X beneath the words “Only you can stop fascist liars.”

Her campaign insisted the message targeted ICE and the Trump administration, not McDonnell, and blamed the video’s editing on left-wing influencer Ed Choi.

The controversy has also exposed conflicting messages about when Raman would replace McDonnell if she defeats Mayor Karen Bass in the Nov. 3 election.

During an ABC7 interview Saturday Raman insisted replacing McDonnell was not among her immediate priorities.

“You know, replacing the chief of police is not on my 100-day agenda. Restoring trust with our law enforcement and the public is on my 100-day agenda,” Raman said.

Pressed about Bass’ warning that firing McDonnell ahead of the LA 2028 Olympics could be disastrous, Raman suggested waiting until 2030.

“I believe his term goes through 2030, if I’m not mistaken, and at that point I think I would be looking to appoint a new chief,” she said.

But when The California Post sought clarification Saturday, Raman offered a different timetable.

“Chief McDonnell’s term ends in 2030 and I would expect to replace him prior to that,” she told The Post, promising a “careful, orderly transition.”

Raman said she did not know where the Gascón rumors originated, but multiple law enforcement and political sources told The Post his name has been circulating inside City Hall and among rank-and-file cops as a possible replacement.

The prospect has alarmed law enforcement officials, who warn appointing him could trigger a mass exodus from the already understaffed LAPD.

“Gascón would turn the LAPD upside-down,” Dennis Zine, 79, a former LA City Councilman and longtime LAPD officer, told The Post. “He basically flipped from one extreme to the other — law enforcement to pro-criminal.

“I would think you’d see a mass exodus of officers with less than five years on the job,” Zine warned. “It’s like the ship is sinking. Let’s get out while we can.”

Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park also said that the choice of police chief could worsen the department’s staffing crisis.

“Decisions about leadership and the appointment of the chief and command staff is something that will absolutely directly impact our staffing levels at LAPD,” Park said.

The Los Angeles Police Protective League was even more forceful.

“Apparently, Nithya Raman’s public safety plan consists of appointing the author of Proposition 47, George Gascón, to be our Chief of Police,” the union’s board of directors charged.

“We’d be laughing if it wasn’t so frightening that after getting bounced two-years ago as District Attorney by a landslide, Raman wants to flip her nose at voters and return Gascón to power.”

Gascón, 72, has longstanding ties to LA’s democratic socialist movement, with the DSA’s Los Angeles chapter urging voters to support him in 2024.

A well-connected senior LAPD officer claimed Gascón is widely believed within the department to be Raman’s preferred replacement.

“It’s not a secret. Everyone knows that. Everyone saying that she’s in touch with him,” the officer said. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli blasted the prospect during a Skid Row press conference.

“I think when you talk to the residents of LA, they want law and order, the days of lawlessness are over,” Essayli said. “Mr. Gascón lost an election over that. So the decision will be made by the voters.”

Political strategist Michael Trujillo questioned whether voters would accept Gascón’s return.

“After voters rejected Gascón as being a public safety official as our DA, do they really want Nithya Raman to backdoor him in as being the chief of police?” Trujillo told The Post.

Gascón joined the LAPD in 1978 and rose to assistant chief before leading police departments in Mesa, Arizona and San Francisco.

He later became San Francisco’s district attorney and won the Los Angeles County DA’s office in 2020.

His four years as LA’s top prosecutor sparked bitter battles over sentencing enhancements, juvenile prosecutions and policies critics considered too lenient.

Supporters argued his reforms reduced excessive punishment and racial disparities. Voters ousted him in 2024, electing Nathan Hochman.

Zine warned a Gascón appointment could drive officers into retirement or neighboring departments just as Los Angeles prepares for the Olympics.

“You’re gonna see a lot of them leaving before the Olympics. There’s no question,” he said.

“We don’t have enough officers now to maintain policing the city of Los Angeles, let alone the drain it’s gonna take on the Olympics.”

One current Los Angeles prosecutor delivered an equally stark assessment.

“Law enforcement hates him. Voters hate him. And Raman attempting to resurrect him should terrify residents of Los Angeles who suffered under the crime spree that took place while Gascón was the DA,” the prosecutor told The Post. “It’s a massive step backwards.”

On October 9, protesters gathered in New York City following the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Bronx. Lela Edgar/SOPA Images/AP

The ICE shooting of a 28-year-old in the Bronx Thursday has provoked an uproar among New Yorkers, who rushed to the streets in protest the night of the shooting, clashing with the New York Police Department. At least five protesters were arrested. And though members of the NYPD were not involved in the shooting, they were involved in arresting protesters and, some witnesses say, protecting ICE vehicles—despite a New York State law that prohibits local police departments from collaborating with the federal agency, as well as local “sanctuary city” laws.

Allies of Mayor Zohran Mamdani are now calling on his police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, to step down if ICE does not leave New York City.

Oscar Belgal, the man who was shot in his car while his five-year-old child sat in the backseat, is being hold in the MDC Brooklyn federal detention facility. He was shot at least seven times, according to police. Some ICE agents at the scene were dressed as construction workers; at least one carried a long gun. Belgal, according to his lawyers, was transported first to a local hospital, then to ICE custody in New Jersey and then to the federal prison in New York City in the hours following his shooting. He still has a bullet lodged in his body, one of his attorneys told a federal judge during a hearing Friday.

Though Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for the abolition of ICE shortly after the shooting, his New York Police Department seemed to coordinate with ICE agents, clearing the way for ICE vehicles to pass through a crowd of protesters at a hospital near the scene that evening.

“We cannot call ourselves a sanctuary city when the NYPD clears the path for ICE but goes after protesters like we saw last night,” Devashish Basnet of the New York Civil Liberties Union said at a rally Friday. “Our city can’t claim to stand up for us against the Trump regime when our police commissioner carries water for Homeland Security and smears the name of Oscar Belgal, like she did last night.”

That police commissioner, third-generation billionaire heiress Jessica Tisch, is a holdover from Eric Adams’ mayoral administration who has pushed to expand surveillance infrastructure in New York City. At a press conference Thursday, she highlighted Belgal’s two prior arrests.

Democratic Socialist allies of Mamdani called for Tisch to stop New York police officers from working with ICE either formally or informally—or, failing that, to step down in the aftermath of the shooting. The New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, which propelled Mamdani to his upset victory ten months ago, released a statement Friday saying that “ICE is a terrorist agency that must be expelled from New York City and abolished.”

“Jessica Tisch must get ICE out of New York and end NYPD complicity with these terrorists,” the group wrote. “If the commissioner can’t put a stop to these injustices, she must be fired.”

Congressional candidate Darializa Chevalier of the Bronx, who can be seen on video being shoved to the ground by NYPD officers at a protest the night of the shooting, also called for the police commissioner’s resignation on Friday morning, as did State Assemblymember Claire Valdez.

Yesterday, an ICE agent opened fire in Marble Hill. They shot a member of our community in the neck while he was in his car. His five-year-old kid was in a child seat in the back of the car when ICE agents fired at least 7 rounds into it. This was in the middle of the afternoon,…

“The NYPD spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers,” Chevalier wrote on social media. “Last night, the NYPD and Commissioner Tisch violated the spirit, if not the letter, of our sanctuary city policies and fueled the Trump Administration’s attempt to demonize our communities.”

Mamdani reportedly spent hours on the phone with President Donald Trump Friday attempting to negotiate Belgal’s release, but was unsuccessful.

Federal immigration officials, meanwhile, are defending the shooting—and arguing, as they often have in ICE shooting cases, that Belgal was only shot at because he “weaponized his vehicle.”

Marcos Charles, a top ICE official, said in a statement that Belgal “weaponized his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate toward other officers.” In the statement, Charles says that ICE agents transported Belgal to the hospital; NYPD body camera footage shows that police, not ICE agents, did so.

Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security, asserted that it was not ICE agents who put Belgal’s five-year-old son in danger by shooting into the car, but Belgal who put him in danger by putting him in the car in the first place.

“We weren’t aware the child was in the car,” Mullin said Friday, according to NBC News. “I can tell you that, but you know who was? Oscar.”

Embattled Cornell University is set to become the first Ivy League to offer bachelor’s degrees to jailbirds.

The Cornell Prison Education Program is launching a three-year Bachelor of Professional Studies program at Cayuga Correctional Facility in August 2027.

The medium-security prison for men in Moravia, NY, has housed notorious inmates, including transgender Big Apple serial killer Harvey Marcelin, an 88-year-old who spent 50 years behind bars until his release on parole in 2019.

He was sent away again last June for dismembering his latest victim, and is now in a maximum security prison east of Buffalo.

Cayuga prison is 20 miles from the Ithaca-based university, which is at the center of drug-fueled gang rape allegations at the Chi Phi fraternity house.

The first approved major will be in “Organizations, Markets and Society,” a degree that combines business, policy and social science studies.

A first cohort of 12 to 18 inmates will enroll in classes that will include economics, statistics, data analytics, entrepreneurship, marketing and finance, through a combination of self-paced learning and in-person sessions with Cornell professors at the prison for “discussion and networking.”

Prisoners with an associate’s degree, or the equivalent of two years of undergraduate education, will be eligible to apply, including inmates already housed at Cayuga and those seeking to transfer there.

Asked whether those convicted of violent crimes will be barred from enrolling, Cornell University said, “the antecedent background and ongoing conduct of participants in our program require that strict standards be met.”

“We do this work in the pursuit of breaking the cycles of crime and incarceration- making a safer and more just society for all,” a spokesperson for the Cornell Prison Education Program told The Post.

The Ivy’s prison program has already taught more than 1,000 inmates at Cayuga, Auburn and Five Points correctional facilities — 200 of which have completed an associate’s degree — since it was founded in 2001, giving them waived tuition and fees.

The school was awarded $750,000 over five years by the Manhattan DA’s office through its Criminal Justice Investment Initiative.

Last year’s classes included poetry, astronomy, creative writing, social psychology, world civilization, microeconomics, infectious diseases, introductory math and even meditation.

“We work to create something that feels much closer to a true college experience” said the Cornell Prison Education Program website, boasting about its extracurricular activities, includinga debate club at Cayuga that creates a “thoughtful and nonjudgmental atmosphere” focused on “liberating the mind.”

Meanwhile, New York AG Letitia James has been appointed special prosecutor to look into whether criminal charges should be filed against the seven Cornell fraternity brothers accused of drugging and sexually assaulting a female student.

Two of the defendants filed motions asking she be removed, saying she showed prejudice when she posted on social media that Jane Doe was a “survivor.”

The youth riots across France have already cost the country at least 30 million euros and have resulted in thousands of arrests, the federal government revealed on Friday.

According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities have arrested some 6,877 people since the start of the so-called student demonstrations in France last month. The MoJ revealed that 86 per cent of all those arrested during the riots have been under the age of 18.

So far, 2,376 people are facing charges, 65 per cent of whom have already been brought before a judge. Le Figaro reported that authorities have remanded 21 people in custody, including 15 adults and 6 minors.

Meanwhile, the Élysée Palace has reportedly estimated that the youth riots have cost “at least 30 million euros” ($33 million) since the demonstrations began in mid-September. Although the protests claimed to be about a supposed lack of investment in education, students have damaged hundreds of school facilities over the past month.

In the latest example, a school outside of Bordeaux was ransacked on Thursday amid a student protest. Local prosecutors claimed that around 30 to 40 people broke into the school, smashed or stole around a dozen computers worth around 3,000 euros a piece, before setting fires within the building. In total, the school estimates that it suffered “between €100,000 and €200,000” in damages.

Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray said on Friday that more than 100 school staff have been injured so far during the riots.

Police have also been a major target of the youth unrest. The Paris prosecutor’s office said that a 15-year-old boy will face juvenile court on February 23 for allegedly attacking a female police officer. During the viral altercation, people could be heard shouting “Wallah, kill her”.

The Ministry of Interior reported this week that the level of public street violence hit record levels in September, likely in party as a result of the youth demonstrations, with some 20,000 violent incidents being recorded last month alone, or 700 instances per day.

Although the protests appear to be growing and spreading, with similar demos staged in Belgium and Italy on Friday, the government reportedly expects the riots to slow.

However, a student at Paris 8 University told France24 on Thursday: “We’re here, we’re demonstrating, and we won’t stop. Until October, November, December if necessary. Nothing will stop us.”

Paris police have accused the far-left, including the radical La France Insoumise (France in Rebellion/LFI) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, of helping organise and spread the protests nationally.

Conversely, opponents, including U.S. President Donald Trump, said this week that the riots were a result of mass migration and the importation of millions of Muslims.

“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” he warned.

(Francisco Kjolseth  | The Salt Lake Tribune) People recite the rosary as they gather to oppose the death penalty at a free speech zone outside the Utah State Correctional Facility shortly before the scheduled execution of Taberon Honie in Salt Lake City, Wednesday, Aug. 7, 2024.

Comment

Add as Preferred Source

What happened to Christa Pike in a Tennessee prison late last month was much more than just a “botched execution.”

It was — and, if she is still alive when this is published, remains — an act of unspeakable torture.

And it focuses national attention on a question that should always remain before us, whether capital punishment is something that has any place in a civilized society.

It doesn’t.

The Utah Legislature last seriously considered the issue in 2022, when then-Rep. Lowry Snow and Sen. Dan McCay sponsored a bill to end the death penalty in the state. They argued, rightly, that capital punishment is too prone to serious error and, as public attention is drawn to ongoing legal battles, may only increase the anguish for the loved ones of those murdered.

The bill didn’t get out of committee.

It is unlikely that the Republican supermajority of the Legislature will consider the matter again any time soon. But the issue should always weigh on the conscience of our lawmakers, and the rest of us.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

The Tennessee case is an extreme one. Pike was 18 when she and two others murdered a classmate. Now 50, she was to die by lethal injection Sept. 30. After two attempts, she remained alive. After several days, she woke up in a hospital bed, unable to swallow, with swollen limbs and likely brain damage.

It is an experience no government should inflict on anyone, no matter what crime they have been convicted of.

Far less gruesome, but still of great concern, is the case of Douglas Stewart Carter. He walked out of a Utah jail late last month, 41 years after he was sentenced to death for a crime that, as more evidence unfolds, he may not have committed.

There are not very many executions in Utah, and only three prisoners remain on our death row. Those sent there are about as likely to die of old age as execution. There is little reason to believe that ending the death penalty would harm anyone.

If Utah will not join the majority of the civilized world in abolishing the death penalty, it must maintain its relatively open process of conducting capital cases and do everything humanly possible to be sure no innocent person is sent to their death at our hands. Or by torture.

And, as dreadful as it may be to consider, all Utahns must always be aware of, and responsible for, what the state does in our name.

A new proposal that could bring driverless rideshare vehicles to the streets of the nation’s capital is causing an uproar among union workers, drivers and religious leaders who fear the technology could eliminate jobs.

The protesters urged the council to reject the legislation, arguing that an influx of robotaxis would displace rideshare drivers.

“It’s bulls – – -,” Sabrina from Washington, D.C., said. “Let’s not bring robots taking my neighbor’s jobs. My folks that drive for a living, let’s just not take their jobs.”

Archeologists have located seven coffins containing human remains near the governor’s residence in Bismarck, North Dakota, a site where community members laid their loved ones to rest in the 1800s.

Crews found the coffins and a wooden box after Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Facilities Management Director Brandon Solberg said they investigated over 80 spots before concluding their fieldwork in early September, KFYR reported Monday.

OMB told People that preliminary analysis of the remains inside the coffins showed they were those of two women, two men, two teenage boys, and a toddler.

Per the KFYR article, “The discovery dates back to May 19, when contractors doing excavation on the southwest corner of the property near 4th Street and Boulevard Avenue first uncovered remains, coffin hardware, and fragments. That paused construction and led to a radar scan by the State Historical Society, followed by a dig that started Sept. 1.”

The archaeologists’ analysis of the remains and found items is expected to conclude early next year, and the remains will be carefully stored before they are expected to be reburied at a local cemetery.

The site was the city’s first community cemetery from 1873 until 1877, and the majority of the graves were believed to have been relocated to other cemeteries. However, it has since been discovered that others were left behind at the site.

According to State Historical Society of North Dakota spokesperson Kara Haff, “They had thought in the 1880s that they had exhumed everybody. There’s an article that says ‘we’ve moved everybody but two, and we expect that work to be done within the next week.’ Well, this has kind of proven otherwise.”

In a November 8, 2012 article on Public Prairie Newsroom, writer Jim Davis highlighted the historical aspects of the cemetery and the people buried there:

On this date in 1883, a reporter from the Bismarck Tribune visited the “Old Graveyard on the Hill” and, as he put it, “the meandering scribe walked leisurely about the weather-beaten slabs and soon was lost in wonderment and reflection.” He wrote about the phenomenal growth of the city and how not long ago these humble tombs were far distant from town. And he noted that “here amid these irregular and rapidly decaying wooden headboards… are the lowly graves of the pioneers and frontiersmen who died fighting the battles, which were the passports of those who are now enjoying the peace and luxury on the very ground for which they fell.”

…

The reporter went on to reflect on the plans to move the graves noting that “in a few short years they are forgotten, the weeds and wildflowers cover their graves and soon the music and laughter of wealthy, comfortable homes is heard above their bleaching bones.”

Indeed, KXNET reported in 2021 that abandoned cemeteries including the Bismarck site held some of the state’s history.

“These are the people that came and settled. These people paid a heavy sacrifice to start a life here, they helped build that county and the state of North Dakota,” Morton County Commissioner Andy Zachmeier told the outlet at the time.

The Dominican Republic native shot by ICE agents in The Bronx was a migrant with an alarming rap sheet — who apparently benefited from New York’s lax bail and sanctuary laws, allowing him to remain on the streets, according to sources and court records.

Oscar Belgal, 28, is believed to have entered the US illegally around 2022, robbed someone at gunpoint in Fordham Heights a year later, allegedly sold dangerous drugs within months of his conviction in 2025 and was even allegedly connected to a violent street gang.

None of that stopped Mayor Zohran Mamdani from referring to Belgal as “a New Yorker” in a raging tribute Thursday against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement — a label some Bronx locals took offense to.

“I don’t consider him a New Yorker,” fumed Bronx mom Migdalia Martinez, whose 12-year-old son Jacob Freytas was killed in gangland crossfire while riding his bike in July.

“The only thing I do consider him as is trash, nothing else but trash. And I don’t consider New York, my home, as trash,” she told The Post Friday.

Asked if Mamdani was wrong to call Belgal a New Yorker, Martinez said: “The mayor is wrong in many ways — that’s definitely one.”

Martinez’ son was tragically struck by a stray bullet in Mt. Eden, known Trinitarios territory, and authorities said they suspected the vicious gang was involved in the violence.

US Department of Homeland Security officials have said the same gang was involved in the July 2025 shooting of an off-duty CBP officer at Fort Washington Park — and that they were investigating alleged links to Belgal when they approached him Thursday.

Security footage showed plainclothes ICE agents rushing Belgal’s parked car in Marble Hill at around 4 p.m. with guns drawn, before he peeled away, and out of the view of the CCTV cameras.

Marcos Charles, the head of ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, said Belgal “accelerated” at the agents, “smashing” into two of them.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed the ICE agents were wearing body-worn cameras, but the feds didn’t immediately release the footage.

Federal sources said it’s believed Belgal slipped into the US with a migrant caravan in 2022 without encountering border patrol.

By December 2023, he’d been arrested for the armed robbery a month prior, according to authorities and court records.

Belgal was driving with two people in the backseat along Morris Avenue, when he turned and pointed a gun at them while demanding “give me your jewelry or I will shoot you,” according to the criminal complaint.

The victims handed over jewelry and about $500 cash, and Belgal was later caught — but then released without bail pending trial, records showed.

He pleaded guilty to a lesser rap of fourth-degree grand larceny in April 2025, with the deal landing him a mere month in jail and five years probation when he was sentenced in January, officials said.

That brush with the law apparently did little to reform Belgal — just months after his conviction he was arrested again in August 2025, this time for allegedly selling dangerous drugs like fentanyl, cocaine and heroin in a case that remains open.

Those drug charges were not bail-eligible — meaning Belgal was sprung after his arrest — but prosecutors requested and were granted the highest level of “supervised release,” law enforcement sources said.

But federal sources said detention detainer order was issued for Belgal after his arrest, meaning ICE requested he be handed over to the agency by local authorities — an ask that wasn’t honored.

Mullin said New York’s sanctuary laws — which largely bar local cooperation with federal immigration authorities — prevented them from catching Belgal, and endangered Americans.

“Sanctuary politicians create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for American citizens to be safe,” he said. “When you have sanctuary cities and politicians, you endanger the safety of the public.”

Belgal was back behind bars — this time in federal custody — Friday after an ICE agent shot him in the neck during the attempted arrest where he tried to drive off in his Honda SUV with his 5-year-old son in the backseat.

Intense bodycam footage from the NYPD showed cops rushing to the scene and finding ICE agents tending to the wounded Belgal, while his terrified son screamed in the background.

Seven bullets smashed through the car’s front, side and rear windows, but Belgal survived the injury and was rushed to a hospital. His son was physically unharmed and is now in the care of family.

It was the second time ICE had attempted to arrest Belgal — the agency tried in September, but officials said he managed to flee and get away.

His shooting sparked widespread outrage from lefty New York pols and anti-ICE protesters, who swarmed NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where cops brought Belgal in the aftermath — before he was swept away by the feds in a car.

“A New Yorker was shot by ICE agents in Marble Hill,” the mayor told reporters. “ICE agents surrounded the man’s vehicle before opening fire. They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There was no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents.

“You are hearing from New Yorkers right now — anguish, pain, anger — at the fact that here in this city, the world’s city, immigrants have to wake up every morning and not know if they can live the lives that they should be able to live,” he fumed.

But not every New Yorker shared the mayor’s views — including one of Belgal’s Upper Manhattan neighbors, who answered with a staunch “No” when asked if she considered him a New Yorker.

“What’s going on with the legal system, the jail, letting these people go after they have a whole list of convictions. This is a criminal. Why would you let this person out?” said Rodriguez, a longtime and elderly resident of Belgal’s old Inwood building. “These judges are very radical. We gotta vote red. That’s what I can say to you.”

Belgal was released from the hospital and sent to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn after a court hearing seeking his release Friday.

His name was bafflingly different across various court documents and agencies — which alternatively listed him as Belgal, Bengal or Bergal.

The Associated Press

An armored vehicle with a banner warning citizens against unlawful gathering stands near the venue of a youth protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Manish Swarup)
                
                    
                    Manish Swarup/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.

The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.

Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.

Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.

Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.

"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.

Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"

The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.

"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.

India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.

The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.

The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.

The commission and the government deny the allegations.

India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi

For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

After a loss in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial primary, Hong is focused on ensuring a Democratic trifecta in the state.

The Wisconsin gubernatorial race was one of the most closely watched Democratic primaries in the country this year, pitting a democratic socialist, state Rep. Francesca Hong, against Milwaukee Democrat David Crowley, who received the endorsement of the state’s sitting Democratic governor, Tony Evers.

Hong lost the race, setting up Crowley to face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in the general election this fall. But she’s already back on the campaign trail, this time trying to help Democrats win a trifecta in the state: the governor’s race and both legislative chambers.

Unifying the state’s voters to achieve that won’t be easy, though. Hong spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about her own loss, Evers’s role in it, and whether or not the voters who felt so passionate about her own campaign would find enough to love in Crowley’s campaign — in particular on the increasingly important issue of data centers.

Astead and Hong also talked about what Wisconsin means for the Democrats nationally, and what lessons the party should take from her race, including her loss.

“I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around,” Hong said. “But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign. I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic.”

Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Hong, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.

Part of the reason we wanted to come here was because we saw you were getting back on the campaign trail, and specifically around that idea of energizing Wisconsin toward a trifecta.

Now, just tell me the difference in terms of the importance of Democrats winning it all — not only the governor’s mansion, but both houses of the state legislature — versus just the governor’s mansion. How does that change the possibilities of what the party could do?

For the last 16 years, a Republican majority in the state legislature has meant that passing the types of policies that we know can drastically improve the lives of everyday folks here in Wisconsin stalled. And we have a historic opportunity to flip the assembly and the state Senate and hold the governor’s mansion and the entire executive branch to a Democratic majority, meaning the opportunity to pass the policies that the majority of our state supports — things like increasing minimum wage, things like legalizing marijuana, codifying abortion.

We also need to repeal Act 10 [which dramatically restricted collective bargaining rights for public-sector employees]. Wisconsin is where workers’ rights, things like unemployment insurance, Social Security were born, and we moved backwards with the Republican majority. That’s all on the table with the Democratic trifecta.

It also, though, raises the political standard of what Democrats would have to do to achieve that, and some of it goes through these more rural communities.

Why do we think the party has fallen behind in more rural communities, and what could be done to reverse that?

I think it’s important to look at what’s happened in the rural communities when we’ve seen manufacturing jobs leave the state, when we’ve seen fewer and fewer supports for our small farmers.

And so much of this — what connects it — is actually the growth of massive wealth and corporate control and corporate greed, and more people feeling the impacts of that. There’s an opportunity right now to say, ‘Hey, Republicans have been in the legislature, they’ve been in power, and things have not improved for you or your community … Now’s the opportunity to make sure that we’re actually able to see our shared Wisconsin values of working hard and taking care of our kids be reflected back in Madison through laws.’

So much of your campaign was focused on data centers, stopping data centers. Should I think of that as a rural issue?

I think the issue around data centers is an everyone issue. It’s a democracy issue. It’s people wanting to feel like there are folks who care about what happens to communities, and that they have control and an actual say in what happens in their communities.

To that point, is it a mistake for David Crowley, the Democratic nominee, to have not gone as far as you did and say, “We won’t be building more data centers for a period of time”?

He’s fighting for communities and community control when it comes to data centers.

But it’s not a moratorium.

But it’s not a moratorium. It isn’t, but he’s also committed to 100 percent renewable energy, clean energy to power data centers.

And achieving that is going to be incredibly difficult, and it is going to be the developers having to pay their own way, and these are things that he’s committed to that we know can slow down the growth and development of data centers.

Have you had time to reflect on your primary loss? If you had to diagnose, why do you think you lost?

I’m still doing a lot of reflection. But I think that I want to continue to look forward. And what I’ve learned from our election is that it’s so important to continue to stay grounded in becoming accessible to people. I think that as an organizer and an elected official, it’s my responsibility to continue to go to the people and remain very in touch with what’s going on on the ground.

I have a couple more questions about the nature of the loss. Evers’s endorsement changed that race, so much so that your opponent David Crowley was able even to win in some smaller communities, like places where you were pitching yourself as the voice of more rural communities.

Does that disprove any of this thesis around, say, data centers? If that was the top priority for Wisconsin voters, wouldn’t you be the nominee?

I think it wasn’t all rural communities. It wasn’t all suburban communities. We saw certain demographics but also ZIP codes where we outperformed David significantly.

And I think that where the governor’s endorsement played a bigger role was areas where he was also more popular.

Did it surprise you when Evers endorsed Crowley?

I was disappointed.

Why?

I was disappointed because I was getting a lot of feedback from folks who hadn’t committed to any candidate yet that this felt like the governor was putting his thumb on the scale.

I wanted to ask about electability, because it seemed as if Evers’s endorsement was about a fear that maybe you couldn’t win in November.

So much of the primary concern was around the DSA label, even campaigning with folks like Hasan Piker. In retrospect, was any of that a mistake?

We knew going in that we would have to encourage new voters to come out, folks who typically do not come out for primaries, quote-unquote low-propensity voters. And we knew that we would have to campaign in places where folks weren’t expecting to see a gubernatorial candidate. And those included Twitch streams.

Those also included going to dive bars and bowling alleys and making sure that we were accessible and shaping our policies based on what the people were telling us they wanted to see happen and also what they wanted to see out of their governor. I think electability… I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around.

But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign.

I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic, when Democrats need to be inspiring and project a vision where everyone can see themselves in it as everyday working-class folks.

When you’ve got a party that has struggled with elitism to then cave to an establishment narrative … being more afraid of labels when I’m hearing from people on the ground that they’re interested in solutions and solving problems, maybe somebody who knows the hustle of the service industry and running restaurants and has worked across the aisle to pass bipartisan legislation. There are ways that we can maneuver around labels and what the loudest narrative might be.

I wish our governor hadn’t fed into that.

To be fair, to your point, the establishment label doesn’t fully fit even someone like Crowley, who comes from a working-class background. But am I hearing that you think Evers’s move made your life in the general election more difficult?

Is it harder to re-inspire if young people who are invested in the Hong campaign think that the establishment squashed them out?

We still had over 300,000 votes. We lost by fewer than 4,000 votes. I had more votes than Evers did during his primary. That’s not squashing our voices.

We’re still here, and it’s so important that people find avenues to continue to exercise their voice and their new organizing power. And I’m definitely going to continue to work to make sure that we get results and that we win the trifecta, and that’s the most important thing we should be focusing on right now.

I hear why a trifecta matters in the state context, particularly the state policy.

If I’m someone, though, who’s not in Wisconsin, who’s just worried about Donald Trump running amok in Washington, why should I care if Democrats win the governor’s mansion and the state legislature? Does that matter for folks outside of the state?

Because we will start to see that when you feel government actually working and you see change happening in your lives, these are then voters who are going to continue to come out and vote for Democrats.

We’re a pivotal state when it comes to the federal elections as well. We’re actually in a swing district right now.

We have an opportunity, through Wisconsin, to actually start improving the brand for Democrats. And if we do that here, this trickles out to the rest of the country.

The premise being that delivering creates a connection for Democrats that is helpful in the presidential election, and it’s helpful in all these other ways too.

Yeah. We’re not going to be fighting every single midterm and presidential for our lives based on what’s happening in just one state.

But I think if we can start showing durable power for Democrats in a state like ours because of the policies that we’re prioritizing, and you have more folks coming out to vote for Democrats, that’s good for the health of democracy.

By Max Tillman

By Genevieve Blandin de Chalain

ABC New England

Topic:Child Care

A Tamworth father has spoken out after his child broke their femur at day care.  (ABC News Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

A Tamworth father's trust has been shattered after his five-year-old child suffered a broken femur while in care.

Darcy Galliano says emergency services were not contacted and the incident was not reported to authorities.

The NSW Early Learning Commissioner says they will work with Little Kindy to attempt to bring the operation up to standard during an enforced six-month closure.

Putting a child into the care of another requires parents to take a leap of faith.

For Tamworth father Darcy Galliano, that bond of trust was breached when he was called to collect his five-year-old son from childcare.

Staff at the centre told him the boy had a dislocated knee; his instincts as a parent told him otherwise.

"My son was in excruciating pain; it [looked] like he was going to blackout," Mr Galliano said.

"Me being a father, I realised his knee [wasn't] dislocated, but something else was wrong.

"When I lifted him, [the child's mother] could hear him scream from the Woolworths car park across the road."

According to the centres' incident report, medical personal were not contacted, and the incident was not reported to authorities.  (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

According to an incident report from the Little Kindy Childcare Centre seen by the ABC, Mr Galliano's son was attempting to jump over a wooden bench when he slipped and hit his left knee just before 3pm on September 1.

Staff applied an ice pack and contacted his mother.

According to the incident report, medical personnel were not contacted, and the incident was not reported to authorities.

Subsequent medical examinations revealed the child had suffered a spiral fracture to his left femur.

He underwent emergency surgery and will spend six months in a full leg cast.

Little Kindy Early was suspended for at least six months for multiple compliance breaches.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

Eight days after the incident, the NSW Early Learning Commission (ELC) closed the centre for six months, citing "ongoing non-compliance and child safety risks".

Among the breaches listed in the commission's report were a failure to maintain a safe environment, a failure to report incidents and inadequate child protection practices

NSW Early Learning Commissioner Darryl Currie also highlighted "unclean and hazardous areas presenting significant risks such as inadequate soft-fall surfacing beneath equipment and unstable or unsecured furniture" as well as "non-compliance with record-keeping and restriction of personal devices".

He said the centre was known to the regulator.

"There had been other compliance actions in the past, in this case," Mr Currie said.

"With regards to this matter, it was considered there was an immediate risk to children."

The NSW Early Learning Commission says it will work with Little Kindy to bring the business up to standard over the next six months.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

Mr Currie said the ELC would be "working with the provider to actually attempt to get them up to what is required to be able to provide a safe service in NSW".

Little Kindy operates three centres across Tamworth, in northern NSW, with its remaining centres in East and West Tamworth still operating.

It operates 24 centres across the country, with 13 in NSW.

Little Kindy has been contacted for comment.

The latest data shows a dramatic increase in the number of NSW centres having their approvals cancelled.

Between April 1 and June 30 this year, 174 services were delisted, compared to 20 in the same period last year.

But the ELC said all but one of those cancellations were due to the operator letting their approval lapse by not providing a service for more than 12 months.

Marg Rogers, an associate professor in early childhood education at the University of New England, said the temporary closure of a childcare centre in a regional town could have lasting effects on the community.

"We live in a childcare desert in all parts of Australia that are regional, remote or rural … [which] means there are at least three families applying for one space," she said.

Marg Rogers says closures can have major ripple effects in close-knit communities.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

"That means it has an implication on parents' ability to go to work, and to trust services.

"So a closure, even though it may be very justified, can have a huge ripple effect on the community."

Darcy Galliano fears for his son's long-term health and future job prospects due to his injury. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

Mr Galliano said his trust in others to care for his child had been shattered.

"He's a strong kid, and we can deal with it, but what happens if something happened to a six-month-old baby?' he said.

"Every other child and every other parent [enrolled at Little Kindy] has been impacted, and I'm sure there are single parents who have been displaced because of an inability to keep up to standards.
