nj-voter-rolls-noncitizens:
‘Ladies and gentlemen, … that’s called a cover-up,’ said Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-NJ, during a hearing on New Jersey’s dirty voter rolls.

Backed into a political corner, first-term New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill held a press conference earlier this summer to let everyone know that she was on top of a preventable assault on election integrity. The far-left politician posing as a moderate told reporters that she was “appalled by the reckless failures” that opened the door to thousands of noncitizens showing up on the Garden State’s voter rolls. She was equally disgusted by “the lack of transparency shown by those in charge at the time.”

“We have no evidence at this time that any elections were swayed,” Sherrill said.

Nearly two months later, we still don’t know whether that’s true. We still don’t know if the sparse information the Sherrill administration has provided is true. That’s because the Democrat has been less than transparent about a number of things.

“There’s still a lot we don’t know about, why this happened and why it took so long for the public to know about it,” Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who chairs the House Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Oversight, said this week during a Capitol Hill hearing on New Jersey’s voter registration debacle.

The 6,600 noncitizens on New Jersey's voter rolls show why we need voter ID requirements. pic.twitter.com/6rzV7ouynW

Titled “Restoring Election Integrity: Oversight of Voter Fraud in New Jersey,” the hearing gave Republicans on the subcommittee the chance to shine more light on an issue that Democrats desperately want to keep in the dark, while offering subcommittee Democrats like the ever race-baiting Rep. Jasmine Crockett the opportunity to turn the whole thing into a sideshow on Orange Man Bad. Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, the insufferable blowhard rep. from Maryland, jumped in for his own dose of Trump Derangement Syndrome theater.

In between the grandstanding, election integrity experts testified that the reported noncitizens on New Jersey’s voter rolls are likely just the “tip of the iceberg” in the Garden State — and in a lot of other states. That’s troubling less than 50 days until November’s general election.

In late July, Sherrill held her “it wasn’t me” press conference to confess that some 6,600 noncitizens had landed on New Jersey’s voter rolls in 2023 and 2024 — and about 400 went on to vote. She has since amended the numbers, asserting that only about 340 of the 6,600 “accidentally” registered noncitizens voted. The state has removed and placed approximately 5,100 of the wrongly registered in “deleted status,” the governor said. Another 1,450 or so have had their registration status changed to rejected, pending further review.

Sherill blames the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission’s longtime license printing vendor for what she has described as a software glitch. A spokeswoman for the firm, IDEMIA, which has contracts with several New Jersey agencies as well as the federal government, has said “there was no glitch or software error,” and the problem was not on the vendor’s end.

Van Drew said the company has been cooperating with his subcommittee’s investigation; Sherrill and her administration have not.

6,600 Noncitizens Found On New Jersey Voter Rolls As Democrats Fight Against Voter IDhttps://t.co/tWu257xfQP

Josh Findlay, senior fellow for secure elections policy at the America First Policy Institute, told the subcommittee that in some cases registering noncitizens to vote may have been a feature of the system, not a glitch.

“In New Jersey, the problem is built into the process,” Findlay said.

Election fraud, Findlay and others said, is a likely outcome of states like New Jersey that automatically register voters through their motor vehicle division, which also hands out driver’s license to illegal aliens.

In May 2021, the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission extended standard driver’s licenses and non-drive ID cards to noncitizens. The blue state’s Democrat-dominated legislature passed the bill, which was signed in December 2019 by then Gov. Phil Murphy, another far-left Democrat. The law opened license and ID access to more than 450,000 illegal aliens of driving age, the MVC estimated.

“Increased access to a driver license will do much to improve the lives of many New Jersey residents and enhance public safety,” MVC Chief Administrator Sue Fulton said at the time. “Our roads are safer when drivers are trained, tested, licensed, and insured.”

Fulton also assured a legislative committee that noncitizens would not be able to register to vote. She was wrong.

“The problem is much broader than the state admits,” Jason Sena, a New Jersey election law attorney, told the Judiciary oversight subcommittee.

Even if Sherrill is right about the vendor software error, Sena said the problem isn’t limited to the alleged “glitch.” He said public records show that election offices in Hudson and Bergen counties, two of New Jersey’s most densely populated counties, confirmed that noncitizens registered to vote before and after the timeframe in question —  between June 2023 and June 2024.

“Records show noncitizens were permitted to register to vote outside that timeframe and through other nonMVC methods, which confirms as a matter of fact that the problem is bigger than state has admitted,” Sena told the subcommittee.

Justin Riemer, president of Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections (RITE), testified that New Jersey did not design its automatic registration system to actually verify citizenship. The applicants were registered to vote even after they acknowledged that they were not citizens on the Motor Vehicle Commission form. The front end of the system, he told the subcommittee, relies solely on attestation of citizenship without any further verification.

The Garden State is by no means alone. Checking ‘yes’ on a box is all that stands between election integrity and diluting citizen votes in federal elections.

“New Jersey may be just the tip of the iceberg on this issue,” Findlay said of noncitizens showing up on the voter rolls in states that grant driver’s licenses to illegal immigrants.

According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 19 states and the District of Columbia have put laws on the books allowing illegal aliens to obtain driver’s licenses. Twenty-four states and D.C. operate automatic voter registration, which is supposed to automatically register “eligible individuals” to vote when they interact with participating government agencies. Election integrity experts say the overlap has proved problematic, as New Jersey’s noncitizens “glitch” underscores.

Oregon runs the same backend opt-out registration system as New Jersey. The Oregon Driver and Motor Vehicle division in 2024 “discovered” staff misidentified nearly 2,000 registrants as U.S. citizens on its voter rolls. More human “errors,” this time involving the drop-down menu in the system, according to the Oregon Department of Transportation.

“The mistake occurred in part because Oregon has allowed non-citizens to obtain driver’s licenses since 2019, and the DMV automatically registers most people to vote when they obtain a license or ID,” The Associated Press reported in September 2024, less than two months before the election.

Leftist California’s statewide voter registration system “does not contain” a specific cancellation reason for non-citizenship. So, as The Federalist reported last month, the secretary of state’s office can’t say how many noncitizens have been removed from its voter rolls, if any, because it doesn’t track that information.

California Admits It Doesn’t Track Noncitizens On Voter Rolls As Federal Law Requireshttps://t.co/K2tOUBfGEq

In Tim Walz’s Minnesota, illegal immigrants could cast ballots if they show a valid state driver’s license, granted to them thanks to Minnesota’s inclusive licensure law. During a Minnesota House Fraud Committee hearing last year, Republican Rep. Patti Anderson asked point blank if that was the case. Minnesota Elections Director Paul Linnell couldn’t provide a straight answer. Spoiler Alert: The answer effectively is yes.

“The exchange captures a significant issue facing Minnesota voters. If election officials cannot clearly explain how the system prevents ineligible voting, the public has every reason to question it,” Findlay wrote in a piece for Townhall. “A state’s election system that is lacking basic safeguards is not one to trust.”

Minnesota, ground zero in the government benefits fraud fight, also permits voters to “vouch” for as many as eight other people at the polls — no voter ID, just personal attestation.

The honor system.

The Republican National Committee late last month sent legal notices to New Jersey Secretary of State Dale Caldwell and election officials in Bergen, Essex, Hudson, Middlesex, Somerset, and Union counties after they failed to release records related to noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.

Findlay said that in May, two New Jersey senators noted individuals who identified themselves as noncitizens in the state’s online voter registration system were being prompted to vote. A month later the New Jersey GOP’s election integrity task force found hundreds of noncitizens registered to vote “at least 30 documented cases were uncovered of non-citizens illegally casting votes, in some cases in multiple elections and for many years.”

It would seem Sherrill and the people in her administration, as well as the Secretary of State’s office, knew about ineligible voters on the states voter rolls long before the governor finally came clean Sherrill blames her predecessor, Phil Murphy, who pulled a Sergeant Schultz from Hogan’s Heroes, claiming he knew nothing of the problem.

The GOP’s findings and a letter from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin raising concerns about noncitizens on New Jersey’s voter rolls forced Sherrill’s hand, election integrity experts say. The governor didn’t come forward in the spirit of transparency, as she has insisted. Her CYA actions are not “what accountable government looks like,” as she has said.

Sherrill has since doubled down, refusing to turn over to the Department of Justice the list of the hundreds of noncitizens she has acknowledged. She claims that the DOJ has “no legal basis.”

Not long after, U.S. Judge Zahid Quraishi (a Biden nominee) ruled that New Jersey does not have to release its unredacted voter rolls. It was the latest ruling rejecting similar DOJ requests in 30 states. New Jersey, like the others, have cited privacy concerns.

Republicans have said if the states have nothing to hide, they would release the information.

“Ladies and gentlemen, in political terms, that’s called a coverup. It means you don’t want people to know what’s really going on,” Van Drew said.

Stephen Richer, the former recorder for Arizona’s Maricopa County booted by voters in 2024 Republican primary election, told the subcommittee that noncitizens on voter rolls is a non-issue. Richer, a Republican shill for the leftist “voter rights” movement who worked to water down his office’s key election responsibilities as he was stepping out the door, noted audits that he says confirm his belief that “noncitizens voting in elections is a minute phenomenon.”

“Those who allege widespread noncitizens voting have little support for their position,” Richer, a senior fellow at the Trump-hating Cato Institute.

That argument from the left and some Republican stooges is getting harder to stand by in the wake of increasingly dirty voter rolls, the surge in illegal immigration under the Biden administration, and a well-funded left-wing infrastructure mass registering voters in heavy noncitizen parts of sanctuary cities across the country.

What is particularly disingenuous is the assertion that noncitizen voting is so minuscule it doesn’t impact the outcome of an election.

As Findlay noted, in 2025 alone at least three New Jersey elections were decided by one vote or resulted in a tie.

Elections can come down to one vote.So when hundreds of noncitizens cast ballots in New Jersey, we asked a pretty simple question: how did this happen?Instead of answers, the state has stonewalled us every step of the way. pic.twitter.com/UMu5g350xL

The Public Interest Legal Foundation’s website includes a running list of elections that ended in ties or were decided by a single vote. It has tracked 1,376 elections that have ended in ties nationally, and 533 that were decided by one vote mostly over the past 20 years. There have been 19 races — from New York to Hawaii — that have ended in a tie or in one-vote advantage this year alone. Many of the contests involved smaller elected posts on local boards, commissions and councils, but the tally includes referenda, primary and general elections for state legislative and judicial positions.

Even the Center for American Progress, launched in 2003 as the leftist alternative to the Heritage Foundation and dubbed by Time Magazine as “Obama’s Idea Factory in Washington,” has admonished that “key elections often come down to just a handful of votes.”

While Sherrill has said her administration has “no evidence at this time that any elections were swayed” by the hundreds of votes cast by noncitizens, we don’t know that. While the governor promised a “thorough, complete and fair investigation,” we have no assurances other than her word that such a “fair” investigation is happening. Based on New Jersey Democrats’ handling of the matter up until late July this year, why should anyone trust things will be different? Why, indeed, when New Jersey officials refuse to turn over the records.

The Federalist has filed an open records request with the state seeking the voter registration files in question and communications between Sherrill and others about the debacle.

Riemer said New Jersey’s voter roll debacle is why congress must act.

“First, it should pass real citizenship verification requirements,” the election integrity expert said, pointing to the SAVE America Act that has languished in the Republican-controlled Senate.

“The SAVE America Act would bar a state from registering those who do not provide documentary proof of citizenship. And because the New Jersey [noncitizen] applicants presented none it would have kept them off the rolls,” Riemer said.

New Jersey’s Voter Roll Chaos Makes The Best Case For The SAVE America Acthttps://t.co/q99aNLzxLa

But even narrower reforms directed specifically at motor vehicle registration would “plug a huge hole,” Riemer said. Automatic registration agencies should be required to offer voter registration only to individuals who provide proof of citizenship, he said. At the very least, they shouldn’t be offering registration to people who provide documents indicating they are not citizens.

States, he said, should have to remove noncitizens just as they must remove deceased and nonresident individuals from their voter rolls.

“It could also clarify that the National Voter Registration Act’s pre-election blackout periods restricting certain list maintenance activities do not apply to removing noncitizens,” Riemer recommended.

New Jersey state Sen.  Michael Testa, has called for the legislature to reconvene to pass a voter ID bill. Sherrill has signaled she would sign a voter ID bill if it lands on her desk.

But Van Drew said it comes down to a simple question: Whose side are you on? The congressman said if Sherrill and other Democrat governors truly value transparency and accountability, why do they refuse to open the books on their voter rolls?

“If there is nothing to hide, if there is nothing to see there, there should be no problem. Just turn it over,” he said.

A new SurveyUSA poll released this week shows Democrat Rep. Gabe Vasquez leading Republican challenger Greg Cunningham by three points in New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District, a margin inside the survey’s error range.

The KOB 4-commissioned poll put Vasquez at 46 percent and Cunningham at 43 percent among 554 likely voters, with 11 percent undecided and a margin of error of plus or minus 4.6 points.

That gap leaves the two candidates in a statistical tie. Vasquez, a two-term incumbent, sits below 50 percent against a first-time congressional challenger in a district Republicans have targeted as one of their strongest pickup opportunities on the 2026 map.

The poll showed the race splitting along familiar lines. Vasquez ran up his margins with women and Latino voters, leading by 13 and 20 points. Cunningham countered with men and white voters, up 5 and 11. A Marine combat veteran who later worked as an Albuquerque police detective, Cunningham wants to eat into the Latino number. “Hispanic culture is at its core a conservative culture,” he told Fox News.

The survey also measured President Donald Trump’s standing in the district, finding 39 percent viewed him favorably and 51 percent unfavorably.

Vasquez defeated former Rep. Yvette Herrell 52.1 percent to 47.9 percent in 2024, the same year Trump carried the district 49.9 percent to 48.1 percent. Ballotpedia lists the seat among 23 Trump-won districts Democrats are defending this year.

National Republicans have poured attention into the race. House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigned for Cunningham in New Mexico last week. The NRCC listed the district among five where its internal surveys showed the party leading or tied inside the margin of error.

Republicans have posted similar numbers in other targeted races, with an NRSC survey last week showing former Sen. John Sununu ahead by a point in New Hampshire’s Senate contest.

As of June 30, Vasquez had raised $3.78 million to Cunningham’s $1.51 million.

The stepson of Norway's Crown Prince Haakon has been found guilty of two counts of rape and other crimes.

Marius Borg Høiby, 29, has been sentenced to four years in prison by an Oslo court on Monday.

Høiby pleaded not guilty to the most severe accusations against him and can appeal the verdict.

The stepson of Norway's Crown Prince Haakon has been found guilty of two counts of rape and other crimes.

Marius Borg Høiby, 29, has been sentenced to four years in prison.

An Oslo court made the ruling on Monday.

Høiby was acquitted of two other counts of rape.

He pleaded not guilty to the most severe accusations against him, including rape, while admitting to some lesser ones, and can appeal against the verdict.

Høiby joined the royal family when his mother Mette-Marit married Haakon in 2001.

Norway's Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit. (Reuters: Leonhard Foeger)

Prosecutors had asked that Høiby should be sentenced to seven years and seven months of prison.

He watched the verdict via video link from prison but could not be seen or heard in the courtroom.

The seven-week trial detailed Høiby's drug addiction and self-made videos of sexual encounters. More than 800 electronic messages were entered into evidence.

One rape took place in the basement of the crown prince's family home, the court heard.

"The court finds it is proven she was not able to resist the action," Oslo District Court Judge Jon Sverdrup Efjestad said of the rape in the home basement, while reading the verdict.

Only one of the women accusing Høiby of rape was in court to hear the verdict.

She cried after the judge said Høiby was guilty of raping her and dabbed her eyes with a tissue her lawyer gave her.

The case, which coincided with Crown Princess Mette-Marit's apology for maintaining contact with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein after he was convicted in 2008, has contributed to a decline in popularity for the royals.

The latest release of the Epstein files has revealed the convicted child sex offender was in contact with members of — and people close to — monarchies across Europe and the Middle East.

Interest in the case was also boosted by the contrast between the picture-perfect family and the allegations heard in court, according to Ketil Raknes, an associate professor in political communication at the Kristiania University of Applied Sciences.

"It was … a perfect crisis for the royal family because they had two crises at the same time. And they had a lot of [criticism] for the way they handled the Epstein files," he said.

A Norstat survey published in February during the trial indicated the number of Norwegians favourable to the monarchy had fallen to a record low 60 per cent, down from 70 per cent in January.

The survey also showed a rise to 27 per cent from 19 per cent in those wanting a different system of governance.

In May, the royal family recovered somewhat in popularity, with 64 per cent supporting the monarchy and 23 per cent wanting a different system of governance.

Høiby (left) joined the royal family when his mother Mette-Marit (right) married Crown Prince Haakon in 2001. (AFP: Lise Aserud/NTB)

Høiby's sentence was delivered amid difficult personal circumstances for his mother, Mette-Marit, who is waiting for a lung transplant on Norway's national transplant list.

Mette-Marit suffers from pulmonary fibrosis, a condition that makes it increasingly difficult to breathe, and her health has severely deteriorated.

Without a transplant, she has about a year left to live, her doctors have said.

Her illness had changed people's perceptions ahead of the verdict, Mr Raknes said.

"People are seeing: 'OK, this is a family who's really struggling and this is not the time for … playing … the moral card as high as we maybe have done earlier in this case.'"

Relations between Italy's prime minister and President Trump have worsened considerably since 2025

There is an AI-generated meme doing the rounds on social media in Italy that shows Giorgia Meloni doing all the things you might expect from someone fresh out of a tough break-up.

In one fake photo she has a new haircut; in others she is imagined booking herself on a singles' holiday, training for a marathon and creating a profile on a dating app.

Of course none of the images are real, but the joke has landed because it captures  the very public political fall-out between the Italian prime minister and US President Donald Trump.

Their relationship has over the past few months gone from public attacks to personal insults and back again, cooling what used to be one of the most watched alliances in European politics.

It was not that long ago that Meloni was being called the "Trump whisperer", and she was the only European leader with a front-row seat at his January 2025 inauguration.

Last April, she was also the EU leader of choice to head to the White House for a meeting aimed at easing tensions over US tariffs on European goods.

For someone who started out on the fringes of Italian politics, with her roots in Italy's post-fascist tradition, and who has spent years trying to rebrand herself as a moderate, credible face of the European right, that closeness to Trump was never just seen by observers as a useful diplomatic tie.

It was proof, on the biggest stage available, that she belonged there.

But Trump's unpredictability has proved difficult for Meloni to handle, denting her credibility both nationally and internationally.

The first real fracture came in late March, when Italy's defence ministry refused to let US military aircraft bound for the Middle East use the Nato airbase at Sigonella in Sicily without parliamentary approval, a decision rooted in Italy's constitution and the public's deep opposition to the war.

Weeks later the row deepened.

Trump attacked Pope Leo XIV on Truth Social in April over the pontiff's criticism of the war, calling him "weak on crime".

This video can not be played

What Trump and Pope Leo XIV said about each other last April

Meloni, governing a deeply Catholic country, called the attack "unacceptable".

Trump did not take it well. "I'm shocked at her," he told Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I thought she had courage, but I was wrong." He added: "She is unacceptable... she is not the same person, Italy is not the same country."

By June things seemed to be getting better. At the G7 summit in Ãvian-les-Bains in France, Trump and Meloni were photographed deep in conversation on a sofa, and Italian officials spoke of a "clarifying discussion".

Meloni told reporters the atmosphere had been "very positive," with "no friction".

Giorgia Meloni was pictured talking to the US president on a sofa at the G7 summit in France

Journalists barely had time to file the story before it fell apart again.

Days later, Trump told Italian broadcaster La7 that Meloni had "begged" him for a photo at the summit, in a phone interview dubbed in Italian that was later published on the broadcaster's website in English.

"She wanted a picture with me so badly," Trump's Italian voiceover said. "I wouldn't have taken it, but I felt sorry for her."

Meloni did not wait long to respond. She posted a video, delivered in Italian, calling Trump's account "completely fabricated."

"I don't know why the president of the United States behaves this way toward his own allies," she said. "I can only say it's a pity he doesn't show the same resolve toward the enemies of the West... But there's one thing he must remember: neither I nor Italy ever beg."

'Neither I nor Italy ever beg': Meloni addressed Trump's remarks on the photo of the two of them at Evian

Italy's foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, cancelled a planned trip to Washington.

Reaction in Italy was swift and across the political spectrum.

Italian President Sergio Mattarella phoned her to express solidarity. Meloni's government colleagues and MPs called the remarks offensive, damaging to Italy's dignity and deserving of an apology, while opposition members condemned the comments as an unacceptable affront to the country as a whole.

Trump doubled down from Camp David, insisting on Truth Social that she had asked "over and over" for the photo and accusing her of trying to be "friends again" now that the US had "defeated Iran militarily".

Just as that dispute seemed to be cooling, a separate row re-opened over military bases.

Italy's Meloni says Trump 'made up' story that she 'begged' him for photo at G7

Meloni tells Trump to 'focus on your own popularity' as row escalates

Italian PM condemns ally Trump over 'unacceptable' Pope criticism

Last Wednesday, Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte told Fox News that around 500 US aircraft had taken off from American bases in Italy in support of "Operation Epic Fury", the codename for the US-Israeli campaign against Iran. It was part of what he described as broader European support running into thousands of flights across the continent.

Rome did not take it well.

Italy's defence ministry called Rutte's account "fallacious" and "totally misleading", insisting it had only ever authorised technical and logistical flights, not combat operations, and had refused any request that crossed that line.

A Nato spokesperson later clarified that Rutte had simply meant to highlight how allies, Italy included, had honoured existing bilateral basing agreements.

Those remarks have stirred a political row in Italy where Meloni's government has repeatedly said it did not authorise the use of Italian territory for direct military action against Iran.

For Meloni, who has had a difficult few months following her recent defeat in a constitutional referendum and faces an election in the coming year, some big questions remain.

How will she reposition herself on the international political spectrum? What next for her uneasy alliance with France's Emmanuel Macron, for so long her political "frenemy" but now increasingly important to her standing? And most of all, will she and Trump ever make up?

"This might be a tough situation to turn around," said Gianni Riotta, author and vice chairman of the Council for the United States and Italy.

"Meloni's ability to build a bridge now looks like a mere illusion, she couldn't stand between Europe and the US," he told the BBC.

"She tried to please both sides, on Ukraine, on tariffs. Then the Pope broke it: she had to back him, and Trump doesn't accept that. Trump has had a friend-or-foe outlook since his property days in New York, you're either with me or against me, and once that understanding broke down, he pushed harder, and Meloni played up her tough-woman image."

In Rome's diplomatic circles, nobody wants a full rupture.

Reports earlier this week suggested several government ministers were ready to skip the US Embassy's Independence Day reception at Villa Taverna, brought forward this year to 2 July, in solidarity with Meloni, who is not expected to attend regardless.

That mood has since softened. Tajani has said he will go "with my head held high", and allies of the prime minister now suggest the boycott talk has cooled into a quieter "everyone's free to do as they please".

But the real test will come at the Nato summit in Ankara early next month, when Trump and Meloni are due to be, for the first time since the G7, in the same room again.

meta_rank_one_surveillance:
Meta is testing face-recognition software built by a company that sells surveillance tools to police departments and the United States military, as it explores bringing the technology to its smart glasses, WIRED has learned.

The arrangement is documented in a software license, obtained by WIRED, that was issued by Rank One Computing—a Denver-based company that derives roughly 80 percent of its revenue from government clients—and is tied to a test version of the Meta AI app that powers Meta's Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses.

Rank One’s face recognition has been bought by the US Marshals Service, which uses it to confirm prisoners’ identities without fingerprinting them during transport, and by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service—the Navy’s police force—which purchased the company’s video tool, ROC Watch. Rank One developed long-range face recognition for US Special Operations Command under a government research contract, saying its software could identify a face from as far as a kilometer away. Police departments across the country use its algorithms too, embedded in tools they buy from other vendors.

The license is the first known evidence of a business relationship between Meta and Rank One, and it offers a rare look at the kind of technology Meta is weighing as it considers face recognition for a mass-market consumer device. It also shows how thin the line has grown between the surveillance technology sold to law enforcement and the military and the consumer products sold to everyone else.

Increasingly, the same companies, and the same underlying algorithms, serve both.

The license Meta acquired authorizes use of Rank One's face recognition along with its liveness detection, which checks whether a camera is seeing a real person rather than a photo or mask. It supports up to 10 million facial templates and remains active. Code reviewed by WIRED shows that remnants of Rank One’s integration—the routines that load its license and initialize its software—remained in a version of Meta’s app that shipped this month, dormant, to millions of consumers, alongside the company’s own face-recognition system.

None of the face-recognition systems tied to Meta's smart glasses were ever active for users. Meta deleted them from the app entirely on June 5, a day after WIRED revealed that the company had quietly built an unreleased face-recognition system, internally called NameTag, into the Meta AI app—the companion software for its smart glasses, downloaded to more than 50 million phones. The system was dormant and could not be accessed by users.

Meta would say almost nothing about the arrangement, declining to answer WIRED's questions about its relationship with Rank One. Meta would not say why it licensed the software, when the relationship began, or whether it is ongoing.

Rank One declined to comment for this story.

Rank One Computing was founded in 2015 by a group of engineers who had built face-recognition systems at the nonprofit research institute Noblis—work that included evaluating algorithms for a US intelligence research agency. The company went public on the Nasdaq in February.

Rank One's leadership is drawn from the senior ranks of law enforcement and intelligence. Its chief executive, B. Scott Swann, previously ran the FBI division that operates the bureau's biometric databases. Its board includes a former CIA deputy director for science and technology, a former head of the FBI's science and technology branch, and a former Pentagon official who stood up a multibillion-dollar special-capabilities office.

“There's a long history of military technologies becoming consumer products,” says Joseph Jerome, a former Meta Reality Labs policy official. “That's arguably the story of the internet.”

Rank One’s technology is already running in some notable places. The US Marshals Service has used a biometric identification kit built on Rank One's technology since 2021. In West Virginia, dozens of schools have used the software to screen faces at their entrances against the state's sex-offender registry, the company's CEO said in 2024. Its algorithm is also bundled inside products from DataWorks Plus, a South Carolina firm, and inside LexisNexis's Lumen platform, which lets police officers run face searches against state and regional image galleries and the FBI's national investigative database.

Like other face-recognition systems, Rank One's does not perform equally across demographic groups. In testing by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, a version of the company's algorithm produced false matches at sharply different rates depending on a person's sex and country of birth, which NIST uses as a proxy for race. Error rates were lowest for people born in Eastern Europe and tended to run higher for women than for men.

There are few national rules governing face recognition in the US. Many states require police to get a warrant before accessing such data, and more are folding biometric protections into their general consumer-privacy laws each year, says Eric Null, director of the Privacy and Data Project at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

“But consumer-facing companies clearly crave access to high-powered facial recognition technology,” he says. “And without proper checks, the risks of this tech becoming a common consumer product are significant and largely unbounded.”

Michael Cohen, the former fixer who once vowed to "take a bullet" for Donald Trump before helping to convict him, has done the once-unthinkable: he sat down and interviewed the president.

Cohen spoke with Trump by phone for roughly 40 minutes Thursday morning, with portions set to air that evening on his 77WABC radio show, "When You Know, You Know," and the rest on Sunday. It is, Cohen said, "the first public conversation between the president and myself in eight years."

And he is promising fireworks.

"There are things that he said to me that I have never heard before, it was a great interview, and people will be shocked when they hear it," Cohen told NBC News.

The reunion caps one of the most bitter breakups in modern politics.

Cohen pleaded guilty in 2018 to tax evasion and campaign-finance crimes tied to hush-money payments to women who alleged affairs with Trump, served three years, and became the star witness whose testimony helped convict Trump on 34 felony counts in 2024. For years afterward, Cohen called his old boss "a cheat, a liar, a fraud" and worse, while Trump branded him a "rat."

Cohen now casts the thaw as forgiveness.

"We rekindled our relationship because of a shared experience of betrayal," he said earlier this year, adding that "the ice between us, it didn't just melt, it broke."

Trump has leaned on Cohen's recent claims that he felt pressured to testify as he appeals his conviction, and Cohen's WABC home is owned by Trump ally John Catsimatidis.

michelle-milthorpe-farrer:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

Two years ago, frustrated with our local representation and the sense that politics wasn’t working the way it should, I did something unusual. I googled, “How do you become an independent?”

That simple search set off a chain of events I could never have predicted: more than 800 volunteers knocking on more than 17,000 doors, hundreds of thousands of conversations across one of the country’s largest electorates, in two federal election campaigns.

I did not win in Farrer. But if the major parties conclude from this latest campaign that independents, minor parties or political outsiders are the reason voters are abandoning them, they will have learnt entirely the wrong lesson. And Farrer was a warning.

For two years I travelled thousands of kilometres, from Albury to Wentworth, Griffith to Deniliquin, Hay to Corowa. I sat at kitchen tables, in community halls, sporting clubs, hospitals, businesses and farms. I spoke to lifelong Labor voters, lifelong Coalition voters, and people who had never voted.

The conversations were remarkably consistent. People were lavished with attention during election campaigns, and forgotten between them.

In March I visited Lankeys Creek – a small community of about 60 people, a camel farm and a bed and breakfast. Residents told me they were tired of being wheeled out every election cycle as an example of a community with poor mobile phone coverage. Their frustration was understandable. The infrastructure exists: the mobile tower that was supposed to solve the problem has been standing there for more than five years. Yet it remains switched off – the community is still waiting for reliable coverage.

For many, that tower has become a symbol of a broader problem.

Across the electorate, people spoke about hospitals that no longer meet community needs, water policy disconnected from the realities of farming, towns struggling to attract GPs. They told me about the trouble they had finding healthcare, childcare, aged care and housing.

Underlying all of this was a sense that decisions affecting regional communities were increasingly being made by people who neither understood, nor experienced, the consequences.

That is the source of disillusionment – not social media, independents or political divisions. It’s the feeling that your voice no longer matters. The rise of independents and minor parties is a symptom of that dissatisfaction.

Too often, the response from the major parties has been to ask why people are voting differently, rather than paying attention to what communities have been telling them for years.

The answer is there if they are prepared to listen. It is not complicated: return to your values, to policy shaped by genuine conversations with the people you are supposed to represent. Be present between elections, not just during them.

In another life, I may well have joined a political party. I grew up in a large extended family where politics was discussed around dinner tables, at family gatherings and on long country drives. One of my cousins worked for a Liberal prime minister and another worked for a Labor home affairs minister. One uncle was a National Party-affiliated country mayor, and his wife was president of the New South Wales Country Women’s Association. My mother is a lifelong National Party supporter, while my father, particularly in recent years, tended to vote for whichever candidate he believed would best represent his community.

Like many Australians, I was raised to respect the role of political parties in shaping our nation – they have delivered many of the reforms and institutions that underpin modern life. But many voters feel that parties are losing connection with the people they were created to serve.

In the conversations I had across Farrer, people were typically less interested in ideology than in effectiveness. They wanted representatives who understood their lives, listened to their concerns and would advocate for their communities. They wanted good ideas, regardless of where they came from.

The campaign also exposed a harder truth about the state of our public debate. We talk often about “misinformation” but ... much of what I encountered was not confusion or misunderstanding but deliberate distortion.

That’s what inspired me to become an independent. Not because I reject politics, but because I believe it works best when it is firmly grounded in the needs and interests of the people. Parties are becoming too focused on managing politics, and politics is now too often performative, designed for media cycles, social media clips and internal party audiences rather than trying to solve real problems for real people.

Throughout the campaign I often spoke about the difference between performative politics and genuine representation. Political acumen is not about mastering factional manoeuvring, nor is it learnt from spending decades inside a party machine. Effective representatives listen, understand complex issues, consult experts and build relationships to properly address community concerns. They know when to collaborate, when to challenge and who to bring to the table.

The media, too, has some reflecting to do. At times during the Farrer campaign, narratives appeared to matter more than facts. Some commentators chose not to use my name when discussing my candidacy – an approach that seemed dismissive. I was said to be unwilling to engage with the press; the reality was often quite different. As the field grew to 12 candidates, it was less possible to meaningfully examine all of us.

For weeks, a well-known journalist encouraged listeners to put me last on their ballot, repeatedly claiming I was “too scared” to do an interview. The truth was far less dramatic. I had agreed to participate, but the broadcaster was unavailable at the times I could make work in the middle of a campaign schedule that covered such a large electorate. Yet the narrative persisted.

It took weeks for our national broadcaster to consistently refer to me by my name, rather than reducing me to the label of a “Climate 200 teal”, despite my repeated explanations that I was a community independent with my own policies and views.

In interview after interview, I was required to account for every dollar of campaign funding in a way that was rarely demanded of other candidates. Commentators who had clearly never read my policy positions confidently told audiences what I believed, often getting it completely wrong.

Democracy works best when every candidate is subject to equal scrutiny and has equal opportunity to explain their ideas. That principle should not depend on party affiliation.

Social media has intensified the competition. It has democratised participation, giving communities typically overlooked by traditional media a bigger voice. It has also amplified division, outrage and hostility. My family and I experienced that firsthand.

This campaign exposed a hard truth about the state of our public debate. We talk often about “misinformation”, but much of what I encountered was not confusion or misunderstanding but deliberate distortion.

Nevertheless, what stood out the most for me in this campaign was not the negativity. It was the extraordinary goodwill shown by thousands of people who wanted to participate constructively in our democracy. I deliberately ran a positive campaign. Some people criticised me for that – apparently modern politics requires enemies. I disagree. We can advocate fiercely for our communities without hating those with whom we disagree. We can challenge ideas without dehumanising people. We can pursue change without abandoning decency.

More than 800 volunteers gave their time, energy and confidence. They were not flown in from party headquarters, nor directed by professional campaign organisations. They were local farmers, teachers, nurses, tradies, retirees, business owners, students and parents who believed their community deserved a stronger voice. They stood at polling booths, knocked on doors, hosted events and publicly backed something they believed in, often in front of neighbours, friends and colleagues who disagreed with them. That takes courage.

The public will eventually see every donation to my campaign because I have committed to transparency. They will not, however, see the full value of those volunteers. Nor will Australians truly be able to compare such efforts with the extensive resources deployed by the major parties, which can call on serving members of parliament, senators and their staff to visit polling booths and campaign trails across the country. Greater transparency would strengthen public confidence in our democratic processes.

Despite the intensity of the campaign, one thing is clear to me: Australia is fortunate to have strong democratic institutions. The election in Farrer was hard fought, highly scrutinised and ultimately decided by voters. That is exactly how it should be. I’ve congratulated One Nation on their historic victory. They successfully tapped into frustrations that many people in regional Australia feel. The challenge now is to convert that frustration into results. Representing anger is one thing. Finding solutions is another. The people of Farrer deserve to see the trust they have placed in their new representative rewarded. He has said they can judge him on how he has delivered on his priorities by the next election. They will.

What should concern the major parties is not who won the byelection but why they were barely part of the final contest.

In what was once considered one of the safest seats in Australia, the race was ultimately between an independent and One Nation. Communities that have long been taken for granted are no longer willing to accept being treated like safe seats that require little attention between elections. They are demanding representation, accountability and genuine engagement.

Trust cannot be rebuilt through advertising campaigns, sophisticated targeting or by blaming political outsiders. It is rebuilt the old-fashioned way: by showing up, listening, being accountable and remembering that politics is not about parties.

Regional Australians are not asking for special treatment. They are asking to be seen, heard and represented. If the political class continues to miss that message, Farrer will not be the last place to send it.

Michelle Milthorpe  is a strategic community leader and advocate from regional Australia. She was an independent candidate for Farrer at the 2025 federal election and the 2026 byelection.

michigan-vaccine-waiver-course:
What the course measures as learning is indistinguishable from agreement.

Parents across Michigan who want a nonmedical vaccine waiver for a child to attend school must now complete an online course before the local health department will certify the exemption. The course — built for the state by Michael Rubyan, a University of Michigan professor, and roughly 40 public health nurses — opens with a pre-training assessment. Before a parent has been shown a single slide, video, or fact, three statements appear:

I think vaccines are safe.

I think vaccines are important for children to have.

I think vaccines are effective.

Each is answered on a five-point scale: strongly agree, tend to agree, tend to disagree, strongly disagree, do not know. At the end of the course, a post-training assessment asks all three again. What the course measures as learning is indistinguishable from agreement.

Officials might point out that “do not know” is available, but that isn’t a refusal. It is a claim about one’s own state of knowledge, recorded as data. There is no “that is not the state’s business” button, and no explanation of where the answers go or who reviews them. The only privacy policy apparently available to parents is the county health agency’s HIPAA notice, which nowhere mentions the waiver process, the course, or attitudinal data.

A parent can see the compelled-speech problem without a lawyer’s help. But Michigan needn’t reach a constitutional question, because the rule the state is enforcing never authorized this in the first place.

Michigan’s vaccine exemption is both statutory and old. Under MCL 333.9215(2), a child is exempt if a parent “presents a written statement to the administrator of the child’s school … to the effect that the requirements of this part cannot be met because of religious convictions or other objection to immunization.” That is the whole test: a written statement, to the school. The legislature wrote “or other objection” deliberately, declining to ask what the objection is, whether it’s sincere, or whether it’s any good.

Now, here is question two of the module’s first graded section:

Maria is a parent in Michigan who wants to obtain a non-medical vaccine waiver for her child for religious reasons. To get a valid waiver in Michigan, Maria needs to:

— Ask her family doctor for a letter granting the waiver

— Ask a religious leader for a letter granting the waiver

— Attend a vaccine education session and get a waiver from the local health department

— Fill out and sign a waiver form at home and send it to the school

The third option is the “correct” choice. But the fourth describes what the 1978 statute actually requires. The administrative gloss has so thoroughly displaced the statute that the state now teaches parents the statutory text is the wrong answer. Current practice has drifted far enough from the statute that the statute now reads as a distractor option.

In 2014, with waiver rates climbing, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) added rule R 325.176(12). The rule states that “each nonmedical exemption” “shall be certified by the local health department that the individual received education on the risks of not receiving the vaccines being waived and the benefits of vaccination to the individual and the community.”

The performer of that duty is the health department, but the sentence assigns the parent nothing, and it prescribes no method of certification. MDHHS said as much in its own rulemaking file, anticipating that departments would provide education “using a variety of methods based on local needs.” At least one Michigan county health department has since argued the rule was misread from the start, and that simply mailing the required education to the parent would satisfy it.

But grant the state its strongest counterargument. Say that certifying a parent “received” education implies confirmable delivery. That would mean a parent must receive information and acknowledge receiving it. It does not get you within a hundred miles of a graded course with an attitude survey at both ends.

The rule was never primarily about educating anyone, however. MDHHS worried in its rulemaking file that “the ease of obtaining a non-medical exemption has been associated with an increased number of vaccine exemptions,” and so it built the rule to make exemptions harder. Suzanne Waltman of Michigan for Vaccine Choice, who learned of the rule the day it took effect, called it “a stealth move.”

Nor has the education changed many minds on the issue of vaccines. Juan Marquez, medical director for Livingston and Washtenaw counties, estimated that of roughly 10,000 waivers his two counties issued over 10 years, the in-person sessions that preceded the online course “changed the minds of maybe one or two people.”

Twice since 2014, lawmakers have been asked to write the requirement into the statute, in 2016 and again in 2024. Both bills died. So, the agency is enforcing by rule precisely what the legislature has declined to enact by statute, twice.

A third bill, House Bill 4552, introduced in June 2025 by 11 Republicans, would strip the department of any power to add requirements beyond the statute’s, and bar local health departments from demanding their own forms. It has sat without a hearing for nearly 15 months.

The simplest remedy is to rescind the 2014 rule and fall back on the 1978 statute. Short of that, enforce the rule as written: The department provides the education, the department certifies, and the parent is asked nothing.

If the module stays, three changes are the minimum. Give every attitudinal item an explicit option to decline to answer, so comprehension can be verified without compelled assent. Publish a privacy notice specific to the course before a parent answers the first question. And preserve a genuine in-person alternative in every county.

Nothing here turns on the merits of vaccination. The question is whether a state agency may condition a statutory right on a declaration of belief, and whether it owes an account of what it does with the data it compels.

As it stands a father who wants his daughter in school must first tell the state, on a five-point scale, what he thinks about vaccine safety. He may answer however he likes, but he may not decline to answer. And he will answer. His daughter needs the waiver, and no principle is worth a year of her childhood. He will click something, the state will record it, and later in the week he will have stopped thinking about it.

But the statute he is seeking to comply with only asks him for a written statement. It has never asked what he believes.

minions_pierre_coffin:
As the cute, yellow, gibberish-spouting creatures return in Minions & Monsters, the animator who voices them and has directed five of the films in the franchise will be taking your questions

Bello! Next month sees the return of everyone’s favourite small, cute, bright yellow blob assistants who spout international gibberish, as Minions & Monsters is released in time to clean up over the US Independence Day box office weekend.

It’s the seventh instalment in the Despicable Me franchise and the third standalone outing for Kevin, Stuart, Bob et al. The series has so far earned £12.3bn globally, of which box office accounts for about half (with merchandise sales slightly outstripping it, and DVD sales coming in at a mere $725m).

Pierre Coffin has directed all but two of these films, which he told the Guardian 11 years ago are all rigorously focus-grouped by his own children.

double quotation markEvery time I work on a scene or I work on the overall movie, I had my kids unconsciously in mind. Is that going to please them? Is it going to be funny for them? And if it is funny for them, is it going to be funny for their friends and their friends’ friends? I show them pretty much everything before it gets anywhere near the final cut so they also get to see all the sucky stuff I miserably fail on and the stuff I have doubts on.

“If it’s meant to be provoking some kind of a comedic reaction and if it fails then you say: ‘OK, back to the drawing board.’

“I totally trust their judgment and I suppose I use them in quite a sneaky way to try to get the truth out of them because my theory is that if you put kids in front of a movie or a TV series, they have a tendency to gullibly like everything and if they don’t like it, it’s only a sort of mild dislike. They’re not going to hate it; they’re just going to say it was good. It’s a subtle difference but if that’s the case you can tell something’s not quite right.”

The son of a French diplomat and an Indonesian novelist, Coffin spent his childhood in Cambodia and Japan before the family settled in a Parisian suburb in the 1970s.

Banned from watching TV, Coffin read a lot of comic books and did industrial quantities of doodling, before training as an animator in Paris and having a brief spell in London working on Steven Spielberg’s We’re Back! A Dinosaur’s Story (1993).

The evolution of the minions was an unexpected one. “In the first film, they were depicted as this big army of muscular thugs doing the dirty work of the arch villain Gru,” he said, “and we quickly realised that they were very unappealing and made Gru a totally unsympathetic anti-hero.

“To make him charming, we had this idea that he’d know all of his little helpers by their forenames, even though there were hundreds, and suddenly Gru was sympathetic. We then put goggles on them, added workers’ overalls, making them look like these subterranean mole men-type creatures, gave them an increasingly saturated yellow skin tone and then they became the Minions. And from that first scene we knew they gave the other characters counterbalance, had great comedic potential and were super cute.”

The new film – set in 1920s Hollywood – is pre-Gru, but does feature voice work from Jesse Eisenberg, Trey Parker, Allison Janney, Christoph Waltz and Jeff Bridges.

So please post your questions for Coffin in the comments below by 9.30am BST on 19 June and we’ll publish his responses as part of our regular reader interview series on 3 July.

Political Correspondent

The mystery surrounding Mitch McConnell deepened on Friday after his office refused to say whether a letter sent to President Donald Trump this week was personally signed by the missing Republican—or by autopen.

The July 28 letter, signed by McConnell and every member of Kentucky’s congressional delegation, urged Trump to approve a request from Kentucky governor Andy Beshear for a major disaster declaration following devastating flooding in the state.

But when the Daily Beast asked McConnell’s office if the signature was handwritten or produced using an autopen, his aides, led by the Senator’s $226,000-a-year chief of staff, Terry Carmack, declined to answer.

The silence adds another layer to the growing questions surrounding the 84-year-old senator, who has not been seen publicly since being hospitalized on June 14.

Trump and his allies have also spent months attacking former President Joe Biden over his use of an autopen to sign official documents, arguing that Americans deserve to know whether elected officials are personally signing important correspondence.

But as McConnell’s prolonged absence extends to another week, his office has offered little information beyond two statements and “proof of life” photographs, which some critics believe are AI-generated.

No video or live appearance has been provided, despite demands for greater transparency from Beshear and some of McConnell’s own Republican colleagues who rely on his vote in the Senate.

In one recent confrontation on Capitol Hill, his aides even sought security intervention while a reporter attempted to ask questions related to the senator’s health.

“Mitch McConnell cares about his legacy, and he’s ruining it,” Beshear said on his podcast on Wednesday.

“I don’t think it’s a positive legacy, but I know he thinks his legacy is being the longest-serving majority leader in the Senate’s history,” he continued. “Well, guess what? On his Wikipedia page five years from now, that’s going to be a paragraph. But what we’re going through right now is going to be a page.”

The letter with McConnell’s signature was sent to Trump on July 28, seeking presidential assistance after excessive flooding and tornadoes ravaged Kentucky, leaving six Kentuckians dead and many others injured.

“We write to call your attention to the July 23, 2026 letter from Governor Andy Beshear requesting a Major Disaster Declaration for the Commonwealth of Kentucky… We support this request in the strongest terms and ask for your immediate consideration so that relief may begin,” it says.

The letter featured McConnell’s signature in blue pen, alongside fellow Kentucky lawmakers including Rand Paul, James Comer, Thomas Massie, and Andie Barr.

But this in itself raised more questions—and accusations of a cover-up.

“McConnell claims to be in rehab only for mobility issues, but has a gorgeous signature,” Adam Cochran, a professor and policy consultant, wrote on X.

“An autopen signature is perfectly legal if a Senator of *sound mind* directed his staff to apply his signature.”

McConnell was rushed to the hospital on June 14 after a 911 call suggesting he’d had a heart attack, was unconscious, and had received CPR.

His office did not release a statement and a “proof of life photo” until July 12 – and only after ongoing questions and conspiracy theories about the senator, who some believed was either dead or on life support.

The statement claimed that McConnell—who has had several health problems over the years—had suffered a fall, briefly lost consciousness and later developed mild pneumonia before being transferred to rehabilitation.

But it is not clear if he was transferred to rehabilitation outside of GWU Hospital, or simply into the rehabilitation unit within the facility itself.

Adding to the mystery are the unmarked Capitol Police SUVs that the Daily Beast has observed for days outside the hospital, parked in the same spot.

“I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell said in his last “proof of life statement.”

50 million Africans living in 40 countries now have access to electricity for the first time thanks to a $15 billion development initiative by the World Bank and African Development Bank Group (ADB).

Called Mission 300, it aims to halve the number of people living without reliable electricity by 2030 by pioneering and working to finance and implement National Energy Compacts—fixed agendas for public ministries, commercial operators, and investors to coalesce around.

African development has been a mixed story since the end of colonialism, with shining examples of Botswana and post-war Rwanda clashing with others like Zimbabwe or Sierra Leone.

It’s a testament to these earlier failures that 600 million people could still be living without electricity on the continent. There’s nothing mysterious about why economies grow and why they don’t, in the same way that there’s nothing mysterious about how to finish an ultra-marathon: that doesn’t make it any easier.

Mission 300’s National Energy Compacts may finally be the ticket, at least regarding electrification. Indeed, households are receiving their first stable power supplies twice as frequently now as when Mission 300 began in 2024, and more than 30 countries have now created or are already working under a National Energy Compact.

In Tanzania, for example, 7.5 million people have gained access to power under Mission 300—a five-fold increase in the average annual pace of electrification prior to the initiative.

In Ethiopia, 4.6 million people have been connected, supported by reforms that made grid connections more affordable.

mississauga-data-centre-pause:
Mississauga.ca

Mississauga "one of the first big cities to address this matter and push back against this data rush”

Activists in Mississauga scored a victory in the fight against unregulated data centres last week after city council voted unanimously to pause new large digital infrastructure projects for the next year.

But despite their win, advocates are saying the job is far from over.

On September 16, Mississauga city council voted to enact an interim control by-law (ICBL) to effectively freeze any new data centre project in the city with a peak-power demand above 10 megawatts for up to a year, which is enough energy to power 10,000 homes.

During this pause, the city says it will conduct a “comprehensive policy review for major digital infrastructure facilities.”

Martin Reid, the councillor for Ward 9, where the data centre would be located, told PressProgress that he was really happy to see the ICBL get approved.

“Putting development before planning is never a good idea,” said Reid. “I think we landed at a good place as one of the first big cities to address this matter and push back against this data rush.”

The Toronto suburb was set to host a new 220,000+ square foot, 40 megawatt data centre in its north end. A development application to create the two storey data centre was received by the city at the end of 2025.

The company behind the application, Prologis, is a real estate investment trust with a client roster that includes Amazon, Fedex, and Walmart.

A data centre is a facility that hosts the cloud. They are warehouses full of computers that store personal data from the internet and are integral for the internet and artificial intelligence to function.

There has been an international backlash to data centres for their impact on power grids, drinking water, and carbon emissions. Last year in Ireland, data centres used 22% of the country’s electricity.

Ashly Batista from No AI Mississauga– a grassroots volunteer-run organization against the data centre– told PressProgress that given the current lack of regulations there is no way to tell what company would be using the data centre Prologis built going forward.

“With a colocation data centre like the one Prologis hopes to build, ensuring digital sovereignty can be even more difficult — to my understanding, there is nothing the city can do to legally track which companies leave or enter as tenants once the data centre is built,” said Batista. “[It] could be a Canadian firm now, and an American firm in five years.”

The data centre proposed in Mississauga is a colocation centre, meaning Prologis would build the facility and rent it out to other firms.

A spokesperson from Prologis told PressProgress they were disappointed by the decision from city council, and highlighted the 1,600 potential jobs the data centre would bring. The spokesperson said that Prologis currently didn’t have a client set to use the data centre, but were in talks with a large Canadian company.

Prologis also provided a statement shared with other news organizations indicating the company is reviewing council’s decision and considering next steps. The statement noted the federal government recently recognized data centres as “critical infrastructure” and established new principles for their “responsible development,” which Prologis has signed.

Mississauga’s fight over data centres has been ongoing for months. Over 300 people attended a contentious town hall on June 25. On July 29, after several hours of statements from Prologis and activists, council approved a motion directing staff to prepare an ICBL to pause development on digital infrastructure projects for up to one year.

Before the vote on September 16, several councillors spoke with a dozen or so anti-data centre activists outside Mississauga city hall.

Councillors Martin Reid, Sue McFadden, Joe Horneck, Alvin Tedjo, and Dipika Damerla told activists what to expect from council proceedings: that they’d skip the deputations and get the interim control by-law passed.

City councillor and mayoral candidate Dipika Damerla congratulated the activists, calling this “their victory.”

The agenda item for the ICBL was pushed to the top of the council meeting, and unanimously passed. Activists filed out of the council chambers and debriefed with each other in the city hall foyer, sharing congratulations, talking about next steps and giving each other a chance to say what they couldn’t in council.

Although the activists were pleased with the decision to enact the ICBL, several in attendance were unhappy that they couldn’t say their piece about data centres.

“While we’re very happy about the interim control bylaw, obviously it’s fantastic, it is a bit unfortunate to see the way that our opinions and our voices weren’t allowed to be heard,” Batista said. “I don’t know anyone who didn’t have at least a little bit of disappointment about not speaking.”

Some activists pointed to the imminent municipal election on October 26 as a potential reason why council may have wanted to keep things as uncontroversial as possible.

Rahul Mehta, an activist with Sustainable Mississauga and council candidate for Ward 8, said that passing the by-law can’t be the end of the city listening to the public’s opinion on this issue.

“We want to see consultations, we want to see town halls, we want to see dialogue between different proponents,” said Mehta. “We don’t want this to be a vote that was expedited simply because it’s an election year.”

Councillor Reid said that the council thought by expediting the vote, they’d run less of a risk of having the ICBL not pass.

“In those deputations you [the residents] were saying ‘we want an ICBL,’ Wednesday was saying ‘we heard you’,” said Reid. “Let’s expedite this and get it done as quick as possible and get your desired outcome as fast as possible.”

The ICBL gives the city the time to research, develop and enact regulations for data centres to protect the well-being of people living in the communities where the centres are built. But questions remain about what role the provincial and federal governments will play in data centre development.

Doug Ford’s provincial government has repeatedly circumvented the authority of municipal governments, overruled the city of Toronto on multiple occasions, ripping out bike lanes in Toronto, and removed the city’s stake in Billy Bishop airport when it opposed expansion. Ford also threatened to use the notwithstanding clause to reverse an Ontario Superior Court decision on a Kitchener encampment if it wasn’t successfully appealed.

“What is going to be their role as they create their own frameworks and their own sets of rules and regulations?” Mehta asked. “Will they overrule each other? Will they sidestep some of the rules we have and say ours are no longer needed because theirs go on top?”

A pitch deck from the federal government for international investors detailing Canada’s artificial intelligence “ecosystem” obtained through an ATIP has also been circulated to activist groups. The deck refers to Canada as “an emerging data centre powerhouse” and “the foremost destination for new data centres.”

The province launched a data centre “playbook” on August 13, to “attract data centre investment, create jobs and deliver real benefits to host communities.” In a general committee meeting on September 9, Mississauga city planner Shaesta Hussen described the playbook as “very high level” and that it “lacks details.” Another staff member added that there needs to be clear guidelines from the province, as well as potential legislative changes to the Planning Act, to allow cities to regulate data centres.

“Whether cities want to regulate these is a second question as well,” the staff member said.

In the same meeting, Mississauga mayor Carolyn Parrish suggested that maybe the province should be in charge of regulating these data centres.

“I think somebody at Queen’s Park should be regulating this, rather than us, and give us very clear guidelines so that we don’t have false information circulating,” Parrish said.

Parrish added that given issues with tariffs the city would soon be under pressure to accept data centres, “whether we like it or not.”

In spite of the uncertainty, advocates recognize the victory accomplished in Mississauga. Over the course of the next year, the city will create regulations for data centres, in no small part because of relentless and consistent grassroots community organizing.

“We had councillors talk about the fact that the amount of people in seats filling the chambers was part of what influenced their decision during the first vote,” said Batista.

“So your voice definitely matters, try to use it when you’re allowed to.”

Mistral on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) released the Mistral Large 4 AI model, also known as Le Chonk, to compete against the strongest open-source models, according to the company.

The French AI startup company said that Le Chonk is a 1 trillion-parameter multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters, and described it as its “largest and most capable model to date”.

By comparison, Chinese AI company Moonshot’s Kimi K3 model — launched this July — is a 2.8 trillion-parameter model.

“The model we’re actually announcing today ‌is ⁠actually above the Chinese models on certain aspects, including cyber. So ⁠the narrative that Europe cannot compete is something that is not true,” CEO Artur Mensch told Reuters at a launch event.

The Le Chonk model’s strengths include coding, agentic workflows, and multimodal understanding. Mistral noted that it “significantly” outperforms open-weight models developed in the US or Europe, and that it is fluent in over 160 languages.

Other areas where it excels include cybersecurity, finance, law, and visual grounding.

Mistral explained that its new model was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs, in Mistral data centres in Europe.

The company pitched the new model as a counterweight to the closed frontier models in the U.S. that have been criticised for a lack of accessibility, and the open-weight Chinese models from firms such as DeepSeek and Moonshot that have sparked security concerns in the West.

Mistral further shared that ML4’s combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% put it ahead of Chinese rivals DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Le Chonk’s open weights are expected to release at the end of October, as per Mistral, and the model is currently available as a public preview.

“We will release the weights by the end of the month. Until then, we are red-teaming the model in real-world settings with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners, and state authorities, who will access the same model with reduced moderation and expanded cyber capabilities,” stated Mistral in a blog post.

The French company announced that users could expect “a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models” from here on.

“The pace of progress from here will be fast,” Mistral noted in the blog post, in what is a stark departure from the messages of U.S. AI company CEOs who have been calling for paced frontier development and forced slowdowns in AI capability.
