India has two films competing for the Best International Feature Film Oscar for the first time, following a historic rule change by the Academy.
Marathi thriller 'Gondhal' is India's official submission, selected from 33 contenders for the 99th Academy Awards.
Nagaland drama 'Angh' earned its place after winning the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival.
A new Academy rule allows non-English-language films to qualify independently by winning one of six designated prizes at major international festivals.
The Toronto jury praised 'Angh' "for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking and deeply resonant portrait of a world."

For decades, the route to the Oscar for Best International Feature Film has been straightforward: each country selects one film to represent it at the Academy Awards.

But this year, India has two films in the race.

Marathi thriller Gondhal, directed by Santosh Davakhar, was selected from 33 contenders as India's official submission for the 99th Academy Awards, to be held in March next year. But Theja Rio's Nagaland-set drama Angh has now secured its own place in contention after winning the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday.

Oscars 2027: All the Arab films submitted for Best International Feature

This is owing to a significant rule change introduced by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the 2027 Oscars, creating a second pathway into the best international feature category.

Under the new rules, countries and regions can continue to select one official submission through their Academy-approved selection committees. However, non-English-language films can now also be submitted if they win one of six designated prizes at major international film festivals.

Those are the Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival, the Best Film award at the Busan International Film Festival, Palme d'Or at Cannes, World Cinema Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, Platform Prize at Toronto and Golden Lion at Venice.

As such, Angh's victory in Toronto has given the film a separate route into the same Oscar race as Gondhal.

Angh is set in Nagaland in north-east India, a region rarely depicted on screen. Set in the 1960s, it centres on an ageing Konyak village chief and his son as their traditional way of life is threatened by the arrival of an American Christian missionary.

The film is Rio's feature directorial debut and grew out of a short film he made in 2018. It was among the films considered for India's official Oscar submission before Gondhal was ultimately selected.

The Toronto International Film Festival jury praised Angh “for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking and deeply resonant portrait of a world”.

“We praise the filmmaker’s vision, audacity and courage,” the jury said.

Gondhal is rooted in the traditional Maharashtrian ritual and folk performance from which it takes its name.

Set during a traditional Gondhal ceremony in rural Maharashtra, it centres on Suman, who is desperate to escape an abusive marriage, and conspires with her lover to kill her husband and start a new life.

It was chosen by the Film Federation of India from 33 submissions to represent the country at the Oscars.

Davakhar won the Silver Peacock for Best Director for the film at the International Film Festival of India.

The Academy announced the change in May as part of a broader overhaul of its rules for the 99th Oscars.

Previously, the international feature award category relied on national or regional selection committees, meaning that even internationally acclaimed films could miss out on consideration if another production was chosen to represent their country.

The new system retains that national selection process but supplements it with the six festival awards, allowing qualifying films to be submitted independently.

The change is particularly significant for countries with large and linguistically diverse film industries such as India, where dozens of films can compete for a single official submission slot each year.

There has also been another significant change to the category. From the 99th Oscars, the film itself, rather than its country or region, will officially be credited as the nominee, with the director accepting the award on behalf of its creative team.

Gondhal and Angh must still make it through the Academy's voting process before reaching the final five nominees for best international feature.

The deadline for films to be submitted for best international feature is September 30. Preliminary voting will then take place from December 7 to 11, with the shortlist announced on December 15.

Nominations voting will run from January 11 to 15, with the final five nominees for the category announced alongside the other Oscar nominations on January 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will take place on March 14, 2027.

The spiky agave plant was traditionally used as fencing in India

A desert plant changed the life of Masapalli Venkatesh.

His 10-acre farm in Kandukur is on the Deccan Plateau, which covers a large part of southern and central India. There he grows tomatoes, peanuts and corn.

But in 2010 he was approached by traders looking for a very different crop - the cactus agave americana.

For him and his fellow farmers the agave cactus was just a "stubborn, valueless weed" - planted as fencing to keep wild animals off their crops.

But it is also part of the family of agave plants that feed the $15bn (Â£11bn) global market for tequila and mezcal.

In Mexico, blue agave is farmed to supply the tequila industry. Only plants from select areas, mainly in the state of Jalisco, can be used to make tequila.

Unlike in Mexico, where vast plantations dominate the landscape, nobody grows agave commercially in India - at least not yet.

Instead, Indian farmers and entrepreneurs collect and process agave that grows wild.

For some, like Venkatesh, it's a welcome source of extra income - earning it the name "blue gold".

These days Venkatesh ranges across an area of 100km (60 miles), co-ordinating villagers and farmers.

"By combining the yields of multiple farms, I ensure a steady, high-volume supply that distilleries are willing to pay a premium for," he says.

Harvesting agave plants is a skilled job.

The most important part of the plant is the heart, known as the piÃ±a because it resembles a giant pineapple.

Skilled workers reveal the heart by chopping off the spiky leaves. But getting the timing of the harvest right is crucial.

Once the plant decides to bloom, it channels its entire reserve of accumulated sugar upward into the stalk in a matter of days.

If the flower blooms, the sugar is completely depleted, making the piÃ±a useless for alcohol production.

"Gatherers must accurately identify the exact pre-blooming window to harvest the plant at its absolute peak sugar capacity, making the timing of the harvest incredibly narrow," says Rakshay Dhariwal, founder and managing director of the distiller Maya Pistola Agavepura.

Once harvested agave plants have to be rushed to the processing plant

Once harvested, the clock starts ticking. The piÃ±as must get to a pressure cooker within 24 hours, where the sugars can be extracted.

"Any transport delay can risk ruining the batch. If it takes longer than 24 hours, the internal sugars begin to rot and ferment unpredictably, destroying the delicate flavour profile needed for premium spirits," says Dhariwal.

And transportation is not straightforward, as agave suppliers are scattered across vast distances in states like Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Andhra Pradesh.

"Brands like us cannot simply order from a centralized farming cooperative. We rely on networks of local aggregators to scout, negotiate for, and harvest individual patches of semi-wild agave growing on marginal lands or rural property boundaries," he says.

It's all helping to meet a rising demand for agave spirits. According to Dhariwal, the Indian market for agave spirits is growing at a rate of 31%.

"It's only been a few years now, that India's finally caught the tequila bug," says Vikram Achanta, co-founder of 30 Best Bars India.

"Producers are beginning to experiment with it seriously, and there's a consumer base today that is far more open to exploring new spirits than before," he says.

Agave drinks are unlikely to replace whisky, India's favourite spirit, he says, but they could carve out a market.

"New brands are interesting examples of early experimentation, especially in how they're working with wild agave from the Deccan Plateau and beginning to shape what an Indian agave identity could look like. It's still early days, but they're helping move the category from curiosity to something more credible," he adds.

Indian distiller Maya Pistola Agavepura uses local agave plants

Desmond Nazareth is a pioneer in the Indian agave spirit industry.  His company, Agave India, launched India's first homegrown agave spirit in 2011.

"What started as kitchen experiments eventually became India's first craft agave distillery after nearly 12 years of research and experimentation," he says.

"We were making Indian agave spirit long before the market was ready for it. It was a craft business way ahead of its time."

Now he's taking a scientific approach to developing the industry.

"We have taken satellite images of areas where agave already grows successfully, then matched those environmental patterns with nearby regions to identify more suitable land. That's important because agave grows for 9â13 years. If you plant in the wrong area, you lose a decade," he says.

With growing demand is there a danger that India's wild supplies of agave will become depleted? Not for at least five years, and probably longer says agricultural expert, Miguel Braganza.

He points out that India's domestic industry is still tiny, with just one plant for processing agave hearts, which belongs to Nazareth's Agave India.

Also, the wild agave plant is very good at propagating itself.

"When you look at a wild agave, you aren't just looking at a single plant. Beneath the soil, the mother agave is incredibly busy. Throughout her 10-to-20-year life, she secretly sends out long root-runners into the earth," says Braganza,

And those roots are the source of future plants.

"Every few feet, a mini-clone of herself pops out. Those baby plants grow their own roots and become independent plants, slowly forming large agave colonies over time. So one plant can naturally turn into dozens of plants across an area without any human help,"

India's Loca Loka brand produces tequila in Mexico

India's wild supply of agave plants is far from ideal, points out Indian entrepreneur Sree Harsha Vadlamudi.

Unlike farmed plants the wild plants are "geneticially inconsistent" he says.

"That means sugar yields fluctuate... and that means alcohol output changes. So standardizing production becomes difficult. Mexico solved this over decades through selective breeding. India hasn't yet," he says.

Vadlamudi co-founded tequila brand Loca Loka. It uses Mexican blue agave from the tequila heartland of Jalisco.

"We wanted to leverage the rich, iron-heavy red soil left behind by ancient volcanic eruptions in Jalisco, Mexico. This unique terroir imparts a distinct flavour profile to the agave that cannot be replicated by growing the same seeds in Indian soil," Vadlamudi says.

Mexico's large, organised agave farms are a sharp contrast to India's informal system.

Those big, rich farms can afford hi-tech farming techniques. Some combine drones and AI systems to monitor their crops.

"Drones scan thousands of hectares to accurately count individual crops, assess plant health, spot early signs of disease, and monitor the growth of the piÃ±a to predict the absolute perfect window for harvesting," Vadlamudi says.

Blue agave farms in Jalisco are the foundation of Mexico's tequila industry

Such investment is still a long way off for Indian producers.

Nazareth accepts that building a significant agave spirit industry will take time. But he's confident.

"India could absolutely become a major agave economy. The Deccan Plateau alone has millions of acres suitable for cultivation. We could theoretically rival Mexico if there's long-term vision and patience."

Williams’ lawyer, Robert Kenner, claimed prosecutors tried to “defame” the elected official, just 10 months into his term as Stockbridge mayor, and warned of the repercussions of removing him from office.

“You will be setting a dangerous precedent by removing an elected official that the citizens of this city have duly elected by allowing people to come up with all kinds of accusations, innuendos that are unfounded,” Kenner said.

“Just because you may not like how he moves, you may not like the way he speaks, you may not like the way he speaks, you may not like his lifestyle, but is that enough to take a draconian action to remove the city mayor?”

Robbie Ashe, one of the city’s prosecutors, had argued that the allegations that had been leveled against the mayor constituted a betrayal of public trust. But Williams has not been slapped with criminal charges.

Another resident said he doesn’t believe all the allegations leveled against Williams were true.

BERLIN — Germany is quietly building a national system linking combat aircraft, drones, satellites and sensors after killing a joint project with France and Spain to build a sixth-generation fighter jet.

Internal German defense ministry documents seen by POLITICO show Berlin is preparing a €580 million contract for Helsing, the Munich-based defense company, to develop a core software-and-test architecture for the Combat Fighter System Nucleus, or CFSN for short.

In other documents seen by POLITICO, the contract favors Helsing despite the defense ministry's concerns about locking the development to a single contractor. The ministry also indicates it plans to avoid additional parliamentary scrutiny.

Under the contract, Helsing is supposed to deliver two experimental uncrewed combat aircraft, two ground control stations, a ground segment, operating system software, autonomy software and a government-owned reference architecture that other systems could plug into.

CFSN is a German effort to build its own project on the remnants of the failed Future Combat Air System. When the jet-fighter element of FCAS was scrapped, both France and Germany underlined that the associated combat cloud connecting warplanes with sensors and drones would continue; what's unclear is if that effort will be multinational or done by individual countries.

The documents show that the ministry is treating CFSN as more than a narrow research project. One paper describes it as a backbone for future networked air warfare, but officials see the project as politically delicate.

One internal note warned of “considerable communication needs.” Among the points flagged is why the contract is needed despite unresolved decisions on the wider future combat-air program and how much cash Germany's parliament is asked to approve.

A defense ministry spokesperson told POLITICO the ministry does not comment on procurement projects and companies before pending parliamentary consideration. Helsing declined to comment.

The planned Helsing contract would be one of the first major industrial moves to see what can still be salvaged from the wider FCAS concept.

In modern air war, the jet fighter is only part of the system. An increasingly decisive layer is the software that lets crewed fighters, drones, sensors and weapons share information and act together.

That was supposed to be one of the selling points of FCAS, linking the Next Generation Fighter with the combat cloud. However, the aircraft part of the project collapsed due to deep disagreements between French and German contractors.

According to internal ministry assessments of the project seen by POLITICO, Germany says the CFSN architecture should avoid dependence on any one supplier. Yet the first step is to award the contract to a single company.

One procurement note says four industrial options were examined as potential main contractors: Airbus Defence and Space, Helsing, MBDA Germany and Diehl Defence. According to the note, only Helsing provided all the required evidence and answers.

The documents list MBDA Germany as one of Helsing’s subcontractors, alongside its subsidiary Grob Aircraft, sensor producer Hensoldt and electronics and communications specialist Rohde & Schwarz.

The ministry is also citing a national-security exemption from normal EU procurement rules, arguing that a standard tender would risk Germany’s security interests.

Another procurement note says that the second stage of the contract in 2027 would not need a separate approval by the parliament; under normal rules, the Bundestag's budget committee has to sign off on all projects worth more than €25 million.

In the past, parliament has strongly objected to the defense ministry's efforts to minimize its role in approving projects.

The form of Helsing's contract may also draw parliament's attention. Instead of buying a finished product at a fixed price, the state will reimburse the company for the costs of experimental work.

The documents acknowledge that cost assumptions are not fully clear before the contract is signed. However, they say the risk should be contained through an overall price ceiling and caps on work packages.

The documents seen by POLITICO suggest Berlin is no longer waiting for a revived multinational FCAS. Instead, Germany is moving ahead with a national air-combat architecture that could shape how future European drones, aircraft and sensors operate together.

Internal divisions over whether to buy Boeing Australia’s Ghost Bat or wait for European alternatives could delay Germany’s plan to field a new combat drone.

Germany’s defense minister is preparing to visit Washington and Texas in September after an attempted Pentagon meeting fell through in May.

Merz and Weidel faced off for the first time since Sunday's AfD election victory

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.

Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.

Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".

While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.

Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia KlÃ¶ckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.

Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.

The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

A new book by longtime Bay Area journalist Gil Durán investigates “tech fascism” and its mounting influence on U.S. politics. The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy follows the rise of Vice President JD Vance, the former venture capitalist whose “outsider” campaign for Senate was bankrolled by the billionaire co-founder of PayPal and Palantir, Peter Thiel. Durán traces the ideological lineage of the current Trump administration back from Vance to Thiel and the far-right-wing monarchist Curtis Yarvin, whose “right-libertarian” political theory has long made the rounds among Silicon Valley elite. “These guys were never libertarians,” says Durán. “Now that they are the government, we see their true face: They’re fascists, and they’re authoritarians.”

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

ANJALI KAMAT: The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. That’s the name of a new book by our next guest, the journalist Gil Durán. The book looks at how tech billionaires, including Peter Thiel and Elon Musk, are pushing what Durán calls “tech fascism.”

Gil Durán also documents how Thiel had played a pivotal role in JD Vance’s rise to power. Durán writes, quote, “Vance is almost entirely a creation of Thiel who bankrolled his brief stint as a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and United States senator. With Vance at Trump’s side — Silicon Valley had one of their own in the White House — a tech venture capitalist one heartbeat away from the presidency.”

AMY GOODMAN: Gil Durán joins us here in New York. He’s the former opinion editor of The Sacramento Bee and editorial page editor at the San Francisco Examiner. He now publishes two newsletters: The Nerd Reich and FrameLab.

Welcome to Democracy Now! So, let’s start with the title, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. Why’d you choose it?

GIL DURÁN: Well, in 2024, I wrote a series for The New Republic about the extremist ideological beliefs coming out of Silicon Valley. And after I’d written a story that went really viral and got me under attack by one of these guys, someone reached out to me from the crypto world and said, “You know, we’ve been calling these guys 'the Nerd Reich' for years.” And that blew my mind. And I saw that no one was really using that title, and so I rebranded my newsletter, which had some boring other name, as The Nerd Reich, and that became the main message of it. But I thought it was amazing that from within their own community, this was a label that was applied to them. People understood it was fascist and was echoing Nazism in nature.

AMY GOODMAN: But I want to just say the billionaire tech bros, as they are known, another name for them, haven’t always been the way they are now, in fact, when Trump was first coming into office. Talk about how they have changed.

GIL DURÁN: During the first Trump administration, we saw something called Tech Against Trump, where there were all these tech companies standing up to Trump, filing lawsuits, opposing his crackdowns on immigration. This time around, it’s completely different.

AMY GOODMAN: He was removed from X.

GIL DURÁN: Yeah, removed from X. Facebook banned him. Now we see the opposite happening.

I think what happened is that Trump was able to tap into some undercurrents in Silicon Valley with his return to power. Billionaires had become radicalized by things like the #MeToo movement, by Occupy, by the Black Lives Matter movement, and then by the pandemic. And so, when Trump is able to return to power, they are now in a very different mentality. They’ve made billions and billions of more dollars. They’re even more against taxes and government, even though government is generally the basis for many of their fortunes.

And so, now we see a complete alignment behind Trump. In fact, Trump is being funded and supported by Silicon Valley. He wouldn’t be able to do the things he’s doing without the billions of dollars he’s raking in in open crypto corruption.

ANJALI KAMAT: You know, in the epigraph to your book, you quote Peter Thiel from 2010. So, in a way, they’ve changed, but this also goes back and has a longer history. And the end of that quote is “technology is this incredible alternative to politics.” Can you talk about what he meant by that and what that means in terms of the kind of influence Peter Thiel has?

AMY GOODMAN: And who he is?

GIL DURÁN: Yeah. Some billionaires appear to have changed, but Peter Thiel hasn’t really changed. He’s been right-wing for a very long time. Peter Thiel was born in Germany, came to the United States as a child, went to Stanford, became a lawyer, studied philosophy, and then got very lucky to be in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s as things were about to take off.

In 1997, he read a book called The Sovereign Individual, which predicted that in the 21st century technology would overthrow democracy, specifically something called cybercurrency, or what we would today call crypto, which would undermine government authority, and advanced automation, which we would call AI, which would collapse the economy by destroying most jobs and concentrating wealth in the hands of a savvy few that were called the “sovereign individual.” And Peter Thiel has credited this crazy book with being the inspiration for PayPal, which he saw — which he says was an effort to get ahead of this digital currency.

It didn’t quite work out that way, but it made him a billionaire, eventually, because it provided the basis for his fortune, and he’s been able to use his money to grow this influential cult of right-wing ideas in Silicon Valley, which, by the way, they were always there, this libertarian, it was called, vibe coming out of Silicon Valley in the '80s and the ’90s. There were a handful of writers who wrote about it then. But what we've learned is these guys were never libertarians. They just wanted to be in charge of the government. They weren’t against the government, unless they don’t get to be the government. So, now that they are the government, we see their true face: They’re fascists, and they’re authoritarians.

ANJALI KAMAT: You know, you tell this story in the book, a remarkable story, of a group of these billionaire tech bros. It’s not just Peter Thiel; it’s several other men. Can you talk about some of these other characters that you talk about? And what is their crusade against democracy?

GIL DURÁN: They have this idea, largely stemming from this Sovereign Individual book, that technology means democracy is an obsolete software system, that the United States is an obsolete country, that it won’t survive the 21st century. And I want to say, I know this sounds crazy to people, but much of my book is told in the words of these men, from — in podcasts, in interviews, in long essays, they write about it. And their problem with democracy is that they don’t get to have all the power.

ANJALI KAMAT: So, you didn’t have to get secret documents. I mean, you have some remarkable statements in this book. You have Balaji Srinivasan and also Curtis Yarvin, and Curtis Yarvin, I believe, talking about, in an early blog post perhaps, talking about San Francisco and what to do with the poor?

GIL DURÁN: Yeah. So, this idea is that they’ve got — some call it the network state. Curtis Yarvin called it “patchworks.” Part of their apocalyptic vision for the future is that the country will be broken up. It will no longer be one country. It’ll be broken up into these sort of corporate zones or fiefdoms called patchworks or network states. And the new governing structure will be these autocratic, dictator-like corporations that will have total power over their citizens. Yarvin wrote that they could even turn unproductive people into biodiesel to fuel city buses. But he said he was just kidding about that, but that what we really need for the poor is a humane alternative to genocide.

So, these are the kinds of ideas you see. And what’s disturbing is that Balaji Srinivasan, another Peter Thiel protégé, because Curtis Yarvin is funded by Peter Thiel — that’s the only reason anyone’s ever heard of him — goes on to create this idea called the network state, which is a more startup-friendly version of this, that corporations and billionaires should fund their own cities and countries. And we’re seeing that grow.

AMY GOODMAN: Let’s go to Curtis Yarvin in his own words at the Institute of Art and Ideas, where he explained why he supports monarchical system of government.

CURTIS YARVIN: Let’s debunk this concept of liberal democracy. There’s actually no such thing. Democracy in today’s world just means a good or legitimate government. It means a claim to a legitimate government. Just because you call yourself a democracy doesn’t mean anything. North Korea calls itself the DPRK, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. That is three euphemisms for democracy, one place name, and it’s a monarchy. …

Anything that works is a monarchy. So, for example, if you take your your iPhone and you look at the box that your iPhone comes in, it says, “Designed by Apple in California, manufactured in China.” So, that is two monarchies — Apple has a CEO, and China has a dictator — and one oligarchy, which is the government of California, which is, by the way, basically a single-party state. There are no longer competitive elections in California. So, when you try to imagine the state of California, in which I live, trying to build an iPhone or design an iPhone, the concept is ridiculous.

AMY GOODMAN: Let’s go back to 2021, when JD Vance, then a candidate in Ohio for U.S. Senate, appeared on the conservative Jack Murphy Live podcast. Murphy asked Vance how to root out so-called wokeism from American institutions.

JD VANCE: There’s this guy Curtis Yarvin, who’s written about some of these things. And so, one is to basically accept that this entire thing is going to fall in on itself, right? … I tend to think that we should seize the institutions of the left and turn them against the left, right? We need — we need like a de-Baathification program, but like a de-wokeification program in the United States, right?

AMY GOODMAN: So, that was JD Vance back in 2021. The latest news, this out of The Washington Post, that President Donald Trump recently told donors in private that he wants to see his vice president, JD Vance, win the 2028 presidential election, a sign that he’s open to publicly backing JD Vance. There’s been this kind of war between JD Vance and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. But talk about the significance of this and, as you said, JD Vance being a creation of Peter Thiel.

GIL DURÁN: JD Vance is a dangerous extremist who embraces a set of ideas that should put a chill down the spine of every American. He went on in that interview to say that Donald Trump would likely win the 2024 election, and that when he did, he should purge the federal government, just like Yarvin had recommended, and, in fact, he should defy the courts and the law and challenge the Supreme Court justices to force him to follow their dictates. It’s pretty amazing that you have a man on the political stage in the White House a heartbeat away from the presidency, who has espoused such radically anti-American ideas.

And I think people need to understand the degree to which he is so closely related to Peter Thiel. We wouldn’t have a JD Vance without a Peter Thiel. Peter Thiel is even the reason that JD Vance converted to Catholicism. He’s the reason JD Vance became a venture capitalist and a millionaire. He’s —

AMY GOODMAN: How did they hook up?

GIL DURÁN: Peter Thiel likes to go around speaking to schools and graduate schools. And in 2011, he went to Yale Law School and gave a speech. And JD Vance said it was one of the most significant moments of his life and that Peter Thiel was one of the most intelligent people he’d ever heard. And basically, that speech convinced him to not be a lawyer, and instead to become a venture capitalist. And at every step of JD Vance’s life since then, it has been Peter Thiel who has made him who he is, who has essentially created him whole cloth.

ANJALI KAMAT: And it’s not just JD Vance, right? I mean, it’s — Bloomberg, I think, reported that 16 people connected to Thiel are in the Trump administration. Can you talk about, you know, what kind of effect this has had in terms of policies? Like, you know, when we hear these ideas, they sound a little outlandish, to say the least. It’s hard to see them being translated into policy. But then, what we’ve been living over the past two years, you’re seeing a lot of this coming to fruition. So, can you talk about, you know, DOGE, for example, or the, you know, mass layoffs at federal jobs, what happened to USAID, and where those ideas came from?

GIL DURÁN: The main argument of Curtis Yarvin for a long time has been that a president should act as a dictator. And one of the ways to cement this dictator’s power is to purge the federal government of anyone who is unwilling to follow the orders of the dictator, basically to destroy the civil service. In addition — this is 15, almost 20 years ago — he recommended that the United States pretty much destroy its diplomatic standing in the world and eliminate international aid programs.

We saw all of that happen during DOGE. In fact, Yarvin had updated his idea to say that it should be a CEO who the president should install as a dictator to run rampant over the federal government. And DOGE was an almost perfect expression of that. So, these ideas that used to be —

ANJALI KAMAT: And what did Curtis call it? RAGE?

GIL DURÁN: He called it RAGE — “Retire All Government Employees.” So, even the four-letter, all-caps acronym is an echo of Yarvin. And these are ideas that were on an anonymous, weird blog, marginal in Silicon Valley 15 years ago, and have now become policy under the Trump administration, because when you’re a billionaire, you have the power to impose these crazy ideas on everyone else.

And that’s what’s happening. Peter Thiel’s entire inner circle has infiltrated government at the same time that the Trump family is now becoming tech venture capitalists and crypto cartel moguls. There’s this joining of forces. The corporate is becoming the state, and both of it’s combined with apocalyptic religious movements. And that is the heart of fascism.

AMY GOODMAN: Where does Elon Musk fit into this picture?

GIL DURÁN: Elon Musk and Peter Thiel go way back to PayPal. They started it together. They’ve had some tensions.

AMY GOODMAN: The so-called PayPal Mafia?

GIL DURÁN: The so-called PayPal Mafia. But you’ll note that Peter Thiel is considered the godfather of the PayPal Mafia, even though Elon Musk is the wealthiest man in the world. Musk is certainly aware of these ideas, and when he was thinking of starting his own political party after he left DOGE, he consulted with Curtis Yarvin about how to do that and what the party should say. So, here’s Yarvin, who knows nothing about anything, but he’s considered a genius by these billionaires, largely because he tells them what they want to hear.

So, Elon Musk is clearly radicalized, is clearly open to these ideas. I’m not sure that he reads a lot about these things as much as he just believes the basic idea behind this, which is that wealthy, white technologists should be the ruler of the world, and then the galaxy and the universe. This is the cosmology coming out of Silicon Valley these days.

AMY GOODMAN: Where do women and people of color fit into this picture?

GIL DURÁN: At the bottom of the hierarchy, if they exist at all. Look at what’s happening with the USAID cuts: a targeted hit delivered against the poorest people in the world by the richest man in the world, with millions of people projected to die. These billionaires who promise abundance because of AI, well, we already have abundance, and we’re not sharing it. Look at what they’re doing to the poorest people today. And if you listen to the apocalyptic visions that AI will kill all jobs and transform everything, they say that, “Well, don’t worry. Everyone will get a share of the extreme universal wealth that’s created.” But that’s not what we’re seeing today, and we can’t really believe that when they say that. Fascism is about imposing a hierarchy, a moral order. And white, wealthy, Western men are at the top of that moral order in fascism.

AMY GOODMAN: Gil Durán is author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. If you have time, we’re going to do Part 2 of this discussion, and then we’re going to post it online at democracynow.org. Again, the book, The Nerd Reich.

I’ll be speaking after the screening of Steal This Story, Please! in Middlebury, Vermont, on August 28th. Check our website at democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

New York City has settled two lawsuits with 9/11 Health Watch, committing more than $34 million to build a public portal, which will share records on the city's response to the terrorist attack, including details about air quality around Ground Zero.

Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani's team is firing back at Mayor Zohran Mamdani after Mamdani accused past city officials of misleading New Yorkers about toxic air following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Giuliani spokesperson Ted Goodman accused Mamdani of seeking to "score cheap partisan political points" by directing blame toward local officials who rushed to the scene of the attacks while overlooking the radical Islamic terrorists responsible for killing nearly 3,000 people.

"Now would be a good time to remind Mayor Mamdani that cowardly terrorists acting in the name of Islam are 100 percent responsible for all of the death and destruction on September 11, 2001, and for all of the suffering and illness that have continued since that day," Goodman said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'

Former NYC Mayor Rudy Giuliani attends the annual 9/11 Commemoration Ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York City in Sept. 2024. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

The records released by Mamdani’s administration include more than 170,000 pages documenting the city’s response to the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath. The initial release includes 68 boxes of records from the Department of Environmental Protection that were not located until 2025, and records related to 7 World Trade Center.

The records include documents from Giuliani’s administration, including a memo sent to Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that warned the city faced potentially multimillion-dollar lawsuits from New Yorkers who claimed health advisories failed to protect them from toxic exposure and that the sites were inadequately cleaned up.

MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER

At a news conference announcing the release, Mamdani said the documents showed that officials across multiple administrations had information about hazardous conditions but failed to adequately inform the public.

"I wish there was a limited number of people who misled the public that I could describe them in just a few names," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference. "But the truth is that, as we have heard, this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted, and we are here to release these documents today because, for a long time, New Yorkers have known the truth, and yet they have been unable to see the truth in any document that's been presented to them."

Mamdani said the release was intended to give New Yorkers access to records that had been difficult to obtain for years. His administration said the city had settled two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch as part of the release and created a public portal containing the documents.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani provided an update hours after the explosion in Staten Island, New York, on Friday afternoon. (WNYW)

"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air. And then, when they began to contend with the symptoms of the illnesses that followed, the government that had not hesitated to send them into harm's way was nowhere to be found," Mamdani said.

NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS

Thousands of first responders, residents, workers and others exposed to the World Trade Center site have since developed illnesses recognized by the World Trade Center Health Program as related to 9/11 exposure. The program continues to provide treatment and monitoring for people suffering from certified 9/11-related conditions.

Former Republican New York Gov. George Pataki, who was governor at the time of the attacks, said in an interview with the New York Post this week that he had been diagnosed with restrictive airway disease, which he attributed to his exposure to toxins at Ground Zero.

The newly released records provide additional detail about environmental hazards found in the years after the attacks, including asbestos detected at 15 John Street in Lower Manhattan. The records document asbestos findings at multiple locations and provide additional detail about the city’s environmental response.

The records show that asbestos was detected at some locations at levels below applicable cleanup or exposure benchmarks and at others at levels that appeared to exceed them. Health authorities have said there is no known safe level of asbestos exposure.

Then-EPA Administrator Christie Todd Whitman said in a Sept. 18, 2001, press release that air monitoring results indicated the air near the World Trade Center was safe to breathe, days after the EPA first issued assurances about environmental hazards on Sept. 13.

MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY

Goodman pointed to the federal government’s role in communicating about air quality after the attacks, noting that the EPA issued public assurances about conditions near Ground Zero. An EPA Inspector General review later concluded that the data available at the time did not fully support the agency’s broad assurances about air safety.

"The EPA, a federal agency, issued press releases and public statements declaring that air samples showed the air quality near Ground Zero was safe," Goodman said, referring to Giuliani's response. "The agency later apologized for those statements, saying it did the best it could with the knowledge available at the time."

Firefighters gather near ground zero after the attack on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. (Corbis via Getty Images)

Whitman later apologized for the assurances in a 2016 interview, saying she was sorry for people who became sick or died and that she and the EPA had done the best they could with the information available at the time.

The release of the documents follows a petition with more than 100,000 signatures from 9/11 victims' family members requesting that Mamdani not attend the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero Friday.

"This mayor is not serving us," Charles Wolf, who lost his wife on 9/11, said at a noon news conference. "He's serving himself. We are asking respectfully that he not show up."

"Even though there is going to be other politicians there, these are the politicians that helped us push beneficial laws through and literally held our hand during that time," Wolf continued. "Mayor Mamdani has not shown any of that, none of it. He just wants to be there because he wants to be there."

In 1956, construction of Glen Canyon Dam began. The dam would generate hydropower, promote recreation and keep silt from filling up Lake Mead, but its main purpose was to create Lake Powell to serve as a water savings account and even out the Colorado River’s fluctuating flows. By storing water during wet years for use during dry ones, it would help the Upper Basin states comply with the Colorado River Compact and ensure that the river’s flow at Lees Ferry was not depleted “below an aggregate of 75,000,000 acre-feet for any period of ten consecutive years.”



Now, all its functions — except capturing silt — are imperiled, and, ironically, the dam itself may cause the Upper Basin to violate the compact’s non-depletion clause. 



More than two decades of drought have nearly drained Lake Powell’s savings account. This winter’s lack of snow has made things worse, forcing federal dam operators to take extraordinary measures to keep the reservoir from dropping below critical levels this summer and preserve its hydropower production and Glen Canyon Dam’s viablity as a water storage facility. But once downstream releases are reduced, the Upper Basin could end up violating the compact.

The outbreaks of Ebola and hantavirus highlight the challenges of waning global cooperation on health, and what Australia must do to prepare.

An outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola is proving difficult to control in the Ituri province of the Democratic Republic of Congo, a region beset by conflict and insecurity. The virus has reached epidemic proportions, with 321 confirmed cases, and has spread to Uganda and possibly other countries further afield.

As we know from the experience of Covid-19, travel and trade mean that epidemics anywhere can threaten the whole world. Australia’s first case of the H5N1 bird flu was a child who had caught the infection overseas. Similarly, we now see the hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship Hondius spreading to countries around the world. The severity of their impact depends on how well these Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks can be contained.

The most obvious responses are vaccines and drugs. Though these were developed for Zaire Ebola in response to the 2014 West African epidemic – the largest and worst in history, with about 28,000 cases – there is no commercially available drug or vaccine for Bundibugyo Ebola. The World Health Organization (WHO) is sponsoring clinical trials of an experimental vaccine and treatments. No vaccines are as yet approved for hantavirus.

An epidemic – loosely defined as a widespread outbreak that may affect a whole country – can be controlled, however, with non-pharmaceutical measures. Time and time again we see amnesia about the principles of such measures, which span air quality, disinfection, personal protective equipment, isolation of infected patients and quarantine of their contacts.

The recent epidemic of the Andes strain of hantavirus – which can spread from person to person – on board the Hondius highlights lessons from the Diamond Princess and Ruby Princess outbreaks of Covid-19. Cruise ships can experience explosive outbreaks, with indoor air quality a key factor in the spread of infection.

WHO’s initial recommendation was for passengers to stay in their rooms or wear a surgical mask when leaving their cabins. Later, this was changed to recommend the higher level of protection offered by a respirator, such as an N95 or P2 mask. Nevertheless, ventilation and air quality were not addressed.

The current diphtheria epidemic in the Northern Territory – which is the worst in more than 35 years – highlights the vulnerability of First Nations communities to infectious diseases, in part due to low vaccination rates.

A complicating factor in the case of the Hondius is that the captain announced to passengers that the initial death was from natural causes, not infection. As a result, passengers condoled with the widow, who later also died of hantavirus. A total of 13 cases and three deaths have occurred to date in multiple countries where passengers and crew were repatriated.

There are lessons for the current Ebola epidemic from that of 2014, when a few hundred cases in March spiralled to almost 28,000 by July the following year. For the first six months, there was no concrete action to control the spread, despite a flood of international responders in the era of USAID funding. That September, however, modelling showed that expanding the capacity of hospitals to isolate infected patients could control the epidemic. Until then, Ebola patients were unable to get a hospital bed and were freely infecting others. This prompted international responders to build tent hospitals to isolate and treat more patients, which flattened the curve. Considerable efforts were also made to trace contacts and quarantine them, which is also critical, as it prevents onward transmission.

The use of personal protective equipment (PPE) was a flashpoint in 2014, with the WHO and US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommending surgical masks for health workers. The CDC switched to respirators after two nurses in the United States became infected wearing surgical masks. The WHO advocates lower-level PPE for Ebola, with even their latest guidelines stating, “Paradoxically, wearing excessive PPE can increase a person’s risk of infection.”

In 2014, my colleagues and I published a paper that was the first to openly challenge the CDC and WHO guidelines. We argued that the precautionary principle – that reasonable steps to reduce risk should be taken in the absence of scientific certainty – should be used to protect the occupational safety of health workers treating patients with Ebola, given the high fatality rate and lack of available treatments or vaccines. Aside from the rights of health workers to be safe at work, if your health workforce is disabled or killed by infection, your ability to control an epidemic is drastically reduced. This broken record is played during every serious epidemic or pandemic, from SARS in 2003, to pandemic influenza in 2009, Ebola in 2014, Covid-19 in 2020 and now Ebola again.

By the time Covid-19 hit Australia in 2020, we had used much of our PPE stockpile in the bushfires of the preceding summer, and sent some of our remaining supplies to China to help deal with what was then an epidemic. As a result, we had severe shortages – stockpiles are typically only a few weeks’ supply, but pandemics go on for much longer.

Australia is well prepared for the current threats, however, with a new Centre for Disease Control and quarantine facilities built for the pandemic. Passengers repatriated from the Hondius have been transported there. There are no travel restrictions around the Ebola epidemic as yet, but it is still far smaller than the one in 2014, when visas from the affected countries were temporarily cancelled. Major cities in Australia have specialised medical facilities for patient transport and treatment, which would be used to safely treat an Ebola case in Australia.

That said, not all communities are equally insulated. The current diphtheria epidemic in the Northern Territory – which is the worst in more than 35 years – highlights the vulnerability of First Nations communities to infectious diseases, in part due to low vaccination rates.

One area of weakness for all countries is the risk of failing to diagnose a serious infection in the hospital emergency department. There are many examples of such failures, including the delay in diagnosing Ebola in the US and Nigeria during the 2014 epidemic, and one of MERS-coronavirus in South Korea in 2015, which led to 186 confirmed cases and 38 deaths.

Staff in ERs are busy and stressed and have no routine tools for situational awareness of high-consequence epidemics that could arrive at their door. Febrile patients are often sent back to the waiting room, perhaps for hours, where they can infect others and cause outbreaks.

An electronic decision support system for triage staff can help to improve awareness and prompt early isolation of patients with potentially serious infections. For example, if a triage nurse records a fever, they can be prompted to ask about travel. If the patient has travelled, the country would be logged and the triage nurse would receive a list of outbreaks in the relevant country. This can help prevent major hospital outbreaks.

Another global challenge is that misinformation has exploded since the Covid-19 pandemic, resulting in distrust of medicine, falling vaccination rates and resurgence of vaccine-preventable infectious diseases throughout the world. A trending topic in 2026 was that the Pfizer Covid vaccine caused hantavirus. Governments are left scrambling to keep track of trending misinformation in real time. The impact of health misinformation and disinformation needs urgent solutions.

Perhaps the most confronting issue for health authorities now is that the old era of global cooperation has ended. Until this Trump administration, America had carried much of global health, via USAID and as the single largest nation-state donor to WHO. USAID also helped to subsidise global health research in Australia. When this funding came to a sudden end last year, our own dependence on the US was exposed.

Global health is an industry, with many parties flocking to epidemics and pandemics and many careers built in the field. The proliferation of non-government organisations has contracted after the cessation of USAID funding, and 18 to 20 per cent of WHO’s funding has been lost as a result of the US withdrawal. Moreover, the US pullback was followed by that of Argentina and murmurs from other countries along the same lines.

It is time to re-evaluate the old model of global health and look to new ones that can build sustainable sovereign capacity in low-income countries and encourage all countries to invest in their own health security, while building global cooperation.

Raina MacIntyre is the founder and director of EPIWATCH, an AI early-warning system for global epidemics with real-time tools to monitor vaccine misinformation and community sentiment. She currently receives research funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council.

Raina MacIntyre leads the biosecurity program at the Kirby Institute. She is on the World Health Organization’s SAGE smallpox and mpox advisory group.

An 11-year-old boy died in a freak go-kart accident when his kart flipped into an upstate New York pond and landed on top of him, trapping him underwater.

Parker Mitchell was driving a go-kart with his 8-year-old sister Teagan in Darien, New York, last Sunday when the pair’s kart rolled over into a nearby pond around 2:30 p.m., The Democrat and Chronicle reported.

The kart pinned Parker underwater. First responders pulled the preteen out of the pond and rushed him to Strong Memorial Hospital, where he died just a couple days before he was to start middle school, according to authorities.

Parker’s sister Teagan, who was able to escape the wreck, was treated at the scene before returning to her family, local authorities said.

The boy, from Greece, New York, was a young athlete who played youth football and baseball and “had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcome,” according to his obituary.

His family remembered him as having a “curious spirit and a wonderful sense of adventure” and said he loved spending time with friends and family.

“He truly excelled at everything he did. He had a good heart, and his kindness left an impression on the people fortunate enough to meet him,” his obituary reads.

The young man was also a Buffalo Bills fan and loved playing video games and spending time in nature, his family remembered.

“His life was short, but his impact will last forever,” his obituary said.

Friends of the family have started an online fundraiser to assist them.

A nurse formerly employed with Gold Coast Health has been charged with 12 offences allegedly involving six teenage girls.

A Gold Coast nurse who allegedly abused his position in a youth mental health ward to stalk and sexually abuse teenage girls has been refused bail by a Queensland court.

Derek George Jackson, 58, faced Southport Magistrates Court today via watchhouse video link charged with 12 offences allegedly committed against six teenage girls between November 2020 and May 2024.

Mr Jackson was arrested and charged on Saturday night with six counts of stalking, two counts of indecent treatment of a child, and one count each of sexual assault, abuse of office, possessing child exploitation material, and creating child exploitation material.

The court heard Mr Jackson was arrested in the international departures lounge of Brisbane Airport.

Magistrate Nerida Wilson said Mr Jackson told police he was travelling to Asia for dental work and intended to return to Australia in July but did not yet have a return flight booked.

The court heard Mr Jackson had been suspended from his role at Gold Coast Health since September 2025 when the police investigation into his alleged offences commenced.

Adolescent inpatients with complex mental health concerns are treated at Robina Hospital. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Police prosecutor Jacinta Raven told the court, Mr Jackson had been the subject of several complaints from the family of children treated through Gold Coast Health's Child and Youth Mental Health Service (CYMHS) and from staff within the service.

Ms Raven told the court Mr Jackson targeted vulnerable children who were unable to remove themselves from his presence because they were admitted to a mental health facility.

Ms Raven told the court two children had complained of inappropriate "stroking or touching of the feet or the legs" and data obtained from Mr Jackson's mobile phone appeared to show he had a "foot fetish".

She said further data from Mr Jackson's phone showed he had searched the names of several children involved in the investigation of his alleged offences, as well as some of their siblings.

"He's also searched how to delete the cache on his iPhone, and that would give the court some concern," Ms Raven said.

In considering Mr Jackson's bail, Magistrate Nerida Wilson told the court his alleged victims were compromised by malnutrition.

"[They] were often undergoing re-feeding to restore weight and overall health," Ms Wilson said.

"Many of the children were also experiencing acute mental health crises including suicidal ideations, serious self-harm episodes and suicide attempts.

"These offences occur against the most vulnerable youth within our society, including those with serious mental health issues and disorders."

Giaan Ramsay, who took her own life in July 2025, is one of six teenage girls Mr Jackson allegedly offended against. (Supplied: Steve Ramsay)

Among the six alleged victims named during Mr Jackson's court appearance was Giaan Ramsay, whose death by suicide in July 2025 sparked a Queensland Health investigation.

Police allege Mr Jackson unlawfully stalked, intimidated, harassed or abused Giaan between June 2023 and May 2024.

Ms Wilson denied Mr Jackson's application for bail on the grounds that he was an unacceptable risk of reoffending and of attempting to flee the jurisdiction.

"The court is deeply troubled by the offences before the court," Ms Wilson said.

A Gold Coast Health spokesperson said in a statement it was aware of the "concerning" allegations involving a staff member.

"Immediate measures were taken, including contacting Queensland Police Service (QPS) and removing the employee from the workplace when this was brought to our attention," the spokesperson said.

"As a values-led organisation, staff and patient safety is of the utmost importance to us, and we take these matters extremely seriously.

"We will continue to cooperate with QPS as this matter progresses."

The head of the Gold Coast Vulnerable Persons Group, Detective Inspector Paul Fletcher, said no further victims had been identified.

Paul Fletcher said police were not aware of alleged offending beyond that related to the six teenagers. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

"Obviously, it's deeply concerning that people are having contact with children, especially highly vulnerable people and children in a hospital setting," he said.

"Hence when these allegations came to light they were vigorously investigated straight away."

In a statement, Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the safety and wellbeing of patients and staff was the organisation's highest priority.

"These allegations are shocking and deeply concerning," Mr Nicholls said.

"As the matter is before the courts, it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Mr Jackson has been remanded in custody to face court again next month.

Investigations are ongoing, with detectives appealing for anyone with information to come forward.

83 years ago today, in combat with the Japanese during the Solomon Islands Campaign in World War II, Patrol torpedo boat PT-109 was rammed by the Japanese Destroyer Amagiri. Its commanding officer, a certain Lieutenant John F. Kennedy, undertook almost single-handedly to rescued his crew of 12 men, saving all but two in the process, while being seriously injured. The event won Kennedy multiple decorations for bravery, and made him a bona fide war hero. READ how the event unfolded… (1943)

Inquirers and historians generally do not find the then-future president at fault for the collision. It happened that Kennedy had received orders, along with other patrol boats, to continue patrol operations after dark. Kennedy was idling PT-109 on a single engine to avoid detection by enemy aircraft.

Eventually he realized they were in the path of the destroyer Amagiri, which was returning northward after dropping off supplies and soldiers on Kolombangara. Patrol torpedo boats were not very maneuverable, and with only one engine, there was little time to escape the fast Japanese warship, which Kennedy had not been warned about on the radio.

Kennedy ordered his men to fire a torpedo, along with a 37mm anti-tank gun at the ship, but they had almost no time to do so. Amagiri struck PT-109 on the starboard side and sheared off a large piece of the vessel. The fuel then exploded causing a fireball 100 feet high. Seamen Andrew Jackson Kirksey and Harold William Marney were killed instantly, two other members of the crew were badly injured and burned when they were thrown into the flaming sea surrounding the boat.

Kennedy was able to rescue MM1 Patrick McMahon, the crew member with the most severe wounds and burns, and brought him to the floating bow. Kennedy also rescued Starkey and Harris, bringing them both to the bow. The ship, though, was sinking. The survivors regrouped and used a wooden plank to support their torsos while they swam to the deserted Plum Pudding Island.

Kennedy, who had been on the Harvard swim team, used a life jacket strap clenched between his teeth to tow McMahon behind him for 5 hours. Once on the island, Kennedy eventually undertook another 2 hour swim to hail passing allied vessels until they were found and rescued.

MORE Good News on this Day:

6 years ago today, the women of Saudi Arabia were given the right to travel abroad without a male guardian, a major advance in rights for women in the country. This meant that women over the age of 21 could apply for passports of their own volition, while the Kingdom simultaneously passed laws permitting females to register births, marriages, or divorce.

According to the BBC, Saudi’s male guardianship system gives husbands, fathers, and other male relatives the authority to make critical decisions about women.

It meant women in the Kingdom were required to seek those relatives’ permission to obtain or renew a passport and exit the country. The first woman to become an envoy for the kingdom, Saudi ambassador to the US Reema bint Bandar Al Saud, hailed the changes. (2019)

14 years ago today, Michael Phelps won an unprecedented third consecutive Olympic gold medal in the 200-meter individual medley, his 16th gold medal in total, becoming the first man ever to win the event in three Olympics in a row. This win also marked Phelps’s fifth Olympic title in the individual medley, breaking the record of four shared by Hungarian Tamás Darnyi and Ukrainian Yana Klochkova.

While the 2012 games in London started badly for Phelps, raising considerations that maybe he was past his pomp, he turned the season around by winning gold in the 4×200-meter freestyle relay, and the gold in the 100-meter butterfly.

This meant he repeated his heroics of the 200-meter individual medley, becoming the first man ever to win the 100-meter butterfly in three consecutive games. Phelps’s final event was the 4×100-meter medley relay in which he went on to win his 18th career gold medal, making him the most decorated swimmer, male or female, and Olympian in general, of all time. (2012)

34 years ago today, at the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona, Belarusian artistic gymnast Vitaly Scherbo, representing the Commonwealth of Independent States, became the first gymnast to win 6 gold medals in a single games, collecting for the pommel horse, rings, vault, parallel, team, and all-around, making him also the most prolific athlete that year.

It would have been easy to imagine following the breakup of the Soviet Union that countries lacking in funding and preparation for the games would struggle. Sometimes called the “Unified Team,” it consisted of Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, the Central Asian republics, Moldova and Ukraine.

Beyond his ballistic ’92 Olympics, Scherbo won 9 gold medals across three editions of the World Championships in gymnastics. WATCH his flawless performances in Barcelona… (1992)

35 years ago today, the Viking replica longship ‘Gaia‘ reached the first Norse settlement in North America, almost 1,000 years after Leif Eriksson’s landing, after crossing from Norway.

Eriksson was a Norse explorer from Iceland, credited with being the first European to set foot on the continent, having landed in Newfoundland. Gaia was built in Bjorkedalen, Norway, to be a replica of the original 890 AD Gokstad Ship which successfully made the voyage, but was only unearthed 140 years ago.

Gaia later made the journey to New York via Greenland and Canada, and she sailed on to Rio de Janeiro to mark the first UN World Conference on the Environment.

In 1993 she returned to Norway and was given as a gift to the town of Sandefjord (where the original ship was excavated). Since then, Gaia has been in frequent use, visiting ports in England, Scotland, Germany, France, and The Netherlands. WATCH the amazing historical footage of the boat launch… (1991)

156 years ago today, the world’s first underground tube railway, the Tower Subway, opened in London, a wonder of the Victorian age.

The quarter-mile-long tunnel under the Thames River was excavated in less than a year, thanks to the project’s civil engineer James Henry Greathead who invented a cylindrical, iron tunneling shield technology that still forms the basis of modern machines used to burrow tunnels today.

Though closed to the public in 1898, the passageway with its small brick entrance still stands near the Tower of London.

In just 70 seconds, 12 passengers at a time could be moved from the north to the south bank while 22 feet beneath the riverbed in a rail car pulled by a steel cable powered by stationary steam engines on either side. (1870)

On this day in 1869, Japan abolished its Samurai class system.

Under the massive reforms of the Meiji Restoration (Meiji means “enlightened rule”), all feudal class privileges were abolished, ending the traditional Confucian hierarchical order that had persisted since 600 AD. Under the caste system, society’s classes were not arranged by wealth but by usefulness. Peasants came second because they produced the most important commodity, food; third were Artisans because they produced nonessential goods; and Merchants were at the bottom of the social order because they generated wealth without producing any goods.

One of the primary differences between the samurai (pictured above) and peasant classes was the right to carry swords; this ancient privilege was suddenly extended to every male in the nation.

After the Meiji reforms, which restored direct political power to the emperor for the first time in over a millennium—by seizing control of hundreds of disparate territories and establishing a constitution—Japan underwent a period of sweeping political, military, and social reform. The island nation, with its new capital Tokyo, rapidly industrialized its production methods and became the first Asian state to westernize itself, adopting policies such as creating a national system of public schools.

And, 22 years ago today, Eric Clapton bought a 50% share in Cordings to save the historic British gentleman’s outfitters, based in London since 1839, from closure.

The guitarist said he had been fond of the West End shop since a window display of a tweed suit caught his eye when he was 16, and he became a regular shopper there. Cordings was the originator of the Covert coat and the Tattersall shirt and made riding boots for the Queen Mother. (2004)

Also, on this day in 1973, American Graffiti, the first successful film directed and co-written by George Lucas, premiered. The coming-of-age comedy starring Richard Dreyfuss and Ron Howard also featured Harrison Ford, a young actor who had become a professional carpenter because acting roles weren’t paying the bills. (The gig profoundly changed his career as he was cast in Lucas’s next film, Star Wars.) An Oscar Best Picture nominee, American Graffiti was produced with a tiny budget of $777,000 and became one of the most profitable films of all time.

Set during a single night in 1962, the film glimpses the car-cruising, rock-and-roll culture popular among teens of the post–World War II baby boom generation—and it was the inspiration for Happy Days, the hit TV comedy series also starring Ron Howard. WATCH a clip with the young Harrison…

good-news-in-history-october-9:
On this day, in Game 2 of the 1909 World Series, Ty Cobb stole home base. The details around this famous of all capers are what make it so. Losing Game 1 to the Pittsburgh Pirates, Detroit Tiger’s star and all-time great Ty Cobb was sitting on third base at the top of the second in Game 2, his team already behind by two runs. A reliever had come in named Victor Willis, a giant of a man, who Cobb noticed was paying far too much attention to the batter, giving Cobb the space he needed to steal home before Willis came to his senses. READ more about the circumstances… (1909)

By his own statement, Cobb was not the fastest runner. However, he was the smartest and most aggressive, leading to him hold the MLB all-time record for home base steals at 54 in his career. He studied pitcher’s deliveries constantly and developed the fall-away slide and some six other sliding maneuvers to foil the basemen. He also led the opposition into traps, and feigned injuries to mislead the defense.

All of this was buttressed by his ability to apply psychology to any given situation which gave him the edge on the opposition. As an example of this, the Society for American Baseball Research cites the steal of home in the 1909 World Series against the Pirates.

Cobb stole second, third, and home in the same inning on three separate occasions. The first time was July 22, 1909, against the Red Sox, the second was July 12, 1911, against the A’s, and lastly on July 4, 1912, against the Browns.

MORE Good News on this Day:

589 years ago, the Hangul alphabet was first published in the Joseon Dynasty. It solidified increased literacy by serving as a complement (or alternative) to the logographic Sino-Korean Hanja, which had been used by Koreans since before the Common Era. The Korean alphabet was designed by King Sejong, perhaps Korea’s greatest monarch, so that people with little education could learn to read and write. A popular saying about the alphabet is, “A wise man can acquaint himself with them before the morning is over; even a stupid man can learn them in the space of ten days.”

As with nearly every East Asian culture that bordered China, the early establishment of the Chinese writing system deeply influenced Korea, as it did for Manchuria, Mongolia, Japan, and southern China. However by the height of Korean power in the Middle Ages, King Sejong felt the number of Classical Chinese characters in use was simply too much for the common person, and so developed a “featural alphabet” that wouldn’t stray too far from what most people used, but introduced vowel and constant pieces which stack on top of each other to be read as a single syllable.

Hangul is now the official writing system throughout Korea, both North and South. It is a co-official writing system in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture and Changbai Korean Autonomous County in Jilin Province, China. (1446)

54 years ago today Rod Stewart went to No.1 on the singles chart with Maggie May. From his album Every Picture Tells a Story, it was first released as a B side, but became one of the most memorable songs of the late 20th Century, topping the chart in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia.

The hit, written about an older woman Stewart hooked up with in the 60s, was recorded in just two takes and famously featured a mandolin (and Ronnie Wood on guitar). Despite record company executives not liking the song much, it single-handedly launched Stewart’s career. WATCH his (and Ronnie’s) 1993 unplugged performance… (1971)

And, on this day 15 years ago, Chile’s 33 trapped miners cheered and embraced each other in the darkness as a drill punched into the underground chamber where they had been stuck for an agonizing 66 days while the world came together to engineer a rescue. (2010)

And on this day in 2006, the ORBIS Flying Eye Hospital landed for the first time in Vietnam.

The DC-10 wide-body aircraft had been converted into an ophthalmic surgical center for doctors to give sight to the poor. During its first quarter century— from 1982 when ORBIS took off on its first sight-saving mission—more than three million people have received medical treatment.

Happy 77th Birthday to Jackson Browne, the singer-songwriter-musician who has sold over 18 million LPs in the US alone. Beginning in the 1970s, hits like These Days, The Pretender, Running on Empty, Fountain of Sorrow, Doctor My Eyes, and Take It Easy have been counted among the most honest and emotionally powerful of a generation.

Last year, Browne became the first artist to receive the Gandhi Peace Award for his “extraordinary contributions to the inseparable causes of world peace, environmental harmony, and social justice.” Awarded annually along with a cash prize since 1960, the Gandhi Peace Award medallion is forged from “peace bronze” composed of metals salvaged from the control systems of US nuclear missiles.

Lately, Jackson has turned his attention to the seas as a founding member of the advocacy group Ocean Elders, along with Sir Richard Branson and James Cameron. Among his numerous other awards for public service, Browne received the NARM Harry Chapin Humanitarian Award. Bruce Springsteen inducted Browne into the Rock Hall of Fame in 2004. (1948)

And, 85 years ago today, John Lennon was born in Liverpool, England. As a performer, writer, or co-writer, Lennon had 25 number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100 chart—both with the Beatles and as a solo act. Double Fantasy, his best-selling solo album, won the Grammy for Album of the Year one year after his death in 1980 at age 40.

To celebrate the day, Paul McCartney, Alec Baldwin, and Sean Lennon, son of the famous Beatle, took over SiriusXM’s Beatles Channel. Sean, as the DJ, played his favorite songs by his father, including Imagine, while remembering his favorite childhood memories.

A two-part radio documentary hosted by Sean Lennon in 2020, featured conversations with his brother Julian Lennon, McCartney, and his godfather Elton John. Billed as “a celebratory, musical, family portrait” on BBC. It was the first time Paul and the younger Lennon talked publicly about the legendary Lennon-McCartney songwriting partnership.

“It’s lovely to imagine him at 80,” McCartney told Baldwin on SiriusXM. “I think he would be very literate. I think he would be writing—not necessarily just music ’cause he was starting to get into (writing), he did a couple of little books.” CHECK OUT the interview snippet… (1940)

And, 40 years ago, marking what would have been Lennon’s 45th birthday, Yoko Ono formally opened a three-acre garden in New York’s Central Park—across the street from the apartment building where Lennon was shot.

Dubbed Strawberry Fields, she funded the memorial with a $1Mil donation and had it planted with trees, flora, and flowers gathered from across the world. A large, round mosaic on the pedestrian walkway is emblazoned with one word: Imagine. (1985)

GOOGLE HAS BEEN fined more than €400 million by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) for breaching users’ location data.

The Irish data watchdog launched an inquiry into Google Ireland six years ago, after complaints from multiple European consumer rights organisations about the tech giant’s processing of location data.

The inquiry examined the lawfulness and fairness of its processing of location data and Google’s accountability obligations under general data protection regulation (GDPR).

It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with ads or to infer their interests.

The inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.

The DPC has imposed administrative fines totalling €403 million and ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance within six months.
