A Martínez

NPR's A Martinez speaks with Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., about Sen. Lindsey Graham's legacy.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  We're joined now by a Senate colleague of the late Lindsey Graham. Richard Blumenthal is a Democrat from Connecticut. He recently partnered with Graham on a bipartisan push to ramp up sanctions against Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Senator, I understand you were in contact with Graham just this weekend. Anything you can tell us about that last conversation?RICHARD BLUMENTHAL: In my last conversation with Senator Graham, he was absolutely exultant, calling from Kyiv. In fact, we had a number of conversations seeking final approval from the White House for our Russia sanctions bill, which he was going to discuss with President Zelenskyy. And, in fact, confirmation came through at the very last moment that President Trump would support a bill that we'd drafted in lengthy, painstaking sessions which would impose scorching tariffs and sanctions on purchasers of Russian oil and stop them from fueling Putin's war machine. So he was really over the moon, saying, we've done good. This is a big effing deal. He was in great shape.MARTÍNEZ: Do you think, Senator, that his death could have impacts somehow on that and also U.S. support for Ukraine more broadly?BLUMENTHAL: My hope is very honestly that his Republican colleagues and some of my Democratic colleagues will see it as a fitting tribute to pass this legislation right now. Senator Graham, in his final moments on this Earth, was very aware of the critical moment that we have right now. Ukraine has turned the tide on the battlefield. It is actually gaining net territory. It's inflicting losses of about 30,000 more casualties a month on Russia. It has set back Russia's economy. It's reaching deep into Russia with its drones and missiles. And now these sanctions would be pivotal in getting Putin to the peace table. That was his objective. And my hope is that his death, tragic as it is, will provide an impetus to President Trump and my Republican colleagues to pass the Russia sanctions bill.MARTÍNEZ: That was Senator Graham's tenth wartime trip to Ukraine over the past weekend. Yeah. So - and one other thing, too, because Senator Graham had an interventionist approach to foreign policy that maybe you don't often find in President Trump's America First circle. What do you think his death could mean more broadly for U.S. foreign policy, at least in the short term?BLUMENTHAL: My hope - again, it's a hope, not by any means a prediction or a certainty - is that maybe President Trump will view more favorably the kind of nonisolationist view of the world that Senator Graham believed in so deeply. I hope that his legacy, at least in part, is that America has a vital role to play in defending democracy in Ukraine because it is in our self-interest to stop Putin before he attacks NATO nations - Poland, Finland, the Baltic states - where then we would have an Article 5 obligation to put troops on the ground. So Ukraine is doing the fighting and dying, but it's our fight to stop Putin and defend democracy there, which is vital to our national self-interest. And I hope his death, while not itself necessarily a persuasive factor, will open minds to be more receptive.MARTÍNEZ: Where in other areas - where did you, as a Democrat, also align with Lindsey Graham on?BLUMENTHAL: I worked with Lindsey Graham on internet safety, particularly for children. We supported a measure called the EARN IT Act, which said to Big Tech - which right now, as you know, has immunity under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. This immunity is so exceptional and, in fact, unique, but Big Tech gained it at a time when it was nascent and small. Now it is immune from any real restraint in the harm that it does to children and others. So Senator Graham and I were very insistent that Section 230 should be modified - in fact, eliminated. And he was also a champion of certain gun violence protection measures. We worked together on a red-flag statute that became part of the Safer Communities Act - the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act. He was a defender of his views very staunchly, but willing to work across the aisle.MARTÍNEZ: One more thing, Senator. I want to raise something that's become common in our hyperpartisan climate online. People who disagreed with Graham politically are celebrating his death. You knew him. Can you share your thoughts on the man he was and the legacy he leaves?BLUMENTHAL: I disagreed profoundly and passionately with Senator Graham on many issues - the SAVE Act, Iran, his approach to the budget and taxation. He justified the massive tax cuts. We disagreed often, but we worked together where we could find common ground and where we could advance selected interests. And I think he was a believer in the Senate as an institution in trying to get things done, trying to make it function and work so as to produce measures that benefit the American people. But I will emphasize, you know, our disagreements were vehement and sometimes, in fact, extremely vigorous, to the point of not talking. But, you know, he believed in coming back and trying to get things done.MARTÍNEZ: Senator Graham was also an ally and a friend of Donald Trump. Not always the case. In 2015, he famously called Trump a, quote, "race-baiting, xenophobic religious bigot." Why do you think - Senator Blumenthal, why do you think he ultimately decided to align himself with Trump after he won that first presidential election?BLUMENTHAL: You know, really honestly, I am not going to try to psychoanalyze Lindsey Graham. Obviously, he had some of the most impactful epithets about Donald Trump at various points and, frankly, to the frustration of our mutual friend John McCain, who was staunchly opposed to Trump to the very end of his life. Lindsey Graham had a more favorable relationship with Trump. Obviously, he probably would say that he had to do it because it was necessary to get things done, and he had to have this relationship with the president of the United States - very far from my attitude. I have fought President Trump at almost every turn. I regard him as a grave danger to democracy. And Lindsey Graham and I rarely talked about Trump or his reason - in fact, I don't think we ever talked about his reasons for supporting Trump when he did.MARTÍNEZ: That's Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Senator, thank you very much for your thoughts on this.BLUMENTHAL: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

By Simon Smale

Topic:BMX Racing

Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 11:26am

There's often another spectator at training these days. (Supplied: Instagram/@laurenreynolds)

The opportunity to compete at a home World Championship is always special.

For Australian BMX racer Lauren Reynolds, this one might be doubly so.

The 35-year-old four-time Olympian will, for the first time in her career, take on the challenge of a world championship as a mother to eight-month-old Royce.

"I didn't know or ever think I would have a child at a BMX track," Reynolds tells ABC Sport on the sidelines of the Sleeman Sport complex track, which will host the UCI BMX Racing World Championships on Saturday, July 18 and Sunday, July 19.

"And to have her at the worlds, and a home worlds, is just really, really cool.

Lauren Reynolds's baby, Royce, is eight months old and on her first trip to Australia. (Supplied: Instagram/@laurenreynolds)

"She's a great little girl," Reynolds continues, her face lighting up in a smile.

"She makes me laugh every day, and it's going to be cool to have her on the sidelines."

Given the occasionally rough and tumble nature of BMX racing, it is perhaps not a surprise that mothers have been few and far between in the racing paddock.

Yet Reynolds, whose wife Ryan carried Royce, is one of three racers who now have a baby in tow.

American Alise Willoughby, a three-time world champion and Olympic silver medallist, and wife of Australian former world champion Sam Willoughby, was trackside with a pram, watching training alongside Sam, who now works with the Japanese team.

Sam and Alise Willoughby's sporting fairytale romance takes a tragic twist, with the strength of their love proving that no matter the obstacle, no setback is too big.

Colombian legend Mariana Pajón, a six-time World Champion and two-time Olympic Games gold medallist, also gave birth last year.

"A lot of the guys are dads, but no, there hasn't been [a lot of mums]," Reynolds said.

"My wife carried our baby, but they were all pregnant and gave birth around the same time, and there was no planning, no communication there, so it's very cool."

Cool, of course, but it has certainly been a change.

"I mean, life is completely different," Reynolds says.

"It's the same, but also completely different.

"A different perspective, different priorities in a sense, I've still got work to do, but coming home healthy and coming home to a little girl is precious.

"It takes away the worries and, whatever happens out here, stays there, and I go home to her."

Nobody is getting confused as to who Royce's mum is. (Supplied: Instagram/@laurenreynolds)

These world championships present the first opportunity for young Royce to visit Australia — Reynolds lives in San Diego these days — and a first meeting for her grandparents.

But the Sleeman track is one that Reynolds knows incredibly well, having spent hours training in Brisbane as a teenager, and it still feels like home.

"It's very cool to come back," Reynolds says, looking out over the venue that will be used for the 2032 Summer Olympics, a new temporary grandstand over on the finishing straight that come this weekend will be packed with green and gold-clad supporters.

"I used to live and train out here for years … so tons of memories.

"And I think now I'm just older and wiser, and I look at it differently.

"It's even better. It's refreshing. It's really cool to come back. I mean, Australia is always home, but I've built a life in San Diego, and I love it, but I love coming back. Having a home worlds is incredible, very cool, and I'm excited."

Josh Jolly won silver by less than a second last year in Copenhagen. Now he's striving for gold in Brisbane. (Supplied: AusCycling)

Another rider who is desperately eager to compete on the world stage in front of friends and family is Josh Jolly.

The 20-year-old from Ballarat already has an incredible pedigree in the sport.

Two years ago, Jolly claimed the junior world championship title in South Carolina.

Then, last year, he came desperately close to winning the Under 23 title last year in Copenhagen.

Jolly, then aged 19, was leading through the first half of the race at the Københavns BMX Klub only to be overhauled by 23-year-old Frenchman Alexis Pieczanowsky.

He was one of three Aussies to win silver at last year's championships, with 2024 Olympic champion Saya Sakakibara and Queenslander Izaac Kennedy both finishing second in the elite races behind Britain's Beth Shriever and Frenchman Arthur Pilard respectively.

Josh Jolly is hoping for a passionate crowd in Brisbane. (Supplied: AusCycling)

"I was pretty heartbroken last year," Jolly tells ABC Sport.

"I was leading the first half of the race and then made a mistake by myself and lost the rainbow jersey.

"That's definitely fuelled the training, fuelled my racing, and it's definitely made me a lot smarter.

"It's made me really want to do well in front of a home crowd and finally get the job done here this year."

Jolly, whose family moved from Ballarat to Brisbane earlier this year to help his career progress, has spent the last 12 months dreaming of redemption on home soil.

"I could honestly say for the last 12 months, every day I've thought about this race and what I want to do," he says, the conviction in his voice stirring and reassuring in equal measure.

"This whole sport, if you don't believe that you're going to do it, you won't do it.

"Every night before I go to bed, I'm visualising the race that I want to ride.

"Ever since last year, I've just put my eyes on this event, and yeah, it's time to get it done."

Lauren Reynolds is embracing her experience. (Supplied: AusCycling)

As a 35-year-old, Reynolds is one of the more experienced racers in the competition, winning a silver medal at the world championships 13 years ago behind fellow Aussie Caroline Buchanan in Auckland.

And yet despite perceptions that BMX is a young-persons' sport, Reynolds is bucking the trend spectacularly, arguably riding some of her best races six years after being dropped from the Cycling Australia elite program in 2017.

At the last World Cup event in Papendal last month, just four female riders in their 30s took to the start ramp.

Three of them, including Reynolds, finished in the top seven.

"I definitely lean into it now, and I didn't before," Reynolds says.

"I think, for a long time, I would kind of like ignore it and I denied it, thinking, 'no, I'm young and I'm…', and it goes through waves.

"Don't get me wrong, the young crop is hungry, they're fast, they're energetic. They eat, sleep, breathe, BMX, and I absolutely did that too.

Lauren Reynolds finished fifth and sixth at the recent World Cup event in Papendal. (Supplied: AusCycling)

"But I totally lean into my age now, and I embrace it. I see it as a positive now.

"I'm enjoying it. I know that I don't have long left in my career. But I'm still delivering, and I seem to be finding improvements each time, so that keeps me hungry.

"It's funny, a couple of days before I flew here, I got my PB at my local track to the first jump, and it was a day before my 35th birthday, and I came home from training on Wednesday, and I was like, 'Holy s***, I'm 35 tomorrow, and I just got a PB'.

"It's pretty cool. I mean, I can laugh about it, and it's fun. I know age will eventually get me, but right now I'm just enjoying it, and I adapt.

"I probably don't train as much as the young ones, but I adapt a little and adjust things, and I'm still thriving, I think."

With another Olympics just two years away, an Olympics taking place just up the road from her second home in California, Reynolds is not ruling anything out.

"As of right now, it's there [the Olympics] and nothing's off or on the table.

"For every four Olympics I've been to, it's always been like this Olympics, this Olympics, this Olympics.

"Now I'm focused on next week, and then I'm focused on Utah two weeks after that, where I'm racing and I'm not thinking of going to an Olympics or not."

Boelter had previously pleaded not guilty in last year’s fatal shooting of Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and an armed attack on another lawmaker and his family. He’s set to appear in court Thursday morning.

By Sarah Nelson and

Jeff Day

Vance Boelter, the man charged in the shootings of two Minnesota lawmakers and their families last summer, is expected to plead guilty in his federal murder case, according to a court record filed Wednesday and two sources familiar with the case.

The change comes after the Justice Department revealed it would not seek the death penalty against Boelter, 58, in the attacks last summer that jarred the state. A memo filed Wednesday by Minnesota’s U.S. Attorney’s Office suggests the decision not to seek a death sentence against Boelter was made “in accordance with the terms delineated in a proposed plea agreement.”

Boelter pleaded not guilty last year to his six federal offenses tied to the shootings that killed Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and injured Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, and their daughter, Hope.

The plea hearing in Boelter’s federal case is scheduled for 10 a.m. Thursday in a Minneapolis courtroom before U.S. District Judge John Tunheim.

A source familiar with the hearing said Boelter is expected to enter a guilty plea related to his federal charges of killing the Hortmans and attempting to kill the Hoffmans.

Boelter is not expected to receive any leniency in exchange for his plea, said a second source familiar with the proceedings.

Boelter’s federal case has remained in the early stages since his indictment and no trial date had been set. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster expressed frustration during a hearing in April over how long it took prosecutors to decide whether they would seek the death penalty against him.

According to his indictment, Boelter disguised himself as a police officer when he arrived at the lawmakers’ homes in the middle of the night on June 14. He was arrested near his home in Green Isle, Minn., after the largest manhunt in state history.

The first two counts against Boelter allege that he stalked the Hortmans and Hoffmans through the use of interstate facilities, namely the internet. Prosecutors argued that stalking his victims rose to a crime of violence. Ultimately, the Justice Department said it agreed with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota that a conviction for interstate stalking is not eligible for the death penalty.

A similar decision was made in January by a federal judge in the case against Luigi Mangione. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett in New York dismissed a nearly identical federal murder charge against Mangione in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

Boelter also faces charges in Hennepin County District Court that include two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of first-degree attempted murder, including against Rep. Kristin Bahner, whose home he allegedly visited that night while she was out of town. He also faces one count of animal cruelty against the the Hortmans’ dog, Gilbert, who was shot and had to be euthanized, and one count of impersonating a police officer.

News & Politics

News & Politics

Immediately after his arrest, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty requested to prosecute the state’s murder charges before the federal case but was denied.

Boelter was on the run for 43 hours after shooting the Hoffmans at 2:02 a.m. in the early morning hours of June 14. He interacted with local police officers twice after that, first in New Hope outside the home of Sen. Ann Rest at 2:36 a.m. and again at 3:35 a.m. outside the Hortman home. Brooklyn Park officers fired shots at Boelter as he killed Mark Hortman in the doorway of the home. Boelter proceeded to kill Melissa Hortman before escaping.

The lack of a coordinated response by several law enforcement agencies, including the State Patrol which is charged with protecting state lawmakers, has come under question since the attacks.

Despite the on-and-off downpour, and the fact that he was playing in front of a raucous sold-out crowd on the road, Bo Levi Mitchell looked as comfortable as ever against the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Thursday night.

It was a vintage performance by the future Canadian Football Hall-of-Famer, with Mitchell and the Hamilton Tiger-Cats torching the home side’s leaky defence en route to a 37-27 victory at Princess Auto Stadium.

“When you have a quarterback like Bo Levi back there, they’re going to make plays. But as a defence, we weren’t as sharp as we wanted to be,” said Bombers linebacker Tony Jones.

John Woods / THE CANADIAN PRESS

Hamilton Tiger-Cats quarterback Bo Levi Mitchell throws against the Winnipeg Blue Bombers defence in the first half in Winnipeg on Thursday.

“There were some critical plays that we want back that as a defence where we didn’t operate at our highest level.

“We’re gonna put this one in the past, learn from our mistakes, and not make those mistakes again further down the stretch.”

The Bombers opened the 2026 campaign in enemy territory last week in Calgary and stumbled out of the gates by allowing the Stampeders to gain over 100 yards on the ground and put 21 points on the board after two quarters. It was a similar result in their latest outing, only this time they fell victim to an aerial attack, with Mitchell completing 15-of-19 passes for 233 yards and three touchdowns in the first 30 minutes.

In the second half, Hamilton shifted to the run with CFL newcomer Larry Rountree III gaining 67 of his 124 rushing yards.

The Tabbies ran into a brick wall in Week 1 — a 30-27 overtime loss at home against Montreal — where they were held to a paltry 35 rushing yards and 2.2 yards per carry average. Against Winnipeg, they totalled 171 rushing yards for a 5.5 average.

“When we had the opportunity to get him in the backfield, or get him for short gains, he was bouncing off tackles,” said defensive end Willie Jefferson.

“They showed up this week wanting to prove they can run the ball. We just gotta make the effort to make the tackles.”

The Bombers were expected to have an obvious edge in terms of running the football, and yet, Brady Oliveira was a non-factor with 32 yards on eight carries.

“I think Hamilton started loading the box, adding extra guys in. And when we started going down, we had to start throwing the ball,” said right tackle Jarell Broxton.

The Weekly Wrap: This Is What Full Employment Looks Like

Welcome back to Friday! It’s the first Friday of the month, which means it is Jobs Friday, and it is now Labor Day weekend. This will be a special edition of our weekly wrap focused on the employment situation in America. Plus we’ve got a lot of musical accompaniment to get you through the weekend.

Let’s go!

Eddie Cochran’s 1958 hit “Summertime Blues” was about the problems of summer employment—not the difficulty of finding a job but the trouble of having one. Lots of Americans know just how that feels now. We’re all working and everyone is grumbling.

The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August, compared with the consensus forecast of 55,000. Not only did we add more than three times as many jobs as expected, but we also exceeded even the most bullish forecasts for around 100,000 jobs. What’s more, the prior two months were substantially better than earlier reported. June was revised from 20,000 to 31,000, while July was revised from a 23,000 loss to a 21,000 gain. Together, the revisions added 55,000 jobs and erased the supposed July contraction.

The strength came overwhelmingly from the private sector. Private employers added 127,000 jobs, more than double the 53,000 forecast. July’s private-sector gain was also revised from 30,000 to 71,000.

Also, the forecast unemployment increase never arrived. The unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, while economists expected it to rise to 4.2 percent. As we’ve been talking about for months, jobless claims and the unemployment rate demonstrate unprecedented job security in America.

Bruce Springsteen’s 1984 hit “My Hometown” was a lament about the deindustrialization of America. “They’re closing down the textile mill across the railroad tracks/ Foreman says ‘These jobs are going, boys, and they ain’t coming back,'” Springsteen sang.

It has taken decades and a revolution in trade, tax, and economic policy, but the jobs are coming back. Manufacturing employment rose by 16,000 in August. This followed gains of 13,000 in June and 14,000 in July. Manufacturing payrolls have now risen by 58,000 since bottoming in December. Durable-goods manufacturers added 15,000 workers in August, 24,000 in July, and 52,000 over the past three months.

This marks a genuine reversal. Manufacturing employment was falling during the final quarters of the Biden administration. The losses continued into 2025, although at a diminishing pace. Last year brought the turn away from decline. This year brought job gains.

Construction added another 22,000 workers in August, lifting total goods-producing employment by 41,000.

The evidence of the manufacturing boom is everywhere. Factory orders are up 6.5 percent this year, including gains of 12.3 percent for machinery and 14.3 percent for computers and electronics. The ISM manufacturing index hit 54.6 in August, its eighth consecutive expansionary reading. Its production index was 58.3, and its employment gauge rose to 51.2.  Manufacturing output grew at a 5.4 percent annual rate in the second quarter, the strongest since 2021. Durable-goods output surged 8.9 percent. Productivity is rising, orders are growing, job openings are climbing, and now payrolls are following.

If the Notorious B.I.G. was right when he sang that more money just brings more problems, the American worker better get ready to get jiggy with it.

The jobs report said average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent over the past year. But that understates the improvement in workers’ paychecks because the average workweek also increased.

Private-sector employees earned an average of $37.75 an hour in August and worked 34.4 hours per week. Multiply the two and average weekly earnings came to $1,298.60. That was up $7.20, or 0.6 percent, from July. Compared with August of last year, weekly earnings increased by $46.20, or 3.7 percent. At an annual rate, the average weekly paycheck now comes to around $67,527.

The gains were even stronger in goods-producing industries. Average weekly earnings for goods-producing workers rose 5.6 percent over the year to $1,566.86. Manufacturing weekly earnings increased 5.1 percent to $1,495.26. Construction workers averaged $1,645.57 per week, up 5.8 percent.

Production and nonsupervisory workers, who account for roughly four-fifths of private employment, earned an average of $32.53 an hour and worked 33.8 hours. That produced average weekly earnings of $1,099.51, an increase of 3.6 percent from a year ago.

This is another sign of an economy operating at full employment. Employers are paying workers to put in more hours in order to meet demand.

Hourly pay measures the price of an hour of labor. Weekly earnings come closer to measuring what lands in the paycheck. In August, workers benefited from both higher hourly wages and longer hours, with the strongest gains going to workers who make, build, and move things.

“I’m American made, I’ve got American parts,” Breitbart’s Jon Kahn sings in his patriotic anthem “American Heart.“ That’s increasingly a fitting anthem for our labor market.

The number of foreign-born workers holding jobs has fallen by nearly one million since President Donald Trump took office. Foreign-born employment stood at 31.774 million in January 2025. By August, it had fallen to 30.780 million, a decline of 994,000, or 3.1 percent.

The foreign-born labor force has contracted even more sharply. It fell from 33.307 million when Trump took office to 31.860 million in August, a decline of nearly 1.45 million.

The missing foreign-born workers have not piled into the unemployment rolls. The number classified as unemployed fell by approximately 453,000 over the period. The foreign-born unemployment rate is now just 3.4 percent.

This represents a dramatic break from the Biden era, when foreign-born workers supplied an enormous share of the growth in employment and the labor force. Under Trump, the number of foreign-born people working or looking for work has moved sharply in the opposite direction.

Perhaps not everyone is happy with the employment report. If you really were hoping that cheap foreign labor would boost your bottom line, there’s nothing but bad news for you. You are going to have to hire Americans and, as we just noted, pay them more to work longer hours.

“Working nine to five, what a way to make a living,” the late, great Dolly Parton sang.

Americans are indeed increasingly working in full-time jobs. Sorry, slackers. We’re all out of part-time gigs.

The number of employed Americans jumped by 569,000 in August. The employment-population ratio rose two-tenths of a percentage point to 59.1 percent, while the labor-force participation rate climbed to 61.6 percent. And the entire gain came from full-time employment. The number of Americans working full-time rose by 735,000. Part-time employment fell by 223,000.

There was also a sharp decline in so-called involuntary part-time work. The number of people working part-time because their hours had been cut or they could not find full-time employment fell by 414,000 to 4.39 million.

This too is a sign of full employment. Part-time jobs are being converted to full-time jobs.

Paul McCartney once wondered whether anyone would still need him when he was 64. In August, American employers supplied an emphatic answer. Employment among people 55 and older rose by 354,000. That was more than 60 percent of the overall increase of 569,000. Prime-age employment, covering workers from 25 to 54, was essentially unchanged, which is what you would expect in an economy already at full employment.

But it wasn’t just aging boomers finding work. Gen Z found jobs as well. Employment among 20- to 24-year-olds rose by 140,000.

In a full-employment economy, more and more of the jobs go to workers in the dawn and twilight of their careers.

For months, we have been hearing the nattering nabobs of negativity whine that the unemployment rate looks low only because people have stopped looking for work.

That just ain’t the way it is. While the published labor-force participation rate has declined by 0.5 percent since January and 0.7 percent from a year ago (although it edged up in August)—the labor force is smaller, and the number of people outside it is larger—it’s just not because people are so down that they have given up hopes of finding a job.

Economist Guy Berger pointed out on his MacroMostly Substack that the number of marginally attached workers has not risen. It fell by 132,000 over the past year. The number of discouraged workers fell by 78,000. The broader number of people outside the labor force who say they currently want a job dropped by 600,000.

The rise in nonparticipation therefore appears to be mostly voluntary. And this is not due to some surge in free-loaders or people on public assistance. These are likely retirees, students, caregivers, and parents. An economy that gives more people the choice to work outside the payroll economy is a welcome development rather than something to worry about.

The black unemployment rate fell to 6.0 percent in August, down from 7.6 percent a year ago. That is a large decline. The number of unemployed black Americans fell by 376,000 over the past year, to 1.32 million.

The improvement has occurred among both men and women. The unemployment rate for black men over 20 fell from 7.1 percent to 5.6 percent. The rate for black women declined from 6.8 percent to 5.6 percent.

Not surprisingly, you probably will not see Trump getting much credit for falling black unemployment in the legacy media. It violates their narratives about systemic racism.

One big reason for the decline in black unemployment: less competition with foreigners. The other is simply the full-employment economy creating more opportunities.

On September 6, 1901, President William McKinley was shot by anarchist Leon Czolgosz while greeting visitors at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo. He died eight days later.

McKinley had built his political career around protective tariffs. As chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, he gave his name to the McKinley Tariff of 1890, which raised average duties on many imported products to nearly 50 percent. As president, he signed the Dingley Tariff, raising rates again. McKinley understood tariffs were key to expanding American industry, maintaining high wages, and providing employment for American workers.

William McKinley and Teddy Roosevelt 1896 campaign poster. The Republican presidential and vice presidential candidates told voters that prosperity had returned because of their high protective tariffs and sound money policy.

The years after the McKinley Tariff became law brought an extraordinary expansion of American industry. Steel production more than doubled by the turn of the century and exceeded 30 million tons by 1913, feeding new railroads, factories, bridges, skyscrapers, and shipyards. Electrical equipment, chemicals, machinery, and automobiles emerged as major industries. By 1913, the United States produced roughly one-third of the world’s industrial output, roughly as much as Britain, France, and Germany combined. This quietly turned the U.S. into the arsenal of democracy, providing the economic might that won two world wars and the Cold War.

The economic achievements made possible by the tariff also led to a political upheaval. McKinley’s victory over William Jennings Bryan in 1896 broke the near-deadlock that had characterized national elections since the Civil War. He assembled a coalition of industrial states, cities, businessmen, professionals, prosperous farmers, and skilled factory workers. He won re-election in 1900 by an even larger margin.

The result was one of the greatest political realignments in American history. Republicans won seven of the nine presidential elections from 1896 through 1928 and controlled Congress for most of that period, interrupted principally by the Woodrow Wilson years. Republican dominance lasted until the onset of the Great Depression, which was brought on and then exacerbated by errant Federal Reserve monetary policy.

Brendan Trew felt out of place when he walked into the cardiac rehabilitation gym at his local hospital.

The 47-year-old considered himself fit and was one of the youngest patients in the room.

“I went on a 37-kilometre bike ride and then the following night I was having a heart attack,” said the single father from Hampton in Melbourne’s south-east.

But the six-week program – which involved a combination of exercise, education, and counselling – helped rebuild Trew’s strength and, more importantly, slashed his risk of having another heart attack and dying.

A new landmark study, published in the International Journal of Cardiology, found that attending cardiac rehabilitation programs reduced patients’ risk of dying from another heart attack by 75 per cent.

But the study of 7100 Victorian patients across 13 public hospitals found that only one in five eligible patients accessed these programs.

Lead author Dr Susie Cartledge, from Monash University, suspects patients are skipping the programs because advancements in medical technology have minimised the severity of their heart condition.

“If you have a heart stent put in now, it’s just a little wound on your radial artery,” Cartledge said, referring to the small incisions that have replaced many open-chest operations.

“Because the treatment is so minimally invasive, it actually minimises what has occurred for the patient. They think, ‘I’ve just got this little scratch on my wrist that healed in a week, I must be OK.’”

But Cartledge said heart disease, which leads to blocked arteries and stent procedures, is something patients need to manage for life.

“We are simply failing to get patients through the door,” she said. “If we could boost attendance to just 60 per cent, the health system would see massive financial savings, and thousands of families would be spared the tragedy of a preventable second attack.”

She said shorter hospital stays following heart procedures also meant patients found it overwhelming to process the information given to them at discharge. “We know patients only remember about one-fifth of what we tell them in the hospital,” said Cartledge.

“Then they get home, the sick leave finishes, they go back to work, and they fall right back into old habits – which is exactly what we don’t want.”

Patients attending cardiac rehabilitation benefited from lower mortality and fewer unplanned readmissions. These health benefits increased with every additional session they attended.

“Mortality was four times higher in those who didn’t attend any sessions compared to those who attended the full six-week program,” she said.

A typical program in Australia runs for six to eight weeks, and offers supervised cardio and strength training with health professionals and education. Counsellors help patients process the emotional impacts of suffering a cardiac event and facing their own mortality.

The programs are run in public and private hospitals and through community health services.

Trew initially dismissed his chest pain as reflux. But when the pain intensified, he decided to visit Sandringham Hospital’s emergency department.

He was then taken by ambulance to The Alfred and was told he had suffered a heart attack.

The news came as a shock. Trew had no risk factors for heart disease: he exercised regularly, ate reasonably well and had normal blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

He felt vulnerable when he was discharged from hospital two days later. He’d had a stent placed in his previously blocked coronary artery and had been put on medication to control his blood pressure and cholesterol.

“I had a heightened awareness of how frail we all are,” he recalled.

A counsellor at the cardiac rehabilitation program helped him work through these feelings, while an occupational therapist put in place strategies to help Trew ease back into his job in corporate sales.

He learnt about nutrition during education sessions, and realised that he was eating too much salt.

Cardiologist Kegan Moneghetti, who works at St Vincent’s Health, said cardiac rehabilitation programs helped patients make behavioural changes that had the same clinical powers as pharmaceutical drugs. This includes altering diets, committing to exercise and stopping smoking.

“Often these things are free and just take our time and our effort, but people need a structure and a support system to be able to achieve it,” Moneghetti said.

He said more funding was needed to ensure that patients could access cardiac rehabilitation programs soon after they were discharged from hospital. He said patients often faced a six to eight-week wait to access these programs.

“There is a small window where you can capture people to engage with change,” he said.

Cardiovascular disease is one of Australia’s leading causes of death and claims a life every 12 minutes, according to the Heart Foundation. About one in six Australian adults live with cardiovascular disease, which includes heart and blood vessel diseases such as coronary heart disease and stroke.

Most risk factors are preventable through a healthy diet, regular exercise and maintaining a healthy weight.

The couple has been named as newlyweds Marie Ebert (left) and Alexander Cromie (right)

A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.

They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.

The private Bell 206 helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.

The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.

Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.

This video can not be played

Footage shows helicopter in the sky moments before crash

A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "Our thoughts are with the families during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and in contact with the Greek authorities."

The BBC has contacted Greek authorities and the aviation company for comment.

Asset management firm Blackstone, where Cromie worked, said in a statement: "We are shocked by the tragic passing of three people including our colleague Alex Cromie and his wife Marie Ebert, who were celebrating their honeymoon.

"Alex was beloved by everyone who knew and worked with him at Blackstone, and our thoughts and prayers are with his loved ones."

Ebert worked as a senior specialist at consultancy brand Bain & Company.

In a statement, the company said: "We are shocked to read reports of a tragic accident in Greece regarding one of our colleagues and her husband.

"Our thoughts and support are with the families involved at this very difficult time."

A senior police official told the Times that the crash came just before the helicopter's scheduled landing time of 18:15 local time (16:15 GMT).

Sifnos' Deputy Mayor, Manolis Foundoulakis, arrived at the scene shortly after the incident and told local news site Newsit there was almost "nothing left" of the aircraft.

He said locals saw the helicopter crash within metres of their homes and had described a "bizarre engine noise coming from the aircraft" as it was about to land.

The island's Vice Mayor for tourism Yiannis Rafeletos told the BBC the people of Sifnos are "devastated" and "deeply shocked".

"So much happiness has turned into sorrow," he added.

He said two of the victims were found in the wreckage, while the third was a short distance away.

Firefighters worked to tackle a blaze which broke out after the crash, and the flames had been extinguished by Monday evening.

Pint-sized peddlers as young as 11 are among the dozens of illegal vendors hawking goods on the Brooklyn Bridge — bumping even licensed military vets.

“They are everywhere,” one stunned tourist told The Post.

At least three dozen unlicensed vendors clogged the Big Apple span Monday to sell fruit, snacks, water, toys and other assorted goods — with many lugging their tiny children along or leaving their youngsters on their own to target passersby and tourists in the underground market.

One boy, 11-year-old Sergio, said he makes anywhere from $100 to $300 every day, typically putting in eight hours four days a week, with his mom selling hats nearby.

He said he emigrated from Ecuador with his family in 2021.

Another boy, who said he’s 12 years old, was selling fruit for $5 a pop. Asked where his mom was, he claimed she went to the bathroom — but the boy remained alone.

“It’s a bit awkward,” Jennifer Thompson, a 53-year-old tourist from Virginia who bought two canvas bags for $10. “I kinda wish it was an adult, but I don’t know their circumstances.”

“I was wondering where their parents are at,” her husband, Larry Thompson, 52, chimed in.

The illicit vendors — many of them immigrants — have been a nuisance on the historic bridge for years. By 2023, the span was jammed with so many peddlers that one frustrated local described it as a “disgusting, mile-long souvenir shop and flea market.”

The vendors were booted in a sweep ordered by former Mayor Eric Adams in 2024.

But the unsightly outdoor market returned, and has been left to prosper by Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The Post spotted at least 42 of the illegal vendors on the bridge on Sunday, with the merchandise mostly spread out on blankets. Nearby, folks of varying ages managed the sales.

Older children were left alone to oversee the transactions, while nearby adults sat next to kids as young as 4 or 5 years old.

The unruly scene has irked local residents and legit vendors, including military veterans trying to make ends meet.

Sammy, a vet and licensed ice cream vendor slinging the cold treat near the bridge, said the city rarely cracks down on the illegal peddlers, and when cops issue tickets, it’s typically a fine of $50 or less — a fraction of the money they make.

“Us being disabled veterans and having a license means nothing over there now because if I go over there, they’re going to kick me out,” he griped. “But they’re not kicking [the illegal vendors] out now.”

The sharp drop in irregular migrant arrivals is evidence that the EU’s policy reforms are working, EU migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said on Thursday (1 October).

But Syria is also no longer the single biggest source of asylum claims after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime 22 months ago, a factor that appears to have been conveniently ignored.

On Thursday, he told reporters after a meeting of EU interior ministers in Luxembourg that irregular arrivals have dropped 55 percent in the past two years.

“So that’s a record low in the asylum applications,” said the former Austrian finance minister, adding that Austria and Sweden have recorded equally low asylum numbers and that Germany is deporting more people than are asking for protection.

“The basis for all of that, and the foundation for all of that, is the pact, the pact on migration and asylum,” he said, in comments that were echoed by Ireland’s migration minister, Jim O’Callaghan.

Morgan McGann is a happy member of the latest generation to enjoy Brunswick's Don Bosco Youth Centre, which opened in Melbourne's inner north in 1939. (Supplied: Kate Longley)

Parents in Melbourne's inner north are rallying to prevent the Don Bosco Youth Centre and Hostel from being sold after nearly nine decades of community outreach.

A petition has been launched, calling on both local and state governments to preserve the Brunswick landmark from property development.

Candidates running for the Brunswick electorate at the November state election have raised concerns about the sale.

A group of parents in Melbourne's inner-north is calling on the state and local governments to step in and save a youth centre that has been offering free accommodation, entertainment, exercise and mentoring to the community for nearly 90 years.

Jesse Bassett is a fan of the indoor trampolines at Don Bosco, one of several activities provided by the Brunswick youth centre. (Supplied: Kate Longley)

The Don Bosco Youth Centre and Hostel on Sydney Road in Brunswick has provided short-term housing for young men, as well as free or low-cost programs, trampolines, basketball and birthday parties, since 1939.

Not to mention a locally famous rabbit.

But in recent weeks, a For Sale sign out the front has been a major talking point for the inner north community.

Patting the pet rabbit is a popular drawcard for younger attendees such as Mila McGann. (Supplied: Kate Longley)

A petition calling on the state government and council to intervene has so far attracted more than 3,300 signatures in a few days.

"Free and low-cost programs aren't a nice-to-have," the petition reads.

"For many kids, they're the difference between taking part and missing out."

Joel Ma has been taking his six-year-old daughter to the centre since she was two, and said the sale of the site was "heartbreaking".

"Don Bosco is part of the fabric of Brunswick," he said.

"[It is] the soul of Brunswick. It connects old Brunswick to new Brunswick."

Joel Ma says the likely sale of the Don Bosco youth centre is "heartbreaking". (ABC News: Billy Draper)

He said his daughter learnt how to take turns at Don Bosco, thanks to the bells that let patrons know their turn on the trampoline had ended.

"We might have a balcony but a space like this is our backyard."

The centre is owned by Catholic organisation the Salesians of Don Bosco, which is advertising the site through Melbourne Acquisitions.

Generations of Sydney Road pedestrians and motorists have passed by the Don Bosco centre. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

The triple-fronted site is being advertised as an "iconic Brunswick landmark" that offers vacant possession over nearly 3,000 square metres, including 74m of street frontage.

It is expected to fetch about $10 million.

It comes as the church faces compensation claims, with the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse finding more than 20 per cent of Salesians were alleged perpetrators.

The Salesians did not respond to the ABC's request for an interview.

Paul Villani said growing up in Brunswick in the 1970s, Don Bosco was a safe place for kids to hang out after school.

"Growing up there myself, there was always supervision, and you got a bit of moral guidance," he said, adding the young men staying in the accommodation would often help with homework.

Paul Villani went to church at Don Bosco with his grandmother in the 1970s. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Mr Villani now works as a lawyer in an office next door to the youth centre.

He said a former priest from the centre married him and his wife, and baptised his children.

"My father, who migrated to the area, used to go there as a kid and play around there, spend time there on the weekends, and then I went there as a child," he said.

Mr Villani said it would be very sad if it were to close.

Merri-bek City Council said in a statement that it did not have a formal position on the sale of the centre, or calls for the council to step in.

"Council is aware the property has been listed for sale, and that the community feels strongly about the centre remaining open," a spokesperson said.

Morgan McGann and Jesse Bassett get a taste of World Cup fever, taking turns on the table football at the Don Bosco centre. (Supplied: Kate Longley)

Labor's candidate for Brunswick in the upcoming Victorian election, Gabe Steger, said the sale was "highly disappointing".

"I'll engage closely on the future of Don Bosco," he said in a statement.

"I am keen to work with the community to make sure its future is given the attention it deserves."

Greens candidate for Brunswick, Adam Pulford, said on social media that Merri-bek Greens would "seek to work with the Victorian Government on how we can save this incredible community asset".

"With so many people barely affording the essentials, having free and cheap community space where kids and families can spend time together and have fun is more important than ever," he wrote on Instagram.

"We need more spaces like Don Boscos, not fewer."

The youth centre's interconnecting double-storey brick buildings have a 75-metre frontage over three titles. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Joel Ma said if the council or government could buy the land, local parents would rally to volunteer to keep the venue operating.

"I can only imagine that parents who have been coming here since their kids have been really young would want to chip in and give back," he said.

Northern Ireland's newly-appointed secretary of state has said he has "a bit of a checklist" of issues he wants to address as he takes on the role.

Sir Chris Bryant was appointed to the job following Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Cabinet reshuffle on Monday.

Sir Chris, the MP for Rhondda and Ogmore, replaced Hilary Benn, and said his appointment came as a quite a shock, describing the role as "daunting".

His predecessor said he wished Sir Chris "all the very best in working with the executive to protect stability, continuing to generate growth and investment and in taking forward the Troubles Bill".

Sir Chris told BBC News NI that his new role demanded "such phenomenal responsibility".

He said his checklist includes "economic opportunity" for young people, a functioning executive, Troubles' legacy legislation and public services.

However, he said a border poll on Irish unity was "not on my list of priorities at the moment".

"I just want to get this legacy legislation through parliament in the way that works for everybody. I want to make sure we have the executive fully functioning.

"We need to make sure every young person in Northern Ireland sees an economic opportunity for themselves in Northern Ireland and for their family," he added.

He said he had visited Northern Ireland numerous times, often for concerts and theatre, and feels the creative industry was "ready for a real boost".

The Northern Ireland role is Sir Chris's first cabinet position, although he held a number of shadow front bench roles under Sir Keir Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn.

In terms of funding for Northern Ireland, Sir Chris said "money is tight" but that it was his "job to fight for Northern Ireland" claiming that he will "do that with every sinew" of his body.

However, he was positive about Northern Ireland's current economic position.

"You've got the best of both worlds being in the single market and in the United Kingdom. We need to exploit all these economic opportunities. Let's lift our eyes to much bigger horizons about economic prosperity."

The DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he hoped Sir Chris Bryant can build on the work done by his predecessor Hilary Benn

Earlier, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme that Sir Chris was in a position "to seize discussions around financial stabilities and around providing a budget and around doing some of the structural changes that Hilary has done the spade work for".

"We don't want to be in a position where we have to start from scratch again," Robinson added.

Robinson added that he had been "disappointed continually by Labour politicians, secretaries of state and prime ministers who talk warmly and richly about reset relations with the EU, but seem to have their eye off the ball about some of the significant issues we have for Northern Ireland".

"This reshuffle has been quite significant, the impact of it I think will reverberate for months and months to come," Robinson said.

Sinn FÃ©in MLA Pat Sheehan said personalities were "irrelevant" regarding the appointment of the new secretary of state and that policy needed to change.

"The name plates may change around the British cabinet table," he said.

"What's important for us is that policy changes and particularly in regard to the full implementation of the Good Friday Agreement, specifically in terms of preparing for a referendum on Irish unity," he said.

Social Democratic and Labour Party leader (SDLP) Claire Hanna MP, who had a meeting with Sir Chris on Tuesday, said there were two "immediate priorities" for the new secretary of state.

"The first is ensuring the executive agrees a budget before the 1 August deadline," she said.

Hanna said the second priority was the "urgent need for institutional reform and calling time on the decay and dysfunctional politics that have held Northern Ireland back for far too long".

TUV MLA Timothy Gaston told the Nolan Show that Sir Chris must be a "secretary of state that is willing to repair the damage done by the Irish sea border".

"What we have seen in the past, over the last number of months is that he is unsympathetic to doing anything about that."

Gaston cited Sir Chris's previous role as minster for trade, when new steel tariffs were introduced earlier this month.

Shaun Woodward, a former Labour MP who served as Northern Ireland secretary in 2009-10, said he has known Sir Chris for more than 25 years.

"He is the kind of secretary of state Northern Ireland needs, I think it is a very astute appointment by the prime minister," he said.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme, Woodward said  Bryant "is  a very fair minded person", adding he is a "fast learner, a very smart guy".

A promise Labour had made in its election manifesto was to repeal and replace the controversial Troubles legacy act.

Passed under Rishi Sunak's government, parts of it including conditional immunity were deemed unlawful by the courts, while victims and political parties in Northern Ireland had no confidence in it.

The legislation is still sitting in the Commons, with no sight of the government's amendments on proposed protections for veterans or how it will command confidence of victims and survivors.

Sir Chris said:  "I want to make sure this is legislation that really, really works."

The NI veterans commissioner, David Johnstone, told the Nolan Show Sir Chris must "fundamentally review" the legacy act.

"Those who followed lawful orders should not be dragged endlessly through prosecutions, court cases and coroners inquests."

Hilary Benn (left) has left his job in Northern Ireland and is being replaced by Sir Chris Bryant

Sir Chris joined the Labour party in 1986 and has served as MP in the Welsh constituency of Rhondda and Ogmore since 2001.

During Gordon Brown's tenure he served as deputy leader of the Commons.

He takes up his new post having moved from the Department for Business and Trade.

Sir Chris is a literature-loving Labour Party veteran who regularly quotes Shakespeare in TV and radio interviews.

He has written 10 books including a two-volume history of parliament.

The Welsh MP is also a former Anglican priest but quit the church in 1991 over its stance on homosexuality.

He and long-term partner Jarred Cranney were the first couple to enter a civil partnership in the Palace of Westminster in 2010.

In 2023 he was awarded a knighthood in recognition of his campaigning work around acquired brain injury and melanoma - a type of skin cancer.

WITH LESS THAN a week to go until Budget 2027, the government knows it must deliver a budget that puts more money in the pockets of working people struggling with the cost of living.

The budget kites have been flying high for a while now, and we know there’ll be changes to the point at which workers start paying the 40% rate of income tax. We know that measures to lower childcare fees are being discussed, that a rent tax credit is on the cards and of course we know that details of Minister Simon Harris’ much anticipated savings and investment scheme will be announced.

But the wind has failed to take one particular kite. 15 years after the Universal Social Charge was introduced, why are we not talking about making real reforms to what was once an emergency measure?

USC came into effect in January 2011, when Ireland was in a difficult financial position. It replaced the income levy and health levy and helped broaden the tax base. Ireland now is a very different country, yet USC is still a permanent fixture on the payslip.

I’ve worked as a financial adviser for more than 25 years. In my experience, most people don’t examine income tax, USC and PRSI as separate questions. They look at what they earn and what arrives in their bank account. I can’t blame them, we’ve made the taxation of work difficult to follow.

Advertisement

googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display('div-gpt-ad-1365092406213-1'); });

Let’s consider one of the most prominent pre-budget kites, the point at which a single person starts paying the higher rate of income tax. It’s currently €44,000, raising that threshold by €2,000 would save up to €400 a year for someone earning enough to receive the full benefit.

Don’t get me wrong, few people would turn down €400, but what does that figure tell them about their finances? They still pay USC and PRSI. Their rent or mortgage may have risen, and we know the cost of food and energy is only going in one direction. A tax change can leave someone better off than they otherwise would have been while still leaving them feeling worse off than last year.

When I meet a client, I look at their overall financial position, and I think we should judge Budget measures in much the same way. The number that matters most to a household is what it’s left with, and what that money can buy.

That doesn’t mean the answer is to scrap USC overnight. Let’s be honest, it would make a compelling headline, but the charge raises billions of euros. Removing it would mean having to replace that revenue in some way, namely reducing spending and cutting public services. Anyone calling for abolition should be honest about that choice.

However, this shouldn’t end the discussion about how the government collects revenue. If the government believes the current arrangement remains the fairest option, it should explain why.

The complexity extends beyond the payslip. People are expected to navigate a whole range of tax and tax credits often alongside rules that change from one Budget to the next. A new Government-backed savings and investment account will compound this. I support helping people save and invest, but its eventual tax rules need to be clear enough for ordinary savers to understand.

And we must be honest with people, there is another reason why this conversation matters now, and that relates to inflation. People hear that their salary has increased and assume they should feel better off. But if your salary rises while food, energy, insurance and housing costs are also increasing, the improvement in your actual standard of living may be considerably smaller.

Hello and welcome to EU Influence! I’m Mari Eccles. Regular readers will know how much time I spend on LinkedIn tracking job moves, deciphering subtweets and, on the most thrilling of days, following incredibly petty below-the-line spats between lobbyists I barely know (please send me your favorites).

But this week I briefly mistook LinkedIn for property site Immoweb after stumbling across this post by Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen’s cabinet member Xavier Coget, who is selling his villa in Uccle. It costs €1.6 million, in case you’re interested.

In non-real estate news:

— EU officials’ use of disappearing messages risks creating “accountability-free zones,” the bloc’s watchdog warns.

— Oslo’s current EU influence strategy isn’t working.

— MCC Brussels announces its successor (just don’t call it MCC 2.0).

NOTHING TO SEE HERE: The EU is increasingly keeping the public in the dark, the bloc’s watchdog has warned — in part because top dogs in Brussels delete their texts. European Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho said text messages, disappearing chats and decisions shaped by artificial intelligence make it harder than ever to scrutinize the EU institutions, and she accused officials of feet-dragging and evasion when it comes to responding to requests for documents.

Time for a rewrite: Anjinho said the bloc’s ancient access-to-documents rules are failing citizens and need updating. “Twenty-five years ago, the regulation was designed for a world of paper trails, physical archives, and analog processes,” she said in a speech on Wednesday. Now, negotiations happen via texts, “where governance increasingly relies on data flows that leave no traditional paper trail behind, and where decisions can even be made by algorithms.”

Funny you mention that: Just last week, the Commission confirmed that it will continue to delete President Ursula von der Leyen‘s texts — even though the ombudsman said doing so amounted to maladministration. Earlier this year, Anjinho’s office told von der Leyen and EU commissioners to retain messages exchanged with heads of state and government after a complaint from outlet Follow the Money, which (unsuccessfully) sought access to texts between the Commission chief and French President Emmanuel Macron. In a private message to von der Leyen in 2024, exclusively reported by POLITICO, Macron attempted to blow up the EU-Mercosur trade deal.

But but but: Von der Leyen’s team on Friday wrote to the ombudsman to say that keeping hold of messages for as long as it might take to challenge a Freedom of Information request refusal — up to two years — “cannot be reconciled with the necessary cybersecurity measures.”

War of words: In her speech this week, Anjinho hit back. “An institution cannot let a security architecture quietly decide what is a document in the first place,” she said, adding: “If the content is relevant to an EU policy and activity, or the decision-making process, it should survive long enough to be assessed, whatever channel it travelled through.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a rake of cost-of-living measures since taking office last week

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet his pledges on defence and the cost of living, a major think tank has said.

Burnham has announced a series of new measures since assuming office last week, including cuts to electricity bills and bringing the bus fare cap in most parts of England back down to Â£2.

But the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) warned the public finances will continue to be squeezed by more persistent inflation as a result of the Iran war.

It questioned whether Burnham had "fully thought through" how his promises would be paid for, but said the prime minister will have to raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere.

Stephen Millard, Niesr's deputy director for macroeconomics, said: "There's clearly no scope for increasing borrowing, so it is about choices."

Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people - including income tax, VAT and national insurance contributions - which Burnham has said he will uphold.

Millard said Niesr was advocating for cost-of-living measures to be funded through higher taxes â "which could involve tax reform rather than higher marginal rates" â or spending cuts.

He said: "People have talked a lot about the welfare bill â that is an obvious place to look.

"The triple lock on pensions, that is very, very expensive, and will get more expensive as we age."

He also pointed to potentially reforming council tax to move towards a land value tax system, or scrapping some VAT exemptions.

"Once you've done all of that, then I'm afraid I would break the manifesto promise and would be looking at the income tax rate."

Niesr also said on Wednesday it expects inflation to keep rising until February 2027, peaking at 3.8% before falling back to the Bank of England's 2% target.

The think tank said in its latest economic outlook that it does not believe the central bank will cut interest rates until 2028.

Its Director David Aikman said that "treading water is not enough" to prevent the national debt from rising.

"Every major shock this century has ratcheted the debt ratio higher, and none of that increase has been reversed," he said.

The Treasury said the government will stick to its fiscal rules while investing in "the public services people rely on".

"Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security," a spokesperson said.

burnham-labour-leadership:
Andy Burnham said he would seek to enter any potential Labour leadership contest should he win the Makerfield by-election on 18 June.

The Greater Manchester mayor made clear his ambitions as he appeared alongside four other candidates during a BBC Question Time special in the constituency.

Reform UK candidate Robert Kenyon said there was a need for a "big move away from career politicians" and warned against using Makerfield as a "stepping stone".

Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has defied calls from some Labour MPs to step down after poor election results last month. No formal challenge has been launched against him.

A No 10 spokesperson said: "The prime minister will not walk away from the mandate he was given just two years ago to build a stronger, fairer Britain."

The by-election was called after then-Labour MP Josh Simons stepped down, a move he said was to allow Burnham to run for Parliament and potentially mount a leadership bid.

The vote in Makerfield is expected to be a race between Burnham and Kenyon, a plumber and local councillor.

Asked about how politicians could restore public trust in them, Burnham criticised "point-scoring before problem-solving" in Westminster before he was pressed about his own ambitions.

The Labour candidate said: "I can't do anything unless I'm lucky enough to get the support of people here.

"But if I get your support, I would seek to represent you at the highest possible level and give this constituency maximum power and influence.

"I think Wes Streeting seems to have launched a leadership contest, so if that is running I would seek to join it, but I'd have to persuade members of the Parliamentary Labour Party to do the same."

Any challenger wanting to trigger a leadership contest must be an MP and have the backing of 81 Labour MPs.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, Justice Secretary and Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy said a leadership contest had not been triggered but "the prime minister has been absolutely crystal clear that if there is a contest he will be in it".

He added that Sir Keir had his "full support" as well as "a mandate from the British people less than two years ago".

Another senior minister, Attorney General Richard Hermer, told the BBC's Political Thinking the prime minister had "consistently been underestimated and had "always proven his critics wrong".

Streeting has confirmed he would enter any potential contest and has encouraged people to back Burnham in Makerfield as he wants a "proper contest with the best candidates on the field".

Kenyon criticised Burnham's record as mayor, saying while Manchester "thrives we're struggling to survive in Wigan" before adding: "We've been left behind."

He said there was a need to "get normal people in politics, people who care about the place, people who live in the place and people who want to stay here and not use it as a stepping stone for other things".

Conservative candidate Michael Winstanley questioned why Burnham was seeking a return to Parliament after previously pledging to serve his current term as mayor, adding he was "disgusted" and "sad that we're having this by-election foisted upon us".

He added: "We will get rid of Keir Starmer whichever politician is elected in this by-election and if you vote for me, it'll speed it up straightaway."

Burnham replied by saying "you cannot control events in politics" as he highlighted Labour's losses to Reform in recent council elections in the area.

Green Party candidate Sarah Wakefield said there was a need for "serious conversations about who is contributing for a better future for our children, to solve the climate crisis, to get our high streets going, to make sure that we have the money back in towns and villages".

Liberal Democrat candidate Jake Austin said the by-election was an "election for a potential future prime minister via the backdoor and that's not the right way to be doing politics".

Elsewhere in the debate, Kenyon said he "won't accept" being labelled sexist after he was asked about his previous online comments – including about women and abortion.

Kenyon said he was "brought up by women", had "nothing but respect for women", adding: "I've made mistakes, I've said things years ago that I wouldn't say now."

The candidates were also asked about the murder of 18-year-old Henry Nowak.

Bodycam footage showed police putting the Southampton University student in handcuffs as he lay dying, after his killer Vickrum Digwa falsely claimed he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Digwa, 23, was given a life sentence for murder with a minimum of 21 years in prison.

He had been carrying a knife in a sheath, as well as a second, larger dagger linked to his tradition as a member of the Nihang order of Sikhs.

Asked if he would support a ban on people carrying knives for religious reasons, Burnham said he thought it needed "to be looked at although it needs a very careful debate".

Violent protests in Southampton on Tuesday night came after the bodycam footage was released.

Kenyon said "violence is never the answer" and also argued the case showed there was a "two-tier policing system".

burnham_bounce_polling_analysis:
Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive

The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election.

Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down.

But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence.

The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented.

All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 â which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II â failed to give her party a boost.

It is not unusual for a new prime minister to enjoy a poll bounce

We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term â even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office.

Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election.

That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election â and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling.

But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process.

But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls.

The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens â much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters â the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving.

When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%.

Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street.

Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring.

Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform.

To do this â and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening.

John Curtice is a professor of politics at Strathclyde University and senior fellow at the National Centre for Social Research and The UK in a Changing Europe
